APL1関連
The ecological features of the Izu Islands and conserving the island ecosystem together with the island people
伊豆諸島の生態的特徴と島民とともに進める保全
Takashi Kamijo
The Izu Islands are a group of volcanic islands located south of Japan's main island, Honshu. The islands stretch from north to south, and the northernmost island, Oshima, is about 25 km from the mainland, but it has never been connected to the mainland and is an oceanic island. The ecological features of the Izu Islands include: (1) forming complex vegetation landscapes due to volcanic activity, strong winds and cloud cover over the peaks, (2) being oceanic islands with many endemic species as well as several species that are partially found on the nearby mainland, (3) having many species presumed to originate from nearby Honshu, while some come from remote regions like the Ryukyus, (4) the absence of medium to large mammals and snakes, creating disharmony of the island ecosystems which varies between islands, and (5) these features make them suitable for comparative studies between the mainland and islands, and among the islands. These comparative studies in the Izu Islands have been conducted on species like the Varied Tit, Okada's skink, and bellflower, contributing academically to ecology. However, invasive species like cats, weasels and muntjacs are undermining the scientific value. In particular, regarding the weasels on Miyakejima, monitoring surveys conducted by researchers have clearly and quantitatively demonstrated the direct impact they have had on birds and Okada's skinks. This lecture will outline the scientific significance of the Izu Islands and the issues surrounding nature conservation there. It will also introduce ongoing conservation initiatives, focusing not only on efforts by government bodies—such as national and local municipalities—and public institutions like the Izu Oshima Geopark, but also on the activities of NGOs specific to each island. Furthermore, the lecture will discuss the importance of sharing successful conservation models—such as dolphin conservation and ecotourism on Mikurajima—across the islands, as well as common challenges, including the shortage of personnel to lead nature conservation efforts. Finally, the discussion will address the sustainable conservation of nature in the Izu Islands.
（要旨集 p.4）

APL2関連
Predator-driven adaptive evolution in the Izu Island skink
捕食者組成が駆動するオカダトカゲの適応進化
島嶼での捕食者による形質の平行進化
Takeo Kuriyama
Island species often exhibit distinctive morphology, life history, and population density compared with their mainland relatives, making islands valuable natural laboratories for studying evolutionary and ecological processes such as predator-prey interactions. Lizards in particular have been extensively studied in this context, revealing broad patterns such as species–area relationships, density compensation following the loss of predators or competitors, and a suite of correlated trait shifts known as the island syndrome. Here I present a case study on the Izu Island skink, Plestiodon latiscutatus, a small terrestrial lizard endemic to the Izu Islands and the adjacent Izu Peninsula, Japan. The Izu Islands are oceanic islands formed by volcanic activity on the Philippine Sea Plate and have never been connected to the mainland. Although P. latiscutatus occurs throughout the archipelago, the composition of its predators, the Japanese weasel Mustela itatsi, the Japanese four-lined snake Elaphe quadrivirgata, and birds, varies markedly among islands, offering a replicated natural experiment for examining how predation shapes multiple traits in parallel. On islands where weasels, snakes, and birds co-occur, such as Izu Oshima, lizards mature early, reproduce annually, and produce many small eggs, whereas on islands where only birds are present, such as Miyakejima and Aogashima, lizards mature late, reproduce biennially, and produce fewer, larger eggs. Islands where snakes and birds are the main predators show intermediate life-history traits. These patterns are consistent with the general prediction that reduced predation intensifies intraspecific competition and favors greater investment per offspring, whereas stronger predation maintains lower population density. Predator composition also shapes juvenile coloration. Populations preyed upon mainly by weasels retain conspicuous body stripes and a vivid blue tail extending to its base. Where snakes are the dominant predator, the tail gradually shifts from brown or green to blue toward the tip, while in bird-only populations the stripes largely disappear and only the tail tip remains blue. This autotomizable blue tail functions to deflect predator attacks, and its coloration has evolved to match the visual sensitivity of the locally dominant predator, underlain by distinct pigment cell organization among populations. Together, these findings demonstrate that a single ecological factor, predator assemblage, can drive parallel adaptive divergence across life history, behavior, and coloration within a single species. Future work will test whether such predator-driven adaptive divergence is a general phenomenon across other Japanese island systems, underscoring the Izu Islands as a powerful model for studying predator-prey coevolution in island lizards.
（要旨集 p.5）

AO2A-01賞候補
Ocean-current-mediated propagule dispersal simulations and genetic analyses reveal contrasting population formation processes in three coastal plant species along the Pacific coast of eastern Japan
海流分散が沿岸植物の遺伝構造に与える影響
Kanako Akimoto*1, Keisuke Tanaka2, Tetsuo I. Kohyama3, Kei Matsubayashi4, Shingo Akita5, Takaya Iwasaki1
Coastal sandy beaches are harsh environments characterized by nutrient-poor sandy soils, high temperatures, and salt exposure, and they support specialized coastal plants with diverse stress-tolerant traits. However, coastal habitats have rapidly declined due to development and erosion, leading to fragmentation and isolation of many coastal plant populations. Because the fruits or seeds of many coastal plants can float in seawater, ocean currents may maintain genetic connectivity among fragmented populations. Nevertheless, how ocean-current-mediated dispersal contributes to spatial genetic structure remains insufficiently understood. We investigated three coastal plant species distributed along the Japanese archipelago: Calystegia soldanella and Lathyrus japonicus, whose propagules can float in seawater for more than 60 days, and Ischaemum anthephoroides, whose floating ability is limited to about 5 days. Focusing on the Pacific coast of eastern Japan, where the Kuroshio and Oyashio currents interact with a complex coastline, we integrated SSR-seq-based population genetic analyses, ocean-current-mediated propagule dispersal simulations, and ecological niche modeling for the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) to evaluate the effects of present-day seascape connectivity and historical range shifts on genetic structure. Private allele richness declined northward in C. soldanella and I. anthephoroides, whereas no clear geographic trend was observed in L. japonicus. C. soldanella and I. anthephoroides showed genetic differentiation between northern and southern regions around the Boso Peninsula. However, their population structures differed: C. soldanella exhibited extensive admixture among populations, whereas I. anthephoroides was subdivided into finer regional groups. In contrast, L. japonicus showed population-specific and geographically discontinuous genetic clusters. Dispersal simulations suggested a potential break in ocean-mediated connectivity around the Boso Peninsula. Simulations assuming a 60-day floating duration produced broad connectivity networks along southern and northern coastal sections, separated around the Boso Peninsula, whereas simulations assuming a 5-day floating duration showed further fragmentation in northern regions. These patterns were consistent with the genetic structure of C. soldanella and I. anthephoroides, but not with that of L. japonicus. Ecological niche modeling suggested that suitable habitats of C. soldanella and I. anthephoroides during the LGM were restricted mainly to southern Kanto, implying postglacial northward expansion, whereas L. japonicus retained broad suitable habitats from Kanto to Tohoku. These results indicate that genetic structure and diversity in coastal plants along eastern Japan reflect the combined effects of historical range shifts and present-day ocean-current-mediated dispersal.
（要旨集 p.123）
BO2B-01賞候補
How many samples do we need for GWAS? A population simulation approach
GWASに必要なサンプル数をシミュレーションで検討
Diego Salazar*1
Understanding the genetic basis of phenotypes is a central goal of evolutionary biology. However, this remains challenging because many traits are likely polygenic and consist of many genes of small phenotypic effects, and it is often difficult to disentangle environmental and genetic influences. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) are a widely used approach in both human genetics and evolutionary biology research to map genotypes and phenotypes. Nevertheless, determining an appropriate sample size remains a central challenge, as researchers must balance sequencing costs with the need for sufficient sampling power to accurately identify the genetic basis of traits. The goal of this thesis is to understand how the genetic architecture of a trait and the population’s evolutionary history influence the number of samples required to detect causal genetic variants. Using simulations of GWAS under a single-population scenario, we show that statistical power depends on the genetic architecture of the trait (number and distribution of causal loci). Under the two-population scenario, we find that population structure can substantially increase false positives on chromosomes without causal SNPs. Finally, we provide a list of recommended sample sizes for each scenario.
（要旨集 p.140）
DO2D-01賞候補
Seed dispersal in the Anthropocene: climbing mountains and crossing cities
テネリフェ島の種子散布網と気候変動影響
Sara Beatriz Mendes*1, Manuel Nogales2, Pablo Vargas3, Jens Olesen4, Patrícia Marrero2, Ruben Heleno5
Global change stressors, such as climate change and rapid urban expansion, are affecting the composition of wild communities and creating novel ecosystems. Animal seed dispersers might be essential to help plants tracking suitable climates to higher elevations, particularly in such a fragmented and urbanised world. Yet the role of seed dispersers in helping plants track climate change remained poorly understood, due to a lack of comprehensive datasets spanning entire environmental gradients. Thus, over one year, we compiled seed dispersal networks along the entire altitudinal gradient of Tenerife island (0-3718 m asl) to explore whether animal seed dispersers could help plants colonise uphill habitats, as well as across the surrounding urban matrix to assess the impact of urbanisation on seed dispersal. Along the mountain, seed dispersers offered viable routes for plants to colonise upper vegetation belts. Eleven plant species were actively dispersed to higher elevations beyond their current distribution range, at vertical distances largely surpassing those required to escape climate change; however, over half of the plants arriving at higher elevations were exotic. Across the city, urbanisation simplified the seed dispersal networks, with exotic plants dominating them (accounting for 61% of interactions vs 15% in the forest). Here too, some dispersers maintained the functional connectivity between urban areas and natural forests, potentially facilitating the spread of exotic species from cities - where they are more common - into the surrounding forests, owing to their generalist and flexible diets. Together, our results highlight that functionally diverse disperser communities are crucial for helping plants escape climate change on mountains and for sustaining connectivity across cities - but exotic plants might particularly benefit from animal seed dispersers’ lift. Finally, our findings underscore the importance of promoting native plants as ornamentals, particularly on oceanic islands, and of sustainable urban planning to preserve ecosystem resilience and persistence.
（要旨集 p.153）
EO2E-01賞候補
Islands within islands: cliff environments and new tools to understand their endemic flora
島の崖生態系と固有植物相の新調査手法
Ben Nyberg*1, Scott Heintzman1
Cliff ecosystems on islands can function as “islands within islands,” forming discrete, vertically structured habitats that promote isolation and high levels of endemism. Despite their importance for island biodiversity, these systems remain among the least systematically surveyed terrestrial habitats due to extreme topography and limited accessibility, resulting in major gaps in baseline data on species composition, distribution, and ecological interactions. Cliffs are recognized as refugia that buffer microclimatic conditions and reduce impacts from introduced ungulates such as goats, thereby safeguarding relict and endemic taxa; however, they are increasingly threatened by invasive plant species, recreational climbing, and climate change. Recent technological advances have substantially improved our ability to access, document, and conserve cliff-associated biota, enabling the discovery of previously undescribed species and generating new insights into the ecology and evolution of these highly specialized “micro-island” systems.
（要旨集 p.168）

AO2A-02必聴賞候補
Complex spatiotemporal history of Cryptops centipedes inhabiting East Asian islands
東アジア島嶼のオオムカデ属の複雑な分布形成史
東アジア島嶼の節足動物系統地理で直接関連
Taro Jonishi*1, Takafumi Nakano1
Cryptops Leach, 1814 is a genus of generally small, blind centipedes that mostly inhabit epigean habitats. With more than 150 species described worldwide, Cryptops is one of the most widespread and speciose genera within the class Chilopoda. Although previous studies have indicated a complex evolutionary history, the biogeography of Cryptops species largely remains unclear owing to the lack of molecular data from some regions such as the easternmost part of Asia. In this study, we addressed phylogeography of Cryptops species from East Asian islands, mainly the Japanese Archipelago and the Ryukyu Islands. Molecular phylogenetic and dating analyses showed that the East Asian species are non-monophyletic, originating from at least three independent lineages. Among them, C. striatus Takakuwa, 1936 is found only in eastern Honshu in Japan, and is closely related to European and North American Cryptops species. The time-calibrated phylogenetic tree indicates that C. striatus represents a relic lineage, which was once more widely distributed across the Holarctic. Another East Asian species, C. japonicus Takakuwa, 1934, widely occurs on the Japanese Archipelago and Taiwan. Molecular analyses revealed deep genetic divergence within this species, suggesting that the intraspecific diversity of C. japonicus has been harbored since the formation of the Japanese Archipelago in the Miocene. By contrast, C. navis Chamberlin 1930, distributed across the Ryukyu Islands and Taiwan, showed almost no genetic differentiation, despite its wide geographic range. The result indicates rampant gene flow among populations of C. navis, possibly mediated by overseas dispersal. The observed differences in the genetic structures among species presumably reflect different dispersal abilities and colonization histories to the East Asian islands. Our results suggest that the species richness of Cryptops on East Asian islands is the outcome of both ancient continental relicts and recent radiations, demonstrating that the current diversity and distribution of Cryptops have been shaped by complex spatial and temporal processes.
（要旨集 p.125）

BO2B-02関連賞候補
Effects of Reference Genome Divergence on Genomic Inference in Pachycephala in the Malay Archipelago
参照ゲノムの分岐度がPachycephala属ゲノム推定に与える影響
マレー諸島の鳥類ゲノム手法、分類群・地域とも非対応
Mona Huguenin*1, José Cerca1, 2, Knud Jønsson1, 3, Martin Irestedt1
The reference genome is the backbone of many evolutionary analyses, but its choice can strongly influence genomic inference through reference bias. Reference bias arises because reads more similar to the reference are more likely to map successfully than reads carrying alternative alleles. Although several studies have quantified reference bias, its magnitude and direction vary across datasets. Here, we investigate how reference genome divergence influences population genomic inference in the bird genus Pachycephala in the Malay Archipelago, a rapidly diversifying clade representing one of the most widespread and complex avian radiations in the Indo-Pacific. Using a whole-genome resequencing dataset, we aligned reads to multiple reference genomes, including Pachycephala references and increasingly divergent outgroup genomes. For each reference, we generated independent variant call sets and inferred phylogenetic relationships, alongside population genomic statistics (e.g., FST, DXY, π, Ne) and reticulation metrics used to detect hybridization and introgression. By repeating these analyses across reference genomes of increasing divergence, we assess how reference bias influences phylogenetic inference, population genomic statistics, and the detection of reticulation, highlighting the importance of careful reference selection in genomic analyses.
（要旨集 p.141）
DO2D-02賞候補
An ecological model to investigate the impacts of urbanization and alien species introduction on plant–frugivore dynamics: a case study from Tenerife
都市化と外来種が植物被食散布に与える影響モデル
Andrea Coppola*1, Lorenzo Mari1, Renato Casagrandi1
Seed dispersal is crucial for biodiversity maintenance, and the mutualistic interactions between plants and frugivores within a community are intertwined in complex networks. However, these communities can be affected by a wide range of anthropogenic impacts, from alien species introductions to habitat loss, and oceanic islands are particularly exposed to these impacts, as evidenced by the high extinction rates observed in island species worldwide. We propose an ecological, process-based mathematical model describing the dynamics of frugivores and plants, properly mediated by reward resources. Our model explicitly accounts for main interactions of both facilitative and competitive nature that occur both within and between the two guilds, allowing us to investigate the ecological mechanisms that link interaction network architecture and community temporal dynamics. We apply our model to a publicly available dataset, describing plant-frugivore networks sampled in the Island of Tenerife, relative to both urban matrix and patches of natural forest, including both native and introduced species. Adopting a mechanistic approach, we first explore how urbanization-driven changes in the interaction network can alter the persistence of both animal and plant species in the community. Secondly, we leverage the model to investigate the impact of introduced species on the native community, and their potential of spread from urban to natural areas. Finally, we explore the links between species’ traits, their position in the network and their ecological performance. Our model provides a quantitative framework to evaluate how anthropogenic disturbances propagate throughout the interaction network, causing cascading effects at community level, therefore representing a tool to investigate the impact of global change drivers in island environments.
（要旨集 p.154）
EO2E-02関連賞候補
“Islands” within an island: An Endangered insectivorous oceanic island bat sustains strongly distinct cavernicolous invertebrate communities
モーリシャスの洞窟コウモリと洞窟性無脊椎動物群集の関係
島の洞窟性無脊椎動物群集、節足動物含むが分類学ではない
Yogishah Bunsy*1, Christian E. Vincenot2, F. B. V. Florens1
Globally, cave ecosystems are often underrepresented in conservation management strategies, despite frequently holding unique biota. As key providers of allochthonous nutrient, cave-roosting bats are important in sustaining cave food webs though guano deposits. However, bat populations are declining worldwide, thereby threatening their associated cavernicolous biodiversity. Oceanic island caves, in particular, face elevated risks due to their additional isolation which may be expected to add vulnerability of their associated biodiversity to extinction. Understanding the influence of cave-roosting bat on eventual cave-dependent biodiversity, especially where a single cave-roosting bat species exists, matters for predicting possible cascading effects of loss or gain of cave-roosting bat colonies. We compared macro-invertebrate diversity and environmental conditions (light intensity, temperature, and relative humidity) between lava tube caves with and without the endemic insectivorous bat, Mormopterus acetabulosus (Molossidae) across Mauritius, sampling from cave entrance to deep sections and across guano piles. Four caves with permanent bat colonies and four unoccupied caves were surveyed. Macro-invertebrates were collected using pitfall traps, and direct collection, and identified to the lowest taxonomic level possible. Species richness, community composition, and beta diversity were compared between bat-occupied and unoccupied caves. Macro-invertebrate richness, abundance, and diversity increased significantly with bat colony size. The three metrics dropped further from guano piles, while light intensity had a positive effect. Community composition differed significantly between bat-occupied caves and unoccupied caves. The observed drop in macro-invertebrate diversity with increasing distance from guano piles reflects nutrient limitation and spatial heterogeneity. The near absence of invertebrates in unoccupied caves highlights bottom-up control, whereby resource availability dictates community composition and trophic interactions. Our results highlight M. acetabulosus as plausible ecosystem engineers that provides guano “islands” whose size and numbers may regulate cave invertebrate diversity, reflecting island biogeography theory. Our study shows the need to prioritise conservation actions in bat-occupied caves, especially where large or multiple guano piles are currently present. This is particularly important given that caves in Mauritius currently receive little consideration in conservation management strategies. Consequently, legal protection of bat-occupied caves, together with restrictions on access to bat colonies and guano deposits, should be considered. Incorporating these measures into conservation policies could help prevent biodiversity declines and serve as a model for other islands experiencing increasing urbanisation and high human population densities similar to those of Mauritius.
（要旨集 p.169）

AO2A-03おすすめ賞候補
Evolutionary history and speciation of the Kurixalus eiffingeri species group (Amphibia: Rhacophoridae) across Taiwan and the Ryukyu Archipelago
台湾・琉球のカエル種群の分岐年代と種分化史
台湾・琉球の分岐年代推定で手法・地史が参考になる
Ryo Kamimura*1, Shu-Ping Wu2, Yi-Huey Chen3, Chi-Shiun Wu3, Natsuhiko Yoshikawa4, Masafumi Matsui5, Atsushi Tominaga1
Understanding how geological history and climatic fluctuations influence species diversification in island fauna is a central question in evolutionary biology. In this study, we investigated the evolutionary history and population structure of Kurixalus eiffingeri species group distributed across Taiwan and the Yaeyama Islands of the Ryukyu Archipelago using mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequences and genome-wide single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) data. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that K. berylliniris diverged earlier within this group, whereas K. wangi is the sister species of K. eiffingeri. Divergence time estimates suggest the colonization of Taiwan by K. eiffingeri species group occurred during the Late Miocene–Early Pliocene transition (ca. 6.7–4.8 Ma). Following the colonization, diversification within Taiwan was likely promoted by the uplift of the Central Mountain Range. SNP analyses of K. berylliniris identified two distinct genetic clusters. Limited gene flow from K. wangi into the southern K. berylliniris cluster was also observed. Within K. eiffingeri, four major lineages associated with Ishigaki Island, Iriomote Island, central Taiwan, and northern Taiwan were consistently identified using both mtDNA and SNP analyses. The Ishigaki and Iriomote lineages formed a Ryukyu clade that was sister to the northern Taiwan lineage, whereas the central Taiwan lineage diverged earlier within this species. Divergence time estimates suggest that the northern Taiwan lineage subsequently dispersed to the Yaeyama Islands via the land bridges. In the Ryukyu clade, despite repeated land connections between the Ishigaki and Iriomote Islands during the Pleistocene glacial cycles, no evidence of gene flow was detected between these populations, suggesting their long-term isolation. In contrast, the absence of genetic substructures within each island indicates that dispersal remained possible within continuous forest habitats, whereas unsuitable environments on exposed land bridges may have restricted inter-island dispersal between the islands. Our results suggest that the K. eiffingeri species group diversified within Taiwan and that the substantial genetic differentiation observed in both K. eiffingeri and K. berylliniris indicates the presence of hidden diversity within this group. Therefore, the geological history and past climatic fluctuations of Taiwan and the Ryukyu Archipelago likely played crucial roles in shaping the genetic structure and diversification processes of this species.
（要旨集 p.126）

BO2B-03おすすめ賞候補
Understanding the impact of bottlenecks on time-calibrated trees using simulated data
島嶼定着ボトルネックが分岐年代推定に与える影響をシミュレーションで検証
分岐年代推定への創始者効果の影響は琉球研究に応用可能
Florian R. Schmidt*1, Alexander Mackintosh1, José Cerca1
Estimating time divergence has classically been performed by constructing coalescent-based phylogenies, especially when fossil records are not accessible. Using neutral models for time-calibrated trees assumes that there has not been a major demographic change in a clade. However, population bottlenecks caused by, for instance, founder effects resulting from island colonization can have major consequences on the genetic diversity and therefore the accuracy of time estimates. An overestimation of island colonization events likely results in an erroneous inference of biogeographic scenarios. We simulated demographic models to highlight the effect of the founder event of island dispersal with and without selection aiming to compare a classic island colonization event to a neutral scenario. To provide an alternative to classical estimation tools we present an ancestral recombination graph (ARG)-based a methodology to estimate divergence time. By estimating deep branch lengths from the simulated models we quantified the effect of how much bottleneck-events confound time-estimated phylogenies. Our results indicate how much phylogenetic software, based on classic neutral coalescent models, underestimate the founder effect.
（要旨集 p.142）
DO2D-03賞候補
Wetlands acting as islands in dispersal networks
湿地を島とみなした種子散布ネットワーク研究
Dániel Popovics*1,4, Nándor Szabó1, Pál Tóth1,2, Gábor Simay1,2, Balázs Koleszár1, Ákos Őrsi1, Lili Sztrehárszki1, Míra Júlia Radnai1, Ádám Lovas-Kiss1,3
Endozoochorus dispersal plays a crucial role in the persistence and metacommunity dynamics of wetlands, as waterbirds can transport the diaspores within their digestive system and subsequently defecate them tens or hundreds of kilometers away from their source location (long-distance dispersal), while the diaspores remain viable after gut passage. This mechanism enables gene flow between otherwise disconnected habitats and increases the probability of successful colonization of newly available sites. In this sense, wetlands can be conceptualized as habitat islands embedded within a terrestrial matrix, since hydrologically they are largely isolated from each other, direct migration of many aquatic species is limited, and the spatial extent of suitable habitat is also limited. Accordingly, the dynamics of local extinctions and colonization events often follow patterns analogous to those described by island biogeography and metapopulation frameworks, where connectivity and patch size jointly determine persistence. In this study, we investigated ecological network structures between three wetland habitats by focusing on interactions between waterbirds and the organisms dispersed by them. Data collection was based on field sampling, during which fecal matter of waterbird species occurring at each habitat was collected and analyzed to identify dispersed species. Based on the resulting interaction data, bipartite networks were constructed and analyzed using network analysis approaches to investigate network structure, species centrality, species contribution to nestedness, and the degree of connectivity among habitats. Our results demonstrated that certain waterbird (dabbling ducks: e.g. mallard) species act as a key species in maintaining ecological connectivity among habitats, as they participate in the dispersal of numerous organisms. The network structure indicated that the wetlands do not function as isolated units but rather as an interconnected system with waterbirds serving as important ecological corridors. Our study contributes to a better understanding of ecological relationships among wetlands and highlights the role of mobile species in maintaining ecological networks and conserving biodiversity.
（要旨集 p.155）
EO2E-03賞候補
Functional composition changes across a tropical island urbanization gradient after 20 years
熱帯島嶼の都市化勾配に伴う鳥類機能的組成の変化
Miguel J. Costas*1, Edgar Vázquez Plass2, Joseph M. Wunderle3, Trevor Fristoe1
Urbanization dramatically alters habitats with complex effects on both native and non-native species. Through fundamentally restructuring landscapes and altering resource dynamics, urban expansion can lead to a loss of biodiversity and homogenization of wildlife. The impacts of urbanization may be further amplified in insular communities with depauperated fauna, high proportions of exotic species, and limited ability to disperse into undisturbed habitats. However, while responses are negative for many species, others benefit from these changes. Thus, a more mechanistic understanding of species responses to urbanization in island systems is of increasing conservation priority. Functional traits mediate species interactions with their environments, and may therefore provide insights into how they will fare in urban habitats. Here we explore how functional traits of birds change across an urbanization gradient (forest -> exurban -> suburban -> urban) that spans northeast Puerto Rico and has been resurveyed after 20 years. Specifically, we take focus on the altered availability and diversity of resources in urban environments by investigating morphological traits linked to diet and foraging – body size and bill morphology. By characterizing species within trait spaces across the gradient, we will test whether the diversity and composition of functional traits vary predictably through time and with the degree of urbanization. We expect most notable difference being between forest and urban habitats. Furthermore, because of habitat heterogeneity may facilitate the co-occurrence of urban generalist and forest specialists, we expect that suburban and exurban habitats will show higher functional diversity, whereas urban habitats will have lower functional diversity due to lower overall richness and higher dominance of generalist species, although presence of exotic species occupy functional space not seen in forest sites. Furthermore, we expect to be able to identify which trait combinations are unique to or excluded from urban sites, this information useful for guiding conservation efforts going forward.
（要旨集 p.170）

BO2B-04おすすめ賞候補
Ancestral recombination graphs in a non-model case: the Scalesia island radiation
祖先組換えグラフで非モデル島嶼放散種の定着史を高解像度推定
ARGによる島嶼定着史の高解像度推定は系統地理研究に有用
Criado-Ruiz David*1, Cerca José1
One of the biggest gaps in island biology is the accurate reconstruction of colonization histories in island taxa. The geological record rarely preserves the resolution needed to date these events precisely, and phylogenetic approaches, where insular taxa are compared to continental outgroups, provide only upper-bound estimates of colonization timing. Ancestral Recombination Graphs (ARGs) offer a powerful alternative: by reconstructing genome-wide genealogies and tracking how lineages coalesce through time, they provide effectively a time-calibrated genealogy at every position across the genome, enabling high-resolution inference of past population dynamics and divergence processes. Critically, island colonization leaves a distinctive coalescent signature: a sharp bottleneck followed by population expansion, that is recoverable from ARG-based analyses, allowing colonization history to be inferred with unprecedented precision. To exploit this, we developed a pipeline integrating variant filtering, haplotype phasing, and ARG inference and dating using the tskit toolkit. We first validated our approach through simulations spanning a range of demographic scenarios, including models with and without population bottlenecks and varying rates of post-bottleneck recovery. We then applied the pipeline to the Galápagos-endemic genus Scalesia (Heliantheae, Asteraceae) as an empirical case study, reconstructing its demographic history and colonization dynamics. Our results reveal the challenges of distinguishing between demographic models in island radiations, where genomic signals are often subtle and overlapping, while also providing new insights into the drivers of diversification in the Galápagos flora.

Continuous and asymmetric connectivity induced by Quaternary sea-level fluctuations as a driver of ecological speciation in oceanic islands
更新世海水準変動が引き起こす非対称な島間連結性と生態的種分化

Marius Albino*1, Robin Aguilée1
Throughout the Quaternary (2.6 Ma), repeated glacial-interglacial cycles drove major climatic changes that resulted in significant sea-level fluctuations. In oceanic islands, these variations profoundly altered inter-island distances, occasionally reducing them to zero, which directly impacted species migration. As glacial periods last significantly longer than interglacials, sea levels declined gradually over tens of millennia as ice sheets expanded, but rose abruptly during deglaciation, leading to continuous and temporally asymmetrical variations of migration between neighbour islands populations. Previous empirical research hypothesised that this specific temporal pattern, by modifying the time available for genetic divergence to accumulate, may strongly shape diversification processes in oceanic archipelagos. Theoretical studies have shown that repeated, discrete shifts between phases of geographical isolation and connection can act as a “species pump”, facilitating speciation. During isolation, populations ecologically diverge, while each secondary contact reinforces prezygotic reproductive isolation because of unfit hybrids. However, these models usually assume temporally symmetrical changes in migration rate and/or instantaneous transitions between high and low migration rate. As a result, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we investigate if continuous and temporally asymmetrical fluctuations in connectivity between two populations favor speciation in a species pump scenario. We developed an individual-based model of a sexually reproducing population split across two patches, where migration fluctuates continuously and can be temporally asymmetric. We also examine empirically inspired scenarios by deriving migration variation from Quaternary sea-level changes to assess their impact on speciation. The two patches have different environments, allowing for ecological divergence. Individuals are characterized by an evolving mating trait allowing for assortative mating based on ecological traits. We showed that Quaternary sea-level fluctuations can act as a powerful driver of diversification. More specifically, continuous and asymmetric connectivity fluctuations shape ecological speciation mainly through the duration of low-connectivity phases and the intensity of contact, with prolonged isolation enhancing ecological divergence and brief periods of moderate contact reinforcing reproductive isolation through moderate hybrid production. This combined effect maximizes speciation probability, particularly for less dispersive species that are most sensitive to these historical shifts in island connectivity. Our findings provide a unified microevolutionary framework that explains the diverse levels of diversification induced by sea-level fluctuations, thereby reconciling the "species pump" paradigm with the diversity-reducing "species vacuum" effect. We demonstrate that, despite complex landscape dynamics, speciation likelihood relies on only two fundamental drivers: the duration of recurrent isolations and the intensity of subsequent contact.

Exceptionally, however, two tree frog species (Dryophytes japonicus and D. leopardus) in the Japanese Archipelago occur widely not only on the four major islands (Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu; hereafter, "the mainland") but also on numerous surrounding small islands, representing rare examples of extensive insular isolation. The results revealed that island populations of both sexes were significantly larger than their mainland counterparts, demonstrating a clear pattern of insular gigantism that was more evident in females than in males. To elucidate the environmental factors driving this variation, we performed model selection using generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) for each sex, setting island SVL as the response variable against five geographic and environmental explanatory variables: habitable area, distance from the mainland, standard deviation of monthly NDVI (NDVIsd), annual mean temperature, and annual precipitation. In males, the top three models explained body size through isolation distance from the mainland (positive correlation) and habitable area (negative correlation). In females, the top three models included habitable area (negative) and NDVIsd (negative), with the top two models also including distance (positive). Notably, in both sexes, habitable area exhibited the strongest effect among these variables, indicating its substantial contribution to body size variation. In this presentation, we discuss these geographic factors and explore the hypothesis that desiccation stress in small-island environments may contribute to the observed gigantism.

We used the KM-GBF indicators categories (i.e., headline, binary, component, and complementary) to assess how well included indicators correspond to the target (i.e., alignment). The indicator that best aligns with a target was used to assess coverage (i.e., how well a set of indicators measures progress toward a target). Four targets had only poorly aligned indicators and thus poor coverage. We then used time series spanning from 1950 to the present to model current and future trends for each indicator, aggregated by target. Preliminary results indicate that 24 indicators (66.7%) appear to be on track to meet their respective targets. However, almost half of the targets have either poor coverage or no indicators at all (n = 11, 47.8%). Taiwan represents a case where a major pollinator shift promoted island colonization but not speciation, whereas Hainan represents a case where speciation was associated with localized pollinator specialization despite little change in pollinator fauna. David J. Pereira*1, Jon P. Sadler1, Joseph P. Wayman1,2, Thomas E. Martin3, Thomas J. Matthews1,2
Biodiversity has faced an ever-increasing crisis in the past 130,000 years, characterised by changes in climate and ecosystems around the globe. This has resulted from, or been exacerbated by, human-driven actions such as the introduction of non-native species to ecosystems, and the modification/destruction of habitats. These actions have, in turn, led to extinctions worldwide and across taxonomic groups. We now know that at least 610 bird species have gone extinct globally, and that 20% of the world’s mammals have been lost through extinctions. However, these extinctions are not mere numbers. They represent a greater loss since species are known to undertake ecological roles that help maintain ecosystem functioning. These roles include pollination and seed dispersal and are thus driven by their functional traits – morphological traits that allow the performance of ecological functions. Unsurprisingly, extinctions have led to the loss of functional traits, and in some cases, led to the complete cessation of ecological functions. On Réunion, the loss of seed dispersal traits following the extinction of the island’s large frugivores has hindered forest regeneration, whereas, in New Zealand, the extinctions of avian pollinators have hampered seed dispersal and pollination of a native shrub. These examples illustrate the functional gaps that may arise following extinctions; however, these gaps can be plugged if other extant species replace the lost functional traits. The deliberate introduction of taxon substitutes – extant species which share a taxonomic relationship with an extinct species they are intended to replace – has been proposed to restore missing ecosystem functions. This approach has been trialled on some islands with varying success. In some instances, the extant species did replace missing ecosystem functions, but in others it replaced some or none. These mixed results are not a surprise given the lack of evidence of taxonomic-ecological function links. However, studies have evidenced functional trait-ecological role links. We suggest incorporating functional traits within the selection process of taxon substitutes, to improve their appropriateness in replacing extinct species’ functional traits and thereby functions. However, there exists no conceptual framework for selecting extant substitutes that account for their functional traits. We address this gap by developing a quantitative trait-based framework using birds as models and illustrate theoretical examples of selecting candidate avian species to replace extinct birds. We provide a conceptual framework, allowing for a rapid, repeatable analysis-based selection of appropriate substitutes for extinct species, thus aiding rewilding efforts around the globe to restore degraded ecosystems.

島の系統地理学への応用だが分類群非対応
Vincent Wilkens*1, Anna Walentowitz1, Carl Beierkuhnlein1
Machine learning has become an important tool in ecological research, with applications ranging from predicting species distributions and classifying remote sensing data to automating IUCN Red List assessments and optimizing habitat connectivity for conservation. Until recently, most applications in ecology have used machine learning models as a data-driven “black box”, taking advantage of its superior predictive performance and effectiveness for learning non-linear relationships and interactions from large training datasets. However, such data-driven modeling is less suited to many island systems, where data are often sparse, limited, and unevenly sampled, and where mechanistic interpretability and transferability across islands and taxa in pursuit of a general theory are desired. A promising way forward is to integrate deep learning with ecological theory and process-based models. This includes approaches that embed process knowledge in neural network architectures or loss functions (i.e., knowledge-guided machine learning), use neural networks to replace or estimate uncertain processes, and use simulations to train neural networks to infer parameters given some empirical data. Such approaches are now gaining traction, but implementations remain scattered across numerous subfields such as forest ecology, phylogenetics, and quantitative paleoecology. Here, we introduce these emerging approaches in the context of island biogeography to stimulate both awareness and further implementation. We highlight two approaches with widespread applicability: (1) hybrid predictive models, which integrate process understanding to improve deep learning models and (2) simulation-based inference, which uses neural networks trained on simulated data to enable likelihood-free inference for complex process-based models. Furthermore, we demonstrate the usefulness of these methods with examples, such as in species distribution modeling of endemic island trees, which are particularly vulnerable to climatic changes and require robust forecasts to inform conservation strategies. In this case, the integration of a process-based model of plant growth in a multi-species deep learning model can improve the transferability of predictions as well as enable few-shot predictions for poorly-observed species.

Islands are natural laboratories for understanding how isolation, environmental conditions, and human influence shape biodiversity and ecosystem structure. While island ecology has traditionally focused on plants and animals, belowground biodiversity remains comparatively unexplored. Root-associated fungi are key components of terrestrial ecosystems, influencing plant performance, nutrient cycling, and species coexistence. Here, we examine root-associated fungal communities and plant–fungal interaction networks across 12 small islands from six archipelagos spanning a broad climatic gradient, from the High Arctic (Svalbard), through temperate (Balearic and Canary Islands) and tropical archipelagos (Galápagos and Seychelles), to the subantarctic region of Tierra del Fuego. These islands span a gradient of human influence, from protected islands with limited human impact to inhabited islands experiencing higher anthropogenic pressure. Together, they encompass a broad range of ages, origins, environmental conditions, and levels of human influence, offering a unique opportunity to investigate plant–fungal communities and interaction networks. We analysed 250 root samples representing 202 plant species using ITS1 metabarcoding, identifying 15,086 fungal ASVs. Plant–fungal interaction networks were constructed separately for three major root-associated fungal guilds: mycorrhizal, saprotrophic, and pathogenic fungi. Across islands, saprotrophic and pathogenic fungi dominated fungal communities and accounted for most plant–fungal interactions. Across archipelagos, fungal richness and diversity were higher on human-influenced islands than on protected islands with limited human impact. Fungal communities exhibited strong biogeographic structuring, with limited taxonomic overlap among archipelagos. Svalbard communities were particularly distinct from all other archipelagos, being strongly dominated by mycorrhizal fungi (48% of fungal reads compared with 5% elsewhere). The Galápagos Islands showed comparatively low within-archipelago overlap, indicating high local turnover. Remarkably, only a single ASV, Acremonium acutatum, a widespread saprotrophic fungus, was detected across all six archipelagos, and its prevalence on human-influenced islands suggests a potential role of anthropogenic activities in facilitating fungal dispersal across oceanic barriers. Plant–fungal interaction networks also varied among islands. Human-influenced islands supported higher fungal richness but less structured networks, exhibiting lower nestedness and specialization (H2’) than protected islands, suggesting that anthropogenic disturbance may promote fungal diversity while simplifying plant–fungal interaction networks. Together, these findings highlight the potential roles of biogeographic history and human influence in shaping belowground biodiversity across islands and reveal substantial variation in fungal communities and plant–fungal interaction networks along a global island gradient.

EO2E-08賞候補
Informing conservation through multi-scale knowledge integration: defining the ecological niche of the critically endangered tara iti (Sternula nereis davisae), in Aotearoa New Zealand
NZの絶滅危惧海鳥タラ・イティの生態的ニッチ統合解析
Nicole Whitelock*1, George Perry1, Ilse Corkery2, Jamie Stavert2, Dianne Brunton1
Globally, seabird populations are in decline, with island-associated species among the most threatened. Aotearoa-New Zealand, considered the “seabird capital” of the world and home to the most diverse seabird community on the planet, exemplifies this crisis, with approximately 90% of seabird species classified as at risk or endangered. Many of these at-risk and endangered populations have undergone severe range contractions due to the anthropogenic pressures of invasive mammalian predators, habitat degradation and the compounding effects of climate change. This reduction challenges conservation practitioners and decision-makers because the habitats where species persist today are unlikely to represent the full breadth of their ecological niche. As a result, conservation decisions are often based on an incomplete understanding of species’habitat preferences. This issue is particularly important for seabird management on island ecosystems, where conservation strategies may need to adapt to the compounding pressures of future climate change. A common approach for ecological niche investigations is species distribution modelling (SDM), often using a multi-scalar approach to include climate and habitat variables. However, while these quantitative modelling tools continue to advance, when used in isolation they can overlook important qualitative knowledge held by people. Expert knowledge, when gathered through transparent and structured elicitation methods, has become an increasingly valuable component of conservation decision-making My research uses Aotearoa-New Zealand’s rarest endemic breeding bird tara iti / New Zealand fairy tern (Sternula nereis davisae) as a case study to explore how combining traditional quantitative data sources with expert knowledge, across temporal and spatial scales can provide a more comprehensive approach to exploring a populations ecological niche. I investigate the ecological niche of the current tara iti population and compare it with historic populations to assess the extent to which the ecological niche of tara iti may have become constrained following population decline. My methodology integrates broad-scale climatic, and fine-scale habitat SDMs with expert elicitation using an iterative questionnaire process to capture micro-scale habitat preferences and important behavioural considerations. The result is a practical, multi-scale framework that integrates complementary knowledge systems to provide a more comprehensive ecological niche assessment. This approach can support management decisions at existing sites while also informing how management may prepare for future environmental change as well as translocation and site expansion initiatives.

Kanon Mizukoshi*1, Kazuto Kawakami2, Hideaki Mori3, Takashi Kamijo4
Seabirds are known as ecosystem engineers on islands, and alter terrestrial ecosystems by guano deposition, seed dispersal, and trampling or burrow digging. Discussing the ability of seabirds as ecosystem engineers, their coloniality is particularly noteworthy. As seabirds form large-scale breeding colonies ranging from hundreds to hundreds of thousands of individuals, a massive number of nests are created within these colonies, and remain in the environment for some time after the chicks have fledged. While such burrows and ground nests left behind in the colonies are considered to have a significant impact on terrestrial ecosystems, there are very few research examples that discuss the ecosystem functions of seabird nests. Burrowing seabirds in particular, they are often noted as soil disruptors, which hinder plant establishment and growth. However, there are very few research cases that address the question of how the burrows that remain even after birds have left the colony affect island ecosystems. In this study, we compared the arthropod fauna inside and outside the burrows of Procellariidae (Ardenna pacifica and Bulweria bulwerii ) nesting on two uninhabited islands; Minamijima and Nishijima Island, belonging to the Ogasawara Islands, to clarify the relationships between burrows and arthropods. Arthropods representing 8 orders were collected from the burrows of Procellariidae, predominantly decomposers such as Lepidoptera (larvae), Blattodea, Isopoda, and Diptera. From the surface nests of boobies, 2 orders were collected: Isopoda and Coleoptera. From the litter collected outside the nests, 10 orders collected, including Geophilomorpha, Isopoda, Orthoptera, Hemiptera, and Araneae. Among these, Tineidae, clothes moths, were found exclusively in the burrows. From the shearwaters’ burrows, Tineidae occurred at high densities, averaging approximately 43 individuals per burrow on Minamijima Island and approximately 18 individuals per burrow on Nishijima Island. For the larvae of Tineidae, which are keratin-eaters with low mobility, the interior of a burrow is considered an excellent habitat that provides not only a supply of food, but also more stable temperature and humidity than the ground surface. In this presentation, we will discuss the possibility that burrows serve as habitats for specific arthropods, contributing to increased biodiversity in islands’ terrestrial ecosystems.

Jan Bernhard Kalusche*1,2,3,4,5, Ana María Bastidas-Urrutia1,3, Patrick Weigelt7,8, Jörg Albrecht2, Alke Voskamp2,4, Maíra Cardoso2, Holger Kreft7, Ulrich Brose4, 11, Katrin Böhning-Gaese2,5,9, Luís Valente12,13, Gregor Scheiffarth6, Lucie Kuczynski14,15, Christian Hof1, 3, Susanne A. Fritz2, 4,10,11
Island assemblages are shaped by biogeographical filters that determine which lineages arrive, become established, diversify and persist. Classical island biogeography has emphasised dispersal limitation, island area, environmental conditions and diversification through in-situ speciation as key processes structuring island biodiversity. In the Anthropocene, however, these filters are increasingly modified by human activities. It remains unclear whether anthropogenic pressures now influence extant island assemblages to the same extent as classical dispersal and environmental filters, and how they alter the functional and evolutionary dimensions of biodiversity. Here, extant island birds are used as a model system to examine how changing filter regimes reshape functional and phylogenetic diversity within an expanded island filter framework. Functional and phylogenetic diversity were quantified for extant terrestrial bird assemblages on 2,719 islands worldwide using morphological traits, avian phylogenies and richness-corrected null models. These metrics capture complementary dimensions of assemblage structure: functional diversity reflects the distribution of ecological roles in trait space, whereas phylogenetic diversity reflects evolutionary history and lineage composition. Multivariate Bayesian models were used to compare classical filters, such as island isolation, island area and productivity, with anthropogenic filters, such as human population density, land-use change, human appropriation of productivity and introduced predators. Functional and phylogenetic diversity were positively correlated globally, but responded differently to individual filters. Functional diversity declined with increasing isolation, whereas phylogenetic diversity increased with island area. This indicates that dispersal and environmental filters affect ecological and evolutionary diversity in distinct ways. Anthropogenic filters, particularly introduced predators and human-driven land-use change, matched or exceeded the influence of classical filters and were consistently associated with functional and phylogenetic clustering. These patterns suggest that human pressures are not merely external disturbances that occur after assembly; rather, they have become pervasive filters reshaping the structure of extant island bird assemblages. This interpretation also connects broader patterns of archipelago endemism and long-term monitoring: in-situ speciation can generate local niche differentiation within constrained trait space, while temporal community change can increase taxonomic diversity but reduce functional diversity. Together, these findings support an expanded island filter framework for the Anthropocene, in which anthropogenic pressures modify processes of assembly, diversification and persistence, thereby shifting extant island biodiversity towards functional and phylogenetic homogenisation.

Here, we investigated genome-wide genetic structure and spatial genetic differentiation across Japanese inland, coastal, and island populations using SNP data generated by multiplexed ISSR genotyping by sequencing (MIG-seq). However, some remote island populations, particularly Hachijōjima and Aogashima, showed localized genetic structure. Island biogeography and population genetic theory predict that insular populations face elevated extinction risk owing to reduced gene flow, stronger genetic drift, and greater vulnerability to environmental disturbance. The Russet Sparrow (Passer cinnamomeus) is a widespread passerine across East Asia and is not globally threatened. However, on the island of Taiwan, this bird is classified as nationally endangered, indicating differential extinction risks across its range. Moreover, citizen science records indicate a distribution gap within Taiwan that separates the northern (TWN) and southern (TWS) populations. It remains unclear how historical environmental change has shaped the current vulnerability of these Taiwan populations, or whether this vulnerability will be exacerbated by future climate change. Long-term demographic analysis revealed population size fluctuations in both the Taiwan and mainland populations broadly consistent with the last glacial cycle, and ENM identified a similar pattern in the dynamics of suitable habitat. Consistent with the expected consequences of long-term isolation, we detected clear genetic divergence between mainland and Taiwan populations. Compared with the mainland populations, Taiwan populations exhibited smaller effective population sizes (Ne), lower levels of genetic heterozygosity and higher levels of inbreeding. Within the island, cryptic genetic structure was detected between TWN and TWS, corresponding to the north–south geographic separation documented in citizen-science records. Demographic analysis focused on recent timescales revealed a gradual and continuous population decline in both TWN and TWS over the past 300 years, reducing the current Ne to merely 260 and 370, respectively—a decline likely attributable to woodland loss driven by recent human exploitation. Under predicted future climate scenarios, both TWN and TSW increased vulnerability from 2041–2060 to 2061–2080, and then stayed at similar vulnerable levels throughout 2081–2100. This study demonstrates that even a continentally widespread species may contain highly vulnerable island populations as a consequence of long-term isolation, local population fragmentation, elevated inbreeding, environmental disruption and future climatic risk.

AO2A-10賞候補

Islands provide excellent systems to investigate how ecological and evolutionary filters reshape functional trait diversity. However, many studies still rely on trait means rather than full trait distributions, potentially overlooking important aspects of functional variation. Using functional distribution-based approaches, we first investigated changes in seed-size distributions across islands in the New Zealand region, testing how geographic isolation, climate, and dispersal mode influence the structure of seed-size assemblages. We found that dispersal syndromes respond differently and non-linearly to insularity: abiotic dispersers tended toward smaller seeds on highly isolated islands, whereas biotically dispersed floras were associated with warmer islands supporting richer and functionally broader bird assemblages. Building on this distributional perspective, we then developed a broader geometric framework to study how insularity reorganizes multivariate morphospace in bird assemblages across the New Zealand region. Species were projected into a common multivariate space describing major ecological and morphological axes using principal component analysis. Rather than analysing traits independently, each island assemblage was treated as a multivariate geometric object characterized by its centroid position, covariance structure, anisotropy, and occupied morphospace volume. This allowed mainland-to-insular transformations to be decomposed into multiple components, including directional shifts in morphospace, contraction or expansion of variance, and restructuring of trait covariation. Preliminary results suggest that islands differ not only in the magnitude of their divergence from mainland assemblages, but also in the direction and internal organization of that divergence, potentially indicating multiple insular trajectories rather than a single generalized island syndrome. Together, these studies illustrate how distribution- and geometry-based approaches can provide a richer understanding of insular assembly processes and evolutionary change than analyses based solely on species means.

Oceanic islands have long served as natural laboratories for understanding evolution owing to their exceptional endemism, ecological heterogeneity, and rapid species diversification through adaptive radiation. Despite this evolutionary importance, genomic studies of oceanic island plants remain scarce, limiting our understanding of the genomic changes underlying island syndrome, ecological specialization, and rapid phenotypic diversification. Among island floras, Macaronesian Echium (Boraginaceae) is one of the most valuable models for island plant evolutionary genomics, comprising diverse island-endemic lineages that vary strikingly in growth form, habitat, and ecology. The assembled genomes ranged from ca. 302 to 456 Mb with high completeness (>95% complete BUSCOs) in all species. Comparative analyses revealed that genome size variation was associated with repeat accumulation, especially LTRs and DNA transposons, whereas the number of predicted genes remained nearly constant as genome size increased. Molecular dating further suggested that Macaronesian Echium species have rapidly diversified across islands and ecological zones within 3.5 Mya. In addition, gene family evolution and enrichment analyses implicated functions related to lignin metabolism, cell wall biogenesis, meristem growth, vascular development, organ morphogenesis, and stress responses, supporting their roles in woodiness evolution and adaptation to novel island environments. Synteny analyses also suggested notable genomic rearrangement and duplication across the lineage. Together, these results provide one of the pioneering comparative genomic foundations for understanding adaptive radiation in oceanic island plants. The genomic basis and evolutionary insights provided in this study will pave the way for future evolutionary genomic studies of genotype-phenotype associations, adaptative radiation, and convergent evolution across diverse island-endemic lineages.

Small and isolated populations on islands often experience reduced genetic diversity and increased vulnerability to pathogen introduction due to long-term demographic constraints and limited gene flow. Understanding how host traits and social structure shape parasite transmission in such systems is essential for predicting disease risks in endangered insular wildlife. However, in wild populations it is rarely feasible to obtain long-term, individual-based background information (for example, kinship, health history, or demographic records) that would allow detailed evaluation of host factors underlying infection heterogeneity. Here, we take advantage of a unique rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta) population maintained in an outdoor, soil-floored enclosure with no immigration for nearly three decades (1993–2021). This closed population exhibits several characteristics typical of small insular systems, including restricted genetic diversity, stable matrilineal social organization, and long-term demographic stability. Importantly, comprehensive individual background information has been accumulated through continuous management, enabling detailed analysis of host-level determinants of parasite infection. Such kin-structured social clustering likely plays a key role in shaping transmission dynamics in small, closed primate populations. Our results demonstrate that, under certain conditions, managed captive populations can function as effective “island model systems” for studying host–parasite interactions. Insights gained from such systems can be directly relevant to understanding parasite dynamics and pathogen invasion risks in small, isolated wildlife populations on real islands. Protected areas are central instruments for conserving island biodiversity, but their effectiveness depends on how well they encompass the distributions of threatened species. To this end, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) defines protected areas in six categories based on how strictly they are managed. These categories range from I, the most strictly protected, set aside mainly for scientific research or wilderness protection, to VI, the least restrictive, permitting sustainable use of natural resources. In the Azores, protected areas span multiple levels, including Natural Reserves and Protected Areas, but their designation has often reflected a combination of ecological, geographical and socio-political constraints. This study aims to assess the extent to which the actual distribution of endemic vascular plants, bryophytes and arthropods in the Azores are covered by these protected areas. Preliminary results reveal marked taxonomic differences in protected-area coverage. Endemic vascular plant occurrences are mainly concentrated in categories IV and V, whereas categories I and III contain comparatively less occurrences. Many species show strong peaks of occurrence in category V (often exceeding 30–50% of their occurrence), while others are almost entirely restricted to that category (~100% of occurrences in V). For bryophytes, species occurrence is strongly concentrated in category I, often representing the dominant share (frequently above 50% and sometimes 100% occurrence), followed by meaningful contributions from categories IV and V. For arthropods, the distribution is markedly towards category I, which frequently holds the largest share of species occurrence, often exceeding 50% and in many cases reaching near or complete dominance (~100%). Areas with categories III and VI though, consistently hold very small proportion of arthropods occurrence. These preliminary patterns suggest that the Azorean protected-area network represents endemic taxa unevenly across management categories. Compared to vascular plants, bryophytes and arthropods species seems to exhibit a much stronger dependence on highly protected areas. Protection levels only partially capture the known occurrences of vascular plants, while showing a stronger association with the distributions of bryophytes and arthropods. Moreover, the limited representation of species in categories III and VI indicates that these areas may play a comparatively minor role in biodiversity conservation, raising questions about whether current protected area design adequately captures the spatial needs of more vulnerable and habitat-restricted groups. Future analyses should also consider protected-area extent, sampling effort and habitat availability to distinguish true biological patterns from artefacts of area size or survey intensity.

While some taxa exhibit distribution patterns consistent with this model, others occur on both islands and the mainland, and several lineages have diversified into multiple endemic taxa. In addition, hybridization with mainland relatives has been suggested in some groups. These observations raise the possibility that repeated dispersal, secondary colonization of the mainland, and hybridization have all contributed to diversification within this floristic element. Genome-wide SNP data are being used to characterize genetic structure, genomic differentiation, and potential signatures of admixture among island and mainland lineages. By comparing multiple independently diversified lineages, we aim to identify common and contrasting patterns of genomic divergence among Fossa Magna element plants and provide a foundation for future studies of their diversification and speciation processes.

Adaptive radiation is one of the principal mechanisms proposed to explain the origin of biodiversity, yet most evidence for this process derives from animal systems, whereas plant radiations remain comparatively understudied. Oceanic islands provide exceptional natural laboratories for investigating diversification because of their isolation, environmental heterogeneity, and dynamic geological histories. In this presentation, we use endemic lineages of the family Asteraceae in the Canary Islands and Madeira as a model system to explore when, how, and why adaptive radiation occurs in plants. The contribution is framed within the DecodADAPT project, which compares adaptive and non-adaptive radiations through integrative phylogenomic, ecological, morphological, and experimental approaches. In particular, we contrast the spectacular adaptive radiations of Sonchus and Argyranthemum with the more limited diversification patterns observed in Reichardia and Gonospermum, in the particular island setting of the Canary Islands. These paired systems provide an opportunity to investigate why some lineages rapidly diversify into multiple ecological and morphological forms, whereas others fail to radiate despite similar ecological opportunities. To address these questions, we carry out Hyb-Seq, sequencing hundreds of nuclear and plastid loci, to perform comparative phylogenomics. We combine these genomic analyses with ecological niche and functional diversity analyses. By comparing adaptive and non-adaptive evolutionary trajectories across Canarian Asteraceae, this work aims to provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying speciation and radiation in plants and highlights the value of oceanic island floras as powerful systems for understanding the origins of biodiversity.

In sympatric regions in central Japan, H. axyridis is a generalist predator feeding on various aphid species, whereas H. yedoensis is a specialist predator restricted to elusive aphids on pine trees. In contrast, in the Ryukyu Islands, where H. axyridis is absent, H. yedoensis utilizes a wide range of habitats, providing an ideal system to test for character displacement. Contrary to expectations, none of these traits showed significant divergence between sympatric and allopatric populations of H. yedoensis, indicating that the observed pattern does not clearly match predictions of character displacement. [Background and Objectives] Acorns, the fruits of oaks belonging to the genus Quercus, are characterized by high concentrations of tannins, which serve as anti-herbivory defense compounds and may have deleterious effects on consumers when ingested in substantial quantities. The large Japanese wood mouse, Apodemus speciosus, a principal consumer of acorns, possesses a tannin detoxification mechanism (i.e., tannin tolerance) that is mediated by acclimatization involving tannin-binding salivary proteins and tannase-producing bacteria. The development of such tannin tolerance is hypothesized to have facilitated the efficient utilization of acorns by this species. However, it is currently unclear whether populations of A. speciosus that lack access to acorns also display high levels of tannin tolerance. Investigating this question is essential for comprehending the selective pressures that have driven the evolution of tannin tolerance. Consequently, we conducted a comparative analysis of tannin tolerance between populations of A. speciosus from regions where acorns are naturally present and regions where they are absent. [Materials and Methods] Pregnant female A. speciosus were captured from both mainland Japan (Iwate Prefecture), where acorns are naturally distributed, and Miyake Island in the Izu Islands, where acorns are absent. Both the parental generation and their offspring, reared under controlled laboratory conditions, were utilized for the experiments (parental generation: mainland, n = 11; Miyake Island, n = 12; offspring generation: n = 12 for each population). Following a two-week acclimation period, the mice were fed exclusively on acorns of Quercus crispula for five days. Survival rates, changes in body mass, food intake, and digestibility— all indicators of tannin tolerance—were measured and compared between the populations. [Results and Discussion] In both the parental and offspring generations, mice from Miyake Island exhibited significantly greater body mass loss following acorn consumption compared to those from the mainland. Conversely, no significant differences were observed between generations. Although not statistically significant, food intake and digestive efficiency also tended to be lower in the Miyake Island population. Additionally, the activities of tannin-binding salivary proteins and tannase-producing bacteria were found to be lower in the Miyake Island mice. Positive correlations were identified between mothers and offspring in terms of body mass loss and digestive efficiency. These findings suggest that tannin tolerance may demonstrate local adaptation in response to the availability of tannin-rich resources, indicating that acorn availability could serve as a important selective pressure influencing the evolution of tannin tolerance.

Oceanic islands represent a paradox in evolutionary biology. Colonization is typically associated with strong founder effects that reduce genetic diversity, yet oceanic archipelagos have generated some of the most remarkable radiations known. One mechanism that may help overcome the limitations imposed by founder events is hybridization, which can rapidly increase standing genetic variation and provide the raw material for diversification. This process may be particularly important in volcanic archipelagos, where the emergence of new islands creates opportunities for previously isolated lineages to come into secondary contact and exchange genetic material. Phylogenetic analyses based on eight nuclear loci identified the central islands as the center of diversification and the source of subsequent colonization events across the archipelago. Microsatellite analyses further revealed that genetic diversity does not follow the pattern expected under a simple founder-effect model, in which diversity progressively declines along the colonization pathway. Instead, populations on younger islands, despite being more recently established, harbour higher levels of genetic diversity than those on older islands. This pattern is consistent with the hypothesis that newly emerged islands facilitate the admixture of divergent lineages, generating genetically diverse populations that subsequently become structured through the speciation process. More recently, large-scale genotyping of dozens of nuclear and chloroplast loci suggested that these patterns extend beyond neutral genetic variation. In fact, RAD-sequencing analyses revealed signatures of introgression associated with ecological traits, suggesting a potential adaptive role for gene flow. These findings are currently being further evaluated using whole-genome sequencing data. Importantly, all marker systems and analytical approaches consistently support extensive admixture among species within the genus. Whereas species provided with calcarean shells (such as molluscs) or bones (such as vertebrates) usually leave traceable fossils behind, other taxa, such as arthropods, bryophytes, fungi, lichens or vascular plants, leave them only exceptionally. Thus, whereas the first group, depending on the taphonomic conditions of the deposition site, can be traced in deep time, the single evidence of the loss of the taxa belonging to the second group is their disappearance from the species lists after having been catalogued in the taxonomic period, i.e. when the firsts list of species were produced for islands’ floras and faunas, what in Macaronesia happened at the transition of the 18th and 19th centuries. However, as the human colonization of Macaronesia preceded clearly this time threshold, with the Canaries being colonized by the Imazighen at the start of the CE, and the other archipelagos by the Portuguese in the XV century, the pristine nature of these archipelagos has been subject for 1500 years in the Canarian case, or for several centuries in the case of Azores, Madeira and Cabo Verde, to the impact of human activities and of the species by them introduced. It is very reasonable to consider that a flora that evolved in the absence of large herbivores was heavily impacted by the arrival of goats, sheep or pigs, and later by cows, rabbits or rodents, among others, not to mention human activities such as burning, gathering, logging or terracing.
