An overview of the diversity of triplefin fishes (Teleostei: Tripterygiidae) in Japanese waters
日本産イソギンポ科ミナミハタンポの多様性概観
Yuna Dewa*1, Hiroyuki Motomura2
Triplefins (Blenniiformes: Tripterygiidae) are small, bottom-dwelling fishes characterized by three separate dorsal fins, ctenoid scales on the lateral surface of the body, and continuous or discontinuous lateral lines. The family currently includes 29 genera and at least 170 species. Triplefins are distributed worldwide from temperate to tropical waters, primarily inhabiting intertidal rock pools and subtidal rocky or coral reefs. The authors have been working on the taxonomy and biogeography of Japanese species of the family Tripterygiidae since 2021. As a result, 36 species belonging to six genera of the family (Ceratobregma: 1 species; Enneapterygius: 22; Helcogramma: 9; Norfolkia: 2; Springerichthys: 1; Ucla: 1) have been recorded from Japanese waters. Several species among them show restricted distributions in the northwestern Pacific: Enneapterygius etheostoma (Jordan and Snyder, 1902) (Japan, Korea and Taiwan); E. leucopunctatus Shen, 1994 and Springerichthys bapturus (Jordan and Snyder, 1902) (Japan and Taiwan); E. miyakensis Fricke, 1987, E. senoui Motomura, Harazaki and Hardy, 2005, Helcogramma flammata Dewa, Muto and Motomura, 2025, and H. nesion Williams and Howe, 2003 (endemic to Japan). Most Japanese tripterygiid species are mainly distributed in island areas. The highest species diversity occurs in the Ryukyu Islands, where 32 species have been recorded, representing 89% of the Japanese tripterygiid fauna. Recent taxonomic studies by the authors have described two new species, E. olivaceus and E. sericus, from the Ryukyu Islands. In addition, at least three undescribed species belonging to the E. tutuilae species group have been recognized. One new species, H. flammata, has also recently been discovered from the Pacific coast of mainland Japan and the Izu and Ogasawara islands. Similarly, E. miyakensis, E. senoui, and H. nesion show a distributional pattern restricted to the Pacific coast of mainland Japan and the Izu Islands, which is probably influenced by the Kuroshio Current. Furthermore, re-examination of specimens previously identified as H. hudsoni (Jordan and Seale, 1906) from Japanese waters revealed that the previous Japanese records of the species were based on misidentifications of H. nesion, H. inclinata (Fowler, 1946), and H. ishigakiensis (Aoyagi, 1954). Consequently, the distribution of H. hudsoni is now known to be restricted to the South Pacific Ocean. This presentation provides an overview of the ichthyofauna of Japanese triplefins and notable species.

How a plant reaches an island system, and what happens when it gets there – the evolution and biogeography of genus Wikstroemia
アジア太平洋域におけるコショウノキ属の進化と生物地理
Ruben Cousins-Westerberg*1, Matthew L. Knope2, Clifford W. Morden2, Niklas Wahlberg1, Colin Olito1
We leverage whole-genome sequencing of 200 herbarium sheets to reconstruct a genus level phylogeny of the Wikstroemia (Thymelaeaceae), a culturally and medicinally significant clade of flowering plants found throughout East, South, and Southeast Asia, as well as on most major Pacific islands. Using this phylogeny and the herbarium records (representing 50 species, 60 islands, and 250 years of botany) as a backbone, we discuss the biogeographic history of the genus: its origin in a common ancestor on the mainland and subsequent dispersal across Asia and the Pacific region. We then zoom in on the Hawaiian archipelago – one of the most isolated island groups in the world and the most notable instance of rapid species radiation in the Wikstroemia genus. Combining the results of phylogenetic and biogeographical analyses with knowledge gained from greenhouse observations and two seasons of fieldwork, we detail the nature and context of the Hawaiian radiation. Discussing aspects of ecology, conservation, and speciation, we put a special emphasis on the evolution of novel sexual systems and on the multiple transitions to dioecy that have occurred in the genus since it reached Hawaiʻi.

Anthropogenic disturbance reshapes pollination networks in the Seychelles: insights from invasive rodents
セーシェルで撹乱と外来齧歯類が送粉網に与える影響を調査
Laura Gómez-Devia*1, Alba Costa1, Christopher Kaiser-Bunbury2, Anna Traveset1
Anthropogenic pressures threaten ecosystem integrity and functioning worldwide, particularly on oceanic islands, where isolated and species-poor biotas are especially vulnerable to biodiversity loss and the disruption of ecological interactions. Plant–pollinator interactions constitute a key ecosystem function that underpins the reproduction of most flowering plants and contributes to the maintenance of terrestrial biodiversity. Understanding how anthropogenic disturbance shapes pollination networks is therefore essential for island conservation. Here, we investigated the effects of anthropogenic pressure on plant– pollinator interactions across nine islands of the Seychelles archipelago spanning contrasting disturbance levels, and whether invasive rodents may also affect these interactions through plant consumption. Anthropogenic disturbance was quantified through an index integrating six components: (1) management intensity, (2) fraction of introduced vertebrates and (3) introduced plants, (4) infrastructure cover, (5) number of permanent inhabitants, and (6) number of fluctuating tourists. Plant–pollinator interaction networks were constructed for each island using focal field observations, and network structure was analysed using quantitative metrics. In addition, we specifically assessed the potential effects of invasive rodents –black rats and mice–, widely regarded among the most damaging invasive vertebrates globally. On invaded islands, rodent faeces were collected and analysed using DNA metabarcoding to characterise dietary composition and evaluate overlap with species involved in pollination networks. Preliminary results indicate that increasing anthropogenic pressure is associated with greater network-level generalisation, suggesting a reduction in specialised interactions and increasing functional homogenization on more disturbed islands. Molecular analyses further revealed that rats and mice diets included approximately 30% and 35%, respectively, of the plant species recorded in the pollination network. Among the plants detected in rats diets, 66% were native, including one endemic species, whereas in the case of mice, all were native. Our study provides new insight into how plant–pollinator interactions on tropical oceanic islands are shaped by anthropogenic pressures and impacted by invasive vertebrates. These findings highlight the vulnerability of island pollination systems to disturbance and underscore the importance of conservation strategies aimed at maintaining resilient and functionally diverse ecological networks.

Charcoal Records of Fire and Environmental Change on Réunion Island: Natural and Anthropogenic Drivers
レユニオン島の火災と環境変化の炭化物記録を分析
Sandra Domingues Gomes*1, Laurent Bremond2, Gael Le Roux3, Fabien Arnaud4, Xiannong Song3, Dominique Strasberg1, Claudine Ah-Peng1
Réunion Island, with a relatively recent history of human settlement, provides a unique natural laboratory for investigating interactions among climate, volcanism, vegetation, fire, and human activities in the Indian Ocean. Yet, the role of fire in shaping the island's ecosystems remains poorly understood owing to the scarcity of palaeoecological studies. Here, we present one of the first late-Holocene reconstructions of fire activity from Réunion Island based on a sedimentary record from Puy de l'Étang (580 m), a wet meadow embedded within the humid montane rainforest. Macroscopic charcoal and pollen were analysed from a 7-m sediment core spanning the late Holocene. High-resolution charcoal analyses provide annual- to decadal-scale reconstructions of local fire activity, while ongoing pollen analyses and additional radiocarbon dating will further refine vegetation–fire relationships and chronological control, particularly across the period of human settlement. The charcoal record indicates persistently low and stable fire activity throughout most of the late Holocene, consistent with a low-flammability humid rainforest ecosystem. Fire activity increased markedly from the seventeenth century onward, signaling a major shift in fire disturbance regimes. A cluster of fire events occurred between ca. 1657 and 1678 CE, followed by sustained elevated charcoal accumulation with peaks around 1760, 1880, and 1980 CE. Despite remaining chronological uncertainties, this pattern broadly resembles unpublished charcoal records from Étang de Saint-Paul, suggesting potentially coherent fire-regime changes across contrasting regions of the island. These increases are tentatively associated with land-use changes following European occupation, including forest clearance for coffee cultivation and the subsequent expansion of sugarcane agriculture. The relative influence of volcanism and climatic variability remain unresolved and requires further investigation. This study contributes to the development of long-term ecological baselines for Réunion Island and provides a framework for testing regional hypotheses on the interactions among fire, volcanism, climate, vegetation, and human activities. The integration of pollen data and comparisons with additional palaeoecological records, including records close to the active vulcano, will help clarify the drivers of ecosystem change across the island during the late Holocene.

Cryptic species previously identified as Pleurosicya mossambica (Teleostei: Gobiidae) associated with sessile organisms, and notes on their ecology
ハゼ属Pleurosicyaの隠蔽種と共生生態の記載

Masayuki C. Sato*1, Hiroyuki Motomura2
The family Gobiidae (Teleostei), comprising approximately 1,360 species, is the second-largest taxonomic group of fishes after Cyprinidae (ca. 1,740 species), with at least 423 species known from Japanese waters. The family includes the species which adapted to estuary and to deep-sea habitats exceeding 400 maters in depth, some of which live in association with sessile marine organisms. The coral-reef gobiid genus Pleurosicya Weber, 1913 is characterized by I, 7–9 second dorsal-fin rays; I, 7–9 anal-fin rays; all scales ctenoid; cup-shaped pelvic fin, fused medially with well-developed connecting membrane between innermost rays and thick frenum between spines; one posterior interorbital pore; edge of lower lip free at sides, fused at chin. The genus is currently known to comprise 17 valid species that live in association with hermatypic, and soft corals, sponges, algae and seagrass. In Japanese waters, 10 of these species have been reported. One of these, Pleurosicya mossambica Smith, 1959 (type locality: Mozambique) shares the diagnostic characters of the genus, but can be readily distinguished from all other congeners by having 17– 19 pectoral-fin rays, relatively shallow body depth, scaled nape, and distinct black blotch on the first dorsal fin. Pleurosicya mossambica is distributed throughout the Indo-Pacific, including the Red Sea, and inhabits on soft corals (e.g., Wrightella sp. and Sinularia sp.), hermatypic corals (e.g., Montipora sp., Millepora sp., Tubastraea sp., and Pachyseris sp.), algae (e.g., Halimeda sp.) and sponges. However, our re-examination of specimens identified as P. mossambica from the Izu to Yaeyama islands, Japan revealed that these specimens included two morphologically distinguishable species. Furthermore, each of these two species formed a separate clade based on the neighbor-joining phylogenetic tree using the 16S regions of the rRNA. Additionally, our examination of the type series of P. mossambica revealed that three specimens represent undescribed species, Pleurosicya sp. In Japanese waters, Pleurosicya sp. has been recorded only from the Ryukyu Islands, where it primarily inhabits on Halimeda sp. This presentation provides a key to these species and re-examines underwater photographs that were previously registered as P. mossambica. It also describes their ecological characteristics.

Sex Chromosome Identification in Hawaiian Wikstroemia: A Comparative Genomic Analysis

Lila Maladesky*1, Nikos Tsardakas Renhuldt1, Bengt Hansson1, Colin Olito1
Wikstroemia is a genus of flowering plants in the family Thymelaeaceae, with a wide distribution throughout Asia, Oceania, and the pacific islands. Most species in this group are hermaphroditic, with the notable exception of those species that have evolved in the Hawaiian Islands. There, nine out of twelve endemic species have physically separate sexes (dioecy). The Hawaiian Islands were most likely colonized by a hermaphroditic ancestor, from which dioecy may have evolved in different lineages independently. Previous greenhouse crossing studies of Hawaiian species have established that sex determination in the dioecious species is controlled genetically, and suggest XY systems in all cases. However, the identity of these sex chromosomes and the genes involved in sex determination are unknown. In this project, I investigate the genomic basis of sex determination in four species of Hawaiian Wikstroemia: W. sandwicensis and W. phillyreifolia from the Island of Hawai'i, W. ohauensis oahuensis from Oahu Island and W. oahuensis palustris from Kaua'i Island. For this study, we first generated high-quality reference genomes for one male and one female of each species using long-read whole-genome sequencing (PacBio HiFi) and HiC sequencing. A combination of methods using Illumina short-read sequence data for males and females were performed to identify the sex-linked region of the genome in each case. Bioinformatic methods used to identify heterozygous regions of the genome were male-female divergence estimates (Fst), reference-based SNP density and GWAS, alongside k-mer analysis to identify male-exclusive regions. In all cases, the sex-linked region found is small (between 1 and 2.5Mb) and associated with an inversion in the Y chromosome. The region is syntenic between three of the species studied (W. sandwicensis, W. phillyreifolia and W. ohauensis oahuensis). Meanwhile, the sex-linked region in W. oahuensis palustris is found in a different set of chromosomes, suggesting that separate sexes have evolved independently at least twice in the Hawaiian Islands. Overall, this study provides the first genomic analyses of the sex-linked region in these species and paves the way for a deeper understanding of sex determination in the genus and the transition from hermaphroditism to dioecy in the context of an island radiation.

Introduction of invasive species can cause strong imbalances in ecosystem functioning, especially in sensitive oceanic islands with high number of endemic species. The Ogasawara Islands of Japan is an oceanic archipelago of World Heritage status (~1,000km South of Tokyo), which in recent decades has faced increasing disturbance from invasive plant and animal species including the insectivore Green anole (Anolis carolinensis) and the European honey bee (Apis mellifera). These invasive species can have strong direct and indirect effects through predation and competition causing disturbances that travel across the trophic chain on the native island pollination system. In this study, we use structural equation models and ecological networks to identify the principal drivers that caused the acute pollinator decline and to explore its effects on the pollination system. Climate-Driven Demographic Shifts in Reproductive Strategies of an Island-Breeding Seagull
ENSOに伴う島営巣カモメの繁殖戦略と個体群動態
Gabriela De la Cruz-Pino*1, Enriqueta Velarde1, Exequiel Ezcurra2, Gabriela Athié1, Alejandro Granados-Barba1
The increasing frequency of ocean-atmosphere phenomena such as the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), and particularly the anomalous rise in Sea Surface Temperature (SST), is becoming more frequent and has more significant impacts on seabirds that rely on marine resources for reproduction and population maintenance. Among female Heermann’s Gulls nesting on Isla Rasa in the Gulf of California, two reproductive strategies have been identified in relation to anomalously warm SST years (SST anomaly > 1°C): bold and conservative. We generated three demographic matrices: all females in normal years (CN), conservative females in warm anomaly years (CA), and bold females in warm anomaly years (AA), to analyze, through iterative models, the population growth rate of each strategy under different scenarios of normal and warm year frequency. The highest population growth rate was recorded for CN (λ = 1.08), intermediate for AA (λ = 0.93), and lowest for CA (λ = 0.83). In the face of environmental anomalies, conservative females prioritize adult survival, while bold females prioritize reproduction at the cost of higher adult mortality. However, both strategies lead to population decline in warm years. The λ values across different recurrence intervals of warm SST anomaly years indicate that the population tends to decline as warm year frequency increases; bold females have lower λ values than conservative ones in most recurrence intervals, except when the warm period occurs annually, in which case bold females show higher λ. In both cases, population decline (λ < 1) occurs if a warm event happens every year. This study found that the presence of both strategies benefits the population, and if current anomalous conditions become the norm with annual recurrence, the population growth rate will be negative for both strategies, but less so for the bold strategy.

Neo-sex chromosome evolution is linked to island colonisation in the Japanese termite Glyptotermes nakajimai
日本のシロアリで性染色体進化と島嶼定着の関係を解析
日本南西諸島の島嶼進化・昆虫系統地理に関連
Maxim W.D. Adams*1, Simon Hellemans2, Kensei Kikuchi2, Aaron R. Jex3, Louise Baker3, Thomas Bourguignon2, Emily J. Remnant1, Kenji Matsuura4 and Nathan Lo1
Chromosomes are a fundamental unit of inheritance, yet their size, structure and number vary dramatically across the Tree of Life. While a “typical” karyotype comprises multiple autosomes and a single pair of sex chromosomes, numerous species have been discovered with multiple sex chromosomes (MSCs), which form non-recombinant, multivalent chains during meiosis. Little is known of the evolutionary processes that drive the emergence and fixation of MSCs within species. Here we test the hypothesis that MSCs preserve heterozygosity and slow genetic erosion in highly inbred populations. We assembled a high-quality reference genome and undertook species-wide genome re-sequencing for the termite Glyptotermes nakajimai. This naturally inbreeding species occurs across the islands of southern Japan and comprises multiple isolated populations with MSC chains of varying lengths (2n = 12–30). By characterising species-wide variation in inbreeding, genetic load, heterozygosity and chromosome structure, we demonstrate that the presence and length of MSCs is positively correlated with genetic diversity. Phylogenomic analyses reveal that MSC chains reflect the historical relationships between island populations, and progressively elongated in successively diverging populations. Likewise, historical demographic reconstructions suggest that the fusion of sex chromosomes may have been driven by historical population bottlenecks due to island colonisation and sea-level fluctuation. Together, these results offer the first empirical evidence that MSC formation preserves genetic diversity under strong inbreeding. They also demonstrate that sex-chromosome evolution can be strongly influenced by historical migration and habitat fragmentation, especially in archipelagic systems. This work offers novel insights into the drivers, processes and tempo of sex-chromosome evolution, as well as the genomic consequences of island colonisation.

Several mammal species on islands are classified as threatened by the IUCN, yet we lack information on which mammalian island faunas are of greatest conservation concern. Here, we identify the islands exhibiting the highest concentrations of mammal species and unique evolutionary history at risk of extinction. We compute threatened species diversity (TSD) and threatened phylogenetic diversity (TPD) for individual islands on a global scale. We aggregate and map biodiversity data on insular non-marine mammals for 327 islands worldwide, representing 1755 native species, including 653 single island endemics and 481 threatened species. TSD and TPD are strongly correlated at the single-island scale, with clear concentrations of threatened native and endemic insular mammalian diversity for both metrics in Madagascar and various islands in Southeast Asia. However, we find several spatial mismatches in TSD and TPD, with unexpected islands showing high TPD compared to their TSD (e.g., Formentera), and others showing the opposite pattern (e.g., Tasmania). Madagascar emerges as the island of highest conservation concern for mammals, ranking high across all metrics, even when taking its large area into consideration. DO3D-08賞候補
Modelling direct and indirect effects of invasive species on island pollination networks

Isaac Planas-Sitjà*1, Marta Quitián2, Adam L. Cronin3
Island ecosystems represent critical hotspots for biodiversity, yet they are disproportionately vulnerable to biological invasions. An important aspect underpinning ecosystem function and stability is the complex network of interactions between plants and pollinators. However, invasive species can restructure these pollination networks, with cascading consequences for native plant reproduction and ecosystem stability. Recent evidence suggests that when multiple co-invasive species co-occur, their interactive effects are often non-additive, amplifying disruption beyond the sum of individual impacts. This study addresses two central questions: (1) How do invasive species influence the pollination networks in island ecosystems? (2) What are the mechanisms underlying cascade effects across trophic levels? To answer these questions, we developed an evolutionary computational model that simulates seasonal changes in pollination networks. We initialised the model with empirical pollination networks from the Ogasawara Islands, which exhibit varying degrees of invasion by a generalist predator (the Anole lizard, Anolis carolinensis) and a floral competitor (the honeybee, Apis mellifera). We then simulated diverse scenarios, including different predation strategies and conditions with or without honeybees, to capture emergent properties of invasional meltdown. Our results demonstrate that biodiversity loss in the Ogasawara Islands is contingent upon the level of invasion, underscoring the urgent need for conservation management in semi-invaded islands. Furthermore, we elucidate the roles of pollinator diet (generalist versus specialist) and activity period (diurnal versus nocturnal) in shaping network resilience. We also explore the honeybee's role as a pivotal actor; previous studies suggest its impact depends on the presence of other invaders—either stabilising networks through functional redundancy or accelerating the competitive exclusion of native specialists. This study confirms that evolutionary network modelling is a valuable tool for predicting shifts in community composition and serves as a powerful instrument for conservation planning, enabling the identification of threatened pollinator and plant groups.

Preliminary observations conducted between September 2024 and August 2025 indicated that turtles entered the river primarily around high tide. Based on these results, visual and quadrat surveys were conducted from January to May 2026 during the two hours before and after high tide on spring, middle, and neap tides. Turtle occurrence and abundance were recorded during 261 30-min observation periods across 15 survey days, together with environmental variables including tide level, temperature, salinity, and human presence. Green sea turtles were recorded during 28 observation periods. Of nine identified individual turtles observed within the river, six (=67%) were recorded repeatedly, and the most frequently observed individual was detected on eight survey days. Some turtles also moved repeatedly between the river and ocean. Mean tide level during turtle occurrence was significantly higher than during non-occurrence periods (183.3 cm vs. 155.5 cm; GLM, p<0.001). Occurrence was significantly higher at night (15.6%) than during the daytime (6.0%; p = 0.002) and was more frequent when river water was cooler than adjacent seawater (p = 0.001). In contrast, human presence, tidal category (spring, middle, or neap tide), river salinity, and monthly algal cover were not significant predictors. Although grazing behavior was repeatedly observed within the river, turtle occurrence was not associated with algal cover. These results suggest that the river functions as a repeatedly-used habitat for green sea turtles and that river use is associated primarily with tide height and between sunset and sunrise. PA3-07必聴
Phylogeography and High Genetic Diversity of the Widely Distributed Springtail, Homidia munda (Hexapoda: Collembola), in the Japanese Islands
広域分布トビムシの日本列島における高い遺伝的多様性と系統地理
日本列島の土壌性昆虫トビムシの系統地理
kenji Ichimura*1, Gaku Ueki1, Koji Tojo1
Geological history and terrain strongly influence genetic diversity of organisms. The Japanese Islands are known to have experienced a complex formation history. Around 20–15 Ma, two different primary landmasses separated from the Eurasian Continent through plate tectonics then collided together in the current “Fossa magna” zone. This complex geological history of the Japanese Islands is due to their location at the intersection four different crustal plates. Therefore, the Japanese Islands are a particularly suitable model for studying how geological events affect genetic diversity. However, studies investigating the genetic divergence associated with the Japanese Islands formation are still scarce. Species having a wide distribution despite low dispersal ability that have survived for a long period are important characteristics to research the relationships between ancient geological events and genetic divergence. Therefore, we focused on springtail (Homidia munda) that is distributed widely in Japanese Islands. Springtails are wingless and vulnerable to drying. So, they have weak dispersal ability. In addition, fossil of the current species has been found between 55–33 Ma layers. Thus, springtails might have experienced a longer evolutionary history than other taxa. In this study, we conducted comprehensive sampling and genetic analyses. Based on mitochondrial DNA analysis (16S rRNA, 12S rRNA), Japanese Islands lineage and Korean Peninsula lineage, each formed monophyletic groups. and the divergence between the Japanese Islands lineage and the Korean Peninsula lineage is very deep. This pattern may be related to the “double-door” opening model of the Japanese Islands’ formation. Furthermore, the Japanese Islands lineage diverged into four geographically structured subclades. In the Chugoku Region located in the western part of the Japanese Islands, these subclades coexist suggesting secondary contact. To examine the possibility of hybridization, we analyzed nuclear DNA markers (28S rRNA, ITS2). Similarly, despite the existence of a coexistence spot, we could not detect any discordance within the mitochondrial DNA and nuclear DNA. This means reproductive isolation has already been established among the clades. This study provides insights into genetic divergence associated with ancient geological events being deeply involved in the mechanisms of biodiversity creation.
（要旨集 p.319）

Tatsuya Yamazaki*1, Gaku Ueki1, Koji Tojo1
Geological events related to tectonic activity, such as continental drift, volcanic activity, and land uplift and subsidence, can separate and reconnect biological populations. Sea-level changes caused by Quaternary glacial–interglacial cycles can also change connections among populations. These processes can promote genetic differentiation and genetic admixture. Biogeographic studies are useful for understanding how biodiversity was formed. The Japanese Islands have a complex and diverse geological history, geography, and topography, and are an ideal region for such studies. Organisms without flight ability are strongly affected by geographic barriers and are therefore more likely to show genetic differentiation. In this study, we conducted a biogeographic analysis based on the molecular phylogeny of Scolopocryptops rubiginosus, a centipede species distributed across the Japanese Islands, Taiwan, the Korean Peninsula, China, and Vietnam. We conducted molecular phylogenetic analyses using mitochondrial DNA (COI, 16S rRNA, and 12S rRNA) and nuclear DNA (28S rRNA and 18S rRNA) sequences. The results showed that samples from central Vietnam occupied the most basal position within the species. Lineages from northern Vietnam and western China diverged afterward. These findings suggest that this species originated on the Asian continent, especially in Southeast Asia. In contrast, samples from the Japanese Islands, Jeju Island, located south of the Korean Peninsula, and Taiwan formed the most derived clade. Ten clearly differentiated genetic lineages were detected within this clade. Each lineage showed a clear geographic pattern. Some straits were suggested to have acted as dispersal barriers between lineages. In addition, different lineages were found in the same areas. These results suggest that populations were repeatedly separated and reconnected even after the species expanded its distribution into the Japanese Islands. Although straits appear to have acted as dispersal barriers, the population on Hachijo Island, an oceanic island located south of mainland Japan, was monophyletic with populations from the Ryukyu Islands located in the southwestern region of Japan. This finding suggests that transoceanic dispersal may have occurred among some regions. Such dispersal may have been facilitated by drifting wood because decayed wood is the main habitat of this species. By focusing on the molecular phylogeny and biogeography of Scolopocryptops rubiginosus, this study showed that both geographic barriers and ocean current-mediated dispersal shaped the evolutionary history of this species. These findings provide new insights into dispersal processes and distribution patterns in soil-dwelling animals. They also contribute to a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying biodiversity formation in the Japanese Islands.

Sera Kobayashi*1, Gaku Ueki1, Koji Tojo1
The Japanese Islands are known to have undergone a complex geological history, which has greatly influenced the genetic diversity of its inhabiting organisms. To clarify the relationship between geological events and genetic divergence, it is important to focus on organisms that are widely distributed despite having low dispersal ability. Rock-crawlers (Insecta: Grylloblattodea) are cold-adapted, soil-dwelling insects with limited dispersal ability and therefore represent a suitable taxon for investigating the relationship between the geological history of the Japanese Island and biogeographic diversification. The results of the phylogenetic analyses revealed four major genetic lineages of rock-crawlers in the Japanese Islands. These lineages were distributed primarily in Hokkaido, Eastern Honshu, Western Honshu and Shikoku, and Kyushu together with the Tsushima Islands, respectively. Among them, the lineage distributed in Kyushu and the Tsushima Islands showed marked genetic divergence from the other three lineages. Furthermore, this lineage was revealed as the sister lineage to Grylloprimevala jilina, a species described from Jilin Province in Northeastern China in 2023. This result suggests that a historical biogeographic connection may have existed between Kyushu and Northeastern China. In addition, populations belonging to the clade primarily associated with Eastern Honshu were identified in the Chugoku region. This result indicates that the distribution of the major genetic lineages of Japanese rock-crawlers is more complex than previously recognized. In particular, the fact that the Eastern Japan lineage is also distributed within Western Japan suggests that the phylogenetic differentiation of leafhoppers cannot be explained solely by simple geographic isolation associated with the formation process of the Japanese Island. Rather, it is highly likely that multiple historical processes—such as past habitat range expansions, multiple dispersal events, or the long-term persistence of ancient lineages—have contributed to the formation of the current genetic diversity. These results suggest that the evolutionary history of Japanese rock-crawlers has been shaped by both geographic isolation associated with the formation of the Japanese Islands and repeated biogeographic connections with the Asian Continent. The ant genus Carebara Westwood, 1840 (Hymenoptera: Formicidae: Myrmicinae) is a species-rich group of predominantly hypogaeic ants, with more than 230 described species distributed mainly in tropical and subtropical regions. Due to their small body size and cryptic lifestyle, taxonomy of this genus is challenging, and taxonomic studies remain insufficient in Asia. Carebara yamatonis Terayama, 1996 is a hypogaeic ant widely distributed in East Asia, including Japan and China. In the original description, specimens from the Sakishima Islands in the southwestern Ryukyus were reported to exhibit morphological differences from the type series collected in mainland Japan. Despite this geographic variation, C. yamatonis has been treated as a single species, and no combined morphological or molecular analysis has been conducted to reassess this variation. The COI divergences were 9% between Groups I and II, and ca. 16% between Groups I and III. Morphological differentiation corresponded to the degree of genetic divergence: Group II differs from Group I only in cuticular sculpture, while Group III exhibits more pronounced differences including the dorsal outline of the propodeum in addition to sculptural differences. Ant colonies provide stable food resources and numerous niches for many organisms that exhibit diverse relationships with ants. However, the sophisticated social behaviors of ants make parasitism difficult for parasitoid wasps. Consequently, parasitoid wasps that parasitize ants are relatively few and show highly specialized morphological and behavioral adaptations. The subfamily Hybrizontinae is a small group of Ichneumonidae comprising four extant genera, Ghilaromma Tobias, Hybrizon Fallén, Neohybrizon Hisasue & Konishi, and Ogkosoma Haupt, with a total of 18 extant species distributed throughout the Holarctic region. All species of Hybrizontinae are parasitoids of ant larvae, and adults exhibit specialized host-searching behaviors around ant nests and trails. Members of the genus Ogkosoma are characterized by their conspicuously large body size and broad, flattened hind tibiae and hind basitarsi, features unique within the subfamily. Three species of the genus Ogkosoma are known from the Palaearctic region. In Japan, only O. cremieri (Romand, 1838) had previously been recorded. This species is also widely distributed in the Western Palaearctic region. However, considering its specialized life history associated with large colonies of Lasius ants, the validity of its wide geographical distribution remains unclear. Furthermore, field observations of Ogkosoma are extremely limited, possibly because of their low population density and autumnal occurrence. Therefore, the behavioral ecology of the genus remains poorly understood, despite the conspicuous hovering behavior of adults around host ant nests. Understanding these behaviors is important for revealing the adaptive significance of the highly specialized morphology observed in the genus. Females of O. cremieri are known to aggressively combat in midair while competing over hosts, although the detailed behavior has remained unclear because these interactions occur instantaneously. We therefore conducted detailed morphological observations of Ogkosoma and used a high-speed camera to investigate competitive interactions among females. Morphological analysis revealed differences in coloration and hind basitarsus structure between Japanese and European specimens identified as O. cremieri, suggesting they may represent separate species. We also newly found O. rufiventris Tobias, 1988, previously known only from Primorye, in Japan. These findings indicate the need for taxonomic revision of Ogkosoma in the Palaearctic region. Field observations conducted in Hokkaido in October revealed details of competitive interactions among O. cremieri around host ant nests. Females of O. cremieri were observed hovering at fixed positions above ant nests and ramming approaching conspecifics with the thorax. These interactions may represent territorial competition over oviposition sites rather than direct competition over hosts.

This approach is based on the strong preference of this species for liquid sugar resources; however, conventional liquid baits are often difficult to handle and apply. The hydrogel formulation overcomes these limitations by preventing absorption into the soil and reducing spillage, while improving ease of deployment. A key advantage of this bait was its simplicity: it could be produced inexpensively and in large quantities from readily obtainable materials, enabling widespread distribution and adoption by residents. The Ryukyu flying fox (Pteropus dasymallus) is distributed across a vast geographical area spanning 1,700 km from the islands of northern Philippines to Kuchinoerabu-jima Island, located south of Kyushu, encompassing the Ryukyu Archipelago. Based on geographical isolation and slight morphological differences, this species has conventionally been classified into five subspecies: P. d. dasymallus (Kuchinoerabu-jima Island and the Tokara Islands), P. d. inopinatus (the Okinawa Islands), P. d. daitoensis (the Daito Islands), P. d. yayeyamae (the Yaeyama and Miyako Islands), and P. d. formosus (Green Island and Gueishan Island in Taiwan). Since the center of distribution for Pteropus species is originally located in the tropics, the Ryukyu Archipelago, where P. dasymallus occurs, represents the northernmost limit of the distribution for this genus. Generally, for many organisms, peripheral regions offer less suitable habitats than central areas, and colonization attempts in such regions often fail even if individuals succeed in reaching new islands. However, bats possess exceptional flight and dispersal capabilities that allow them to cross oceans. This mobility enables them to temporarily leave an island to evade adverse events, such as food resource depletion, and subsequently re-migrate once food conditions improve. Particularly for solitary species like the Ryukyu flying fox, which do not utilize colonial roosts known as "camps" and furthermore rely on spatiotemporally fluctuating ("ephemeral") food resources such as fruits, a mainland-island metapopulation structure facilitates survival, thereby producing geographically complex distribution patterns. Our results were generally consistent with the conventional subspecific groupings; however, they also suggested that the formation of isolated populations has been driven in some areas either by the establishment of new sources through anthropogenic transport or by the emergence of distinct geographic fragmentation resulting from a decline in the species’ dispersal capability.

Reflecting this gradient, mixed conifer–broadleaf forests with distinct species compositions are established. A prominent feature of oceanic island floras is the disproportionately high frequency of dioecious species compared to mainland regions. While most of the approximately 140 Callicarpa species are hermaphroditic, the six species endemic to the Ogasawara islands are uniquely dioecious. However, the specific genetic architecture and the molecular mechanisms that triggered this reproductive-system shift remain unknown. The Y haplotype was approximately 200 kbp larger than the X haplotype, suggesting that this expansion resulted from multiple segmental duplications derived from distinct genomic regions. Comparative genomics revealed that this SDR and its flanking regions maintain high homology with the genomes of closely related hermaphroditic species. The two ecotypes also differ in seasonal development: plants of the forest ecotype first remain as compact vegetative rosettes before flowering, and their transition from vegetative to reproductive growth normally requires prolonged cold exposure, a winter cue known as vernalization. In contrast, plants of the coastal ecotype bypass this rosette stage and initiate flowering without prolonged cold exposure. PA3-15
Evolutionary dynamics of reduced seed dispersal ability in Hydrangea macrophylla following colonization of oceanic islands
アジサイ伊豆諸島系統で種子散布能力低下の進化過程を検証
Shoki Murakami*1, Takuro Ito2, Tatsuya Uemachi3, Shinji Fujii4, Masayuki Maki2
Oceanic islands, which have never been connected to continents, often exhibit unique evolutionary patterns resulting from long-term isolation. Plants on oceanic islands are often differentiated from their mainland relatives. In some cases, insular plants exhibit larger seeds accompanied by reduced seed dispersal ability as a typical example of the “island syndrome” in plants. However, it remains unclear how seed dispersal ability declines during the process of oceanic island colonization. The Izu Islands and the Bonin (Ogasawara) Islands are volcanic islands arranged almost linearly over approximately 1,200 km southward from the Izu Peninsula in Japan. This island chain provides an ideal system for examining the continuous process of reduced seed dispersal ability following oceanic island colonization. This study focused on Hydrangea macrophylla f. normalis (Hydrangeaceae), which distributed along the Pacific coast of the Japanese mainland Honshu, the Izu Islands, and the Bonin Islands. We aimed to (1) infer the colonization history of island populations; (2) quantify seed dispersal ability based on seed size and airborne time, and (3) identify candidate genomic regions associated with seed dispersal traits by detecting outlier loci using whole-genome resequencing data. Population genetic analyses revealed genetic differentiation among mainland and island populations, suggesting that H. macrophylla colonized the islands from north to south via stepping-stone-like dispersal. Seed size and weight in the Izu Islands populations decreased with increasing distance from mainland, whereas those in the Bonin Islands populations tended to be larger and heavier than those in the Izu Islands populations. In addition, airborne time differed among mainland and island populations, indicating geographic variation in dispersal-related traits. Furthermore, significant genetic differentiation was detected near loci involved in seed formation, suggesting that reduced seed dispersal ability may be associated with selective pressure.
（要旨集 p.328）
PA3-16
From genome to populations: reference assembly and population genomics of the Galápagos endemic Darwiniothamnus genus
ガラパゴス固有植物Darwiniothamnusのゲノム解読と集団遺伝
Nicolò Tellini*1, José Cerca1
How is genetic diversity and population structure distributed within a young, multi-species island radiation? The Galápagos endemic genus Darwiniothamnus (Asteraceae, Astereae) comprises three woody species nested within Erigeron s.l. which, on ITS evidence, derive from at least two independent colonisations of the archipelago: D. tenuifolius and D. lancifolius with Caribbean, D. alternifolius with South American relatives (Andrus et al., 2009). Despite being a textbook case of insular diversification, the group has lacked a genomic resource. We present a chromosome-scale reference assembly for D. tenuifolius (1.25 Gb, 18 chromosomes, scaffold N50 83 Mb) and show it to be an allotetraploid. K-mer spectra, 86.5% BUSCO duplication, one-to-one homoeologous chromosome pairing and TE composition all resolve two subgenomes, A and B, consistent with a base number of x = 9. Structural annotation yields 55,647 protein-coding genes on the assembled chromosomes, partitioned asymmetrically: subgenome A is ~25% larger than B yet carries ~10% fewer genes (39 vs 54 genes/Mb) and is missing more conserved single-copy orthologues (10.6% vs 6.5%), perhaps a signature compatible with transposon-driven expansion and biased fractionation. We further resequenced 56 individuals from eight populations spanning all three species across Isabela and Santa Cruz, and use this dataset to describe population structure and the decay of linkage disequilibrium within and between species.

PA3-18関連
An admixed insular lineage of Heliconius cydno from Gorgona Island, Colombia
コロンビア島嶼個体群ドクチョウの混血起源をゲノムで解明
島嶼性昆虫の進化だが東アジア域外の蝶
Geraldine Rueda-Muñoz*1, José Cerca1
Gene flow, demographic changes, and geographic isolation interact in complex ways during population divergence. These processes can be difficult to disentangle, especially in insular systems, where founder effects and small population sizes may increase genetic differentiation while also blurring historical signals of connectivity through drift. In this study, we used a population genomic approach to investigate the evolutionary history of an insular population of Heliconius cydno from Gorgona Island, Colombia. We analyzed whole-genome resequencing data from 46 individuals, including samples from the island population and from three nearby continental populations that share similar wing patterns: H. c. alithea, H. c. weymeri, and H. c. zelinde. We infer that the Gorgona population originated through admixture, after which geographic isolation played a central role in its evolutionary history. Our findings provide multiple lines of evidence supporting this scenario. First, the Gorgona population is genetically distinct, with limited ongoing gene flow with the continental populations. Second, demographic inference indicates a marked reduction in effective population size (Ne), consistent with a single founding episode under conditions of insular isolation. Third, patterns of historical gene flow among the four populations support a hybridization model in which H. c. alithea (59%) and H. c. weymeri (41%) contributed to the origin of the Gorgona population. Finally, we identified genomic regions associated with phenotypic traits in Heliconius, particularly wing-pattern loci (WntA and ivory), where parental contributions align with two specific phenotypic features: the complete forewing band and the intermediate ventral hindwing bar. Keywords: Admixture, demography, gene flow, Gorgona Island, wing pattern, Heliconius cydno.

PA3-20
Some like it hot: Testing the effects of interspecific interactions on divergence of thermal traits in Plestiodon skinks
トカゲ属の種間競争による温度耐性形質の分岐を検証
Shouta Iyoda*1, Ryotaroh Yanagihara1, Teppei Jono1
Interspecific interactions are widely considered major drivers of evolutionary diversification. The thermal niche partitioning hypothesis predicts that species competing for access to thermal environments evolve divergent thermal physiological traits and thermal habitat use. Such divergence can facilitate coexistence by reducing overlap in thermal niches and may thereby contribute to community assembly and diversification, particularly in ectothermic animals. Although this hypothesis provides a valuable explanation for thermal niche partitioning observed in many ectotherm communities, empirical evidence that interspecific interactions drive evolutionary divergence in thermal physiological traits remains limited. To address this question, we investigated the role of interspecific competition in shaping thermal trait divergence using comparative and experimental approaches in Japanese Plestiodon skinks. Specifically, we first conducted interspecific comparisons of preferred body temperature (Tpref) across seven species, including both sympatric and allopatric species with respect to congeners, along a latitudinal thermal gradient spanning from mainland Japan to the Ryukyu Archipelago. Second, we compared microhabitat use and thermal physiological traits in detail between two sympatric species (P. toyamai and P. marginatus) on Okinawa Island. Third, we performed intraspecific comparisons of P. marginatus populations between sympatric and allopatric islands within the Okinawa island group. Across species, environmental temperature did not explain variation in Tpref in Plestiodon species. Instead, species occurring in sympatry exhibited significant divergence in thermal preference. Furthermore, a detailed comparison of two sympatric species showed that P. marginatus possessed significantly higher thermal physiological traits and occupied warmer, more open microhabitat than its congener. While these findings are consistent with predictions of the thermal niche partitioning hypothesis, inter-population comparisons of P. marginatus revealed no significant differences in thermal physiological traits between sympatric and allopatric populations. This contrast indicates a scale-dependent pattern in the effects of interspecific interactions; thermal divergence was evident among species, but absent within species. One possible explanation for this discrepancy is behavioral buffering, whereby precise thermoregulatory behavior weakens selection on thermal physiological traits following release from interspecific interactions. Alternatively, the observed pattern may reflect historical species filtering rather than competition-driven divergence. To distinguish between these alternatives, we conducted laboratory competition experiments to test whether the presence of interspecific competitors directly alters thermoregulatory behavior along an experimental thermal gradient. Our results suggest that the evolutionary significance of interspecific interactions differs between species and population levels, highlighting the need to integrate ecological processes, including thermoregulatory trade-offs, with evolutionary timescales when evaluating the role of competition in thermal niche evolution.
（要旨集 p.334）
PA3-25
Two undescribed fish species of the families Stichaeidae and Pholidae (Teleostei) from the Sea of Okhotsk
オホーツク海産ニシキギンポ科・タウエガジ科の未記載種2種
Seiya Kanai*1, Hiroyuki Motomura2
The pricklebacks (Perciformes: Stichaeidae) and gunnels (Perciformes: Pholidae) are elongated, bottom-dwelling fishes, distributed in the North Pacific, North Atlantic, and Arctic oceans. The family Stichaeidae currently includes 18 genera and at least 45 species. A morphological examination of a specimen of the family collected from Hokkaido, Japan revealed that it is an undescribed species. This undescribed species was identified as a member of Stichaeopsis Kner, 1870 or Ulvaria Jordan and Evermann, 1896 as it had the developed lateral line along the midline of the lateral body. Since no morphological diagnostic characters for these two genera have been identified in previous studies, genetic analysis based on mitochondrial DNA was made during this study, showing that the undescribed species is most closely related to U. subbifurcata (Storer, 1839). The family Pholidae currently includes four genera and at least 15 species. A morphological examination of a specimen of the family collected from the Shantar Islands, Russia revealed that it is an undescribed species. This undescribed species was identified as belonging to the monotypic genus Rhodymenichthys Jordan and Evermann, 1896 [type species: R. dolichogaster (Pallas, 1814)], based on the absence of hypural 5 and the presence of pelvic fin. It however can be distinguished from R. dolichogaster by having the dorsal fin elevated from the 3rd to 27th spines, and black vertical bars on the lateral side of the body. As the dorsal-fin feature is unique to this undescribed species within the family, the question of whether it should be classified as Rhodymenichthys or as a distinct genus, separate from all other valid genera, requires careful consideration.
（要旨集 p.339）
PA3-26
Two undescribed species of lefteye flounders (Teleostei: Bothidae) from Tanega-shima island, southern Japan
種子島産ダルマガレイ科の未記載種2種を形態と遺伝で記載
Kenta Kuriyama*1, Seiya Kanai1, Hiroyuki Motomura2
The lefteye flounder family Bothidae Smitt, 1892 currently includes 18 genera and 150 species which are distributed worldwide in temperate to tropical regions. Based on genetic and morphological analyses, Tongboonkua et al. (2025) divided the previously recognized Bothidae into four families: Bothidae, Grammatobothidae Tongboonkua, Chanet and Chen, 2025, Monolenidae Tongboonkua, Chanet and Chen, 2025, and Taeniopsettidae Amaoka, 1969. They also redefined the valid bothid genera, Arnoglossus Bleeker, 1862, Laeops Günther, 1880, Parabothus Norman, 1931, and Psettina Hubbs, 1915, and resurrected Anticitharus Günther, 1880, Caulopsetta Gill, 1893, Psettinella Fedorov and Foroshchuk, 1993, and Scidorhombus Tanaka, 1915 previously synonymized under the bothid genera. During an ichthyofaunal survey in Tanega-shima Island, two unidentified bothid species were collected sympatrically from shallow sand-muddy bottoms. Although both species undoubtedly belong to the family Bothidae, as evidenced by their distinctly offset pelvic fins and the ocular-side pelvic-fin origin on the tip of the isthmus, their generic allocation remains uncertain. The two species share an ovate body and a very narrow interorbital space, but differ from each other in upper- and lower-jaw lengths on both sides, pectoral-fin lengths on both sides, and the presence or absence of an orbital flap on the lower eye. Molecular analysis based on the COI region also supported their distinctiveness. Comparison of all species of the family with the two species from Tanega-shima Island showed the two to be undescribed species. The generic allocation of the two undescribed species is discussed based on morphological and phylogenetic analyses using mitochondrial and nuclear markers.

PA3-27
Taxonomy and distribution of the bigeye genus Priacanthus (Teleostei: Priacanthidae) in the Indo-Pacific Ocean
インド太平洋産ヒウチダイ属Priacanthusの分類と分布整理
Shintaro Hashimoto*1, Hiroyuki Motomura2
The family Priacanthidae comprises four genera and approximately 20 species that are distributed in tropical to temperate waters worldwide. They occur in rocky and coral reef habitats at depths of 5–400 m. The genus Priacanthus Oken, 1817 currently includes 13 valid species that are distributed in the Indo-Pacific Ocean, with the exception of an Atlantic species P. arenatus Cuvier, 1829: P. alalaua Jordan and Evermann, 1903, P. blochii Bleeker, 1853, P. fitchi Starnes, 1988, P. gracilis Hashimoto and Motomura, 2024, P. hamrur (Fabricius, 1775), P. macracanthus Cuvier, 1829, P. meeki Jenkins, 1903, P. nasca Starnes, 1988, P. prolixus Starnes, 1988, P. sagittarius Starnes, 1988, P. starnesi Hashimoto and Motomura, 2026, P. tayenus Richardson, 1846, and P. zaiserae Starnes and Moyer, 1988. During a taxonomic study of Priacanthus in the Indo-Pacific Ocean, two undescribed species, Priacanthus spp. 1 and 2, have been recognized from the Coral Sea and the western Indian Ocean, respectively. These two species closely resemble P. fitchi, but can be distinguished from it by scale meristic characters, viz., the number of lateral-line scales, scales in the lateral series, and scale rows below the lateral-line. In addition, P. schmittii Bleeker, 1852 (northern and eastern Indian Ocean) and Priacanthus speculum Valenciennes, 1831 (western Indian Ocean), previously regarded as junior synonyms of P. tayenus (western Pacific Ocean) and P. hamrur (Indo-West Pacific Ocean), respectively, are now recognized as valid species. Review of the distributions of Indo-Pacific species of Priacanthus also revealed that P. alalaua, previously known only from island areas of the Pacific Ocean, also occurs off Madagascar. Examination of specimens of P. alalaua from the western Pacific, the Hawaiian Islands, Mexico, and Madagascar revealed slight morphological differences between different localities. However, no diagnostic characters were found, and these differences are herein regarded as geographic variation. The present study confirms that 17 species of Priacanthus occur in the Indo-Pacific Ocean.

PA3-28関連
Genetic Diversity of Razor Clam Populations in Japanese Tidal Flats
日本列島干潟のマテガイ類における遺伝的多様性と地理構造
トカラ海峡等の地理的境界概念が手法的に参考になる
Kotaro Sekino*1, Daishi Yamazaki1, Tomoki Seo2
The Japanese Archipelago comprises numerous islands separated by complex ocean current systems and biogeographic boundaries such as the Tokara Gap. This insular geography provides an ideal setting for investigating the interplay between geographic isolation and gene flow in marine ecosystems. Marine organisms with planktonic larval stages have traditionally been considered unlikely to exhibit significant geographic genetic differentiation because of their high dispersal potential. However, recent population genetic studies have revealed that even such species can develop clear geographic genetic structures. Generally, tidal flats are formed in semi-enclosed coastal environments, where restricted gene flow results in unique genetic structures. Additionally, tidal flats occur widely throughout the islands of the Japanese Archipelago, including the Ryukyu Islands, providing habitats for both subtropical and temperate species across geographically isolated regions. The complex insular geography and oceanographic conditions of the Japanese Archipelago may therefore generate additional patterns of genetic differentiation. Nevertheless, population genetic studies of tidal-flat organisms in Japan remain limited compared with those of other intertidal organisms, and their genetic population structure remains poorly understood. Moreover, tidal flats in Japan have been lost in recent decades, resulting in population declines of many tidal-flat organisms. Understanding the genetic structure of these organisms is important for elucidating how ocean currents and geographic barriers influence population connectivity in insular environments and for providing fundamental information for coastal ecosystem conservation. We therefore chose to focus on organisms with a planktonic larval stage inhabiting tidal flats. The razor clam Solen strictus is a bivalve with a planktonic larval stage that inhabits tidal flats throughout East Asia. Although widely distributed along the Japanese coast, its distribution on Okinawa Island is restricted to only two localities, Haneji Inland Sea and Shioya Bay, making it a useful model for investigating the genetic structure of tidal-flat organisms. We analyzed the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) gene of Solen strictus collected from multiple localities along the Japanese coast to clarify the population genetic structure of this species in insular tidal-flat ecosystems and to provide fundamental information for its conservation. The analyses revealed extensive haplotype sharing among localities, with no clear geographic genetic structure detected. However, genetic differentiation was observed between some populations, suggesting that localized population divergence may occur alongside the overall high level of connectivity among populations.
（要旨集 p.342）
PA3-29
Moss community composition along an elevational gradient: a biogeographical comparison between Pacific and Indian Ocean islands
インド洋・太平洋諸島のコケ群集を標高傾度で比較
Saioa Ricou--Dreneuc*1, Nicholas Wilding1, Terry Hedderson2, Jean-Yves Meyer3, 4, Dominique Strasberg5,
Elevational gradients have long been central to studying environmental influences on biodiversity, particularly on young volcanic islands with steep climatic transitions over short distances. This study aims to quantify moss diversity and assess how elevation, substrate availability, and climate drive moss community composition along two isolated elevational gradients: Piton des Neiges on Reunion Island (Mascarene Archipelago, 3,069 m a.s.l.) and Aorai on Tahiti (French Polynesia, 2,066 m a.s.l.). Moss communities were sampled using the standardized hierarchical design BRYOLAT, which includes four levels: elevational belts, plots (10 × 10 m), quadrats (2 × 2 m), and microplots (10 × 5 cm). Within each microplot, all bryophyte-colonized substrates were surveyed, including rock (rupicolous), soil (terricolous), humus (humicolous), decaying wood (lignicolous), and tree bark (epiphytic). A total of 828 samples across 15 elevations were collected on Reunion and 570 across 7 elevations on Tahiti. Moss species richness differed markedly between the two gradients, with 191 species recorded on Piton des Neiges and 80 species on Aorai. Along the Piton des Neiges gradient, species richness displayed a bimodal pattern, with peaks at both 1,350 and 2,550 m a.s.l., whereas a unimodal pattern was observed on Aorai, where richness reached its maximum at mid-elevation around 1,300 m a.s.l. On both gradient, richness peaks coincided with humid environments and moderate temperatures that likely promote the coexistence of both lowland and montane taxa. On Piton des Neiges, the tree-line may reflect changes in forest structure and substrate availability explaining the observed bimodal pattern. Aligning with previous works our results indicate that community composition changed substantially along both gradients, indicating strong species turnover with increasing elevation. Our findings show that fine-scale elevational variation drives strong ecological differentiation, underscoring the value of these ecosystems and their moss communities as sensitive indicators of environmental change in tropical oceanic islands.
（要旨集 p.343）
PA3-30
Floral and life-history diversity in Japanese endemic Aster species
日本固有シオン属の花形質と生活史の多様性
Sayaka Nakagawa*1, Shigeto Dobata2, Kiyomi Nakagawa3, Takaya Iwasaki1, Minami Yamasaki4, Shota Sakaguchi5, Seikan Kurata6, Kanami Yoshida1, Satuki Kobayashi1, Maika Kinoshita1, Takuro Ito7, Hidenori Deto8, Atushi J. Nagano9, Junko Okazaki10, Tadashi Miyashita11, Hiroaki Setoguchi5, Noboru Kuramoto12, Yuji Isagi5, Akiko Soejima4, Motomi Ito2
Most species in section Pseudocalimeris of the genus Aster (Asteraceae) are endemic to the Japanese Archipelago and occur in diverse habitats, such as grasslands, coastal areas, riverbanks, serpentine soils, and rocky sites. This section also shows diversity in floral morphology and life-history traits. For example, some taxa exhibit the “long tubular ray floret” variation, characterized by elongated tubular peripheral florets of the capitulum. In addition, some taxa previously regarded as biennial semelparous plants can reform rosettes at the base of flowering stems, suggesting the potential for survival and reproduction in subsequent years. Thus, Pseudocalimeris provides a useful system for understanding how trait diversity arises and is maintained in island plants. In this study, we focused on the A. hispidus species complex, A. kantoensis, and A. arenarius to clarify trait diversity within Pseudocalimeris using three approaches. First, we analyzed genetic relationships among tetraploid taxa using ddRAD-seq. Second, we conducted field surveys to examine whether the long tubular ray floret variation occurs in taxa other than those previously known. Third, focusing on rosette formation in flowering individuals, we examined its relationship with habitat type and whether this trait is associated with reproduction in subsequent years. The population genetic analyses showed that the genetic structure of the tetraploid taxa mainly reflected geographic structure rather than habitat differences. However, in coastal A. arenarius and serpentine A. hispidus var. leptocladus, morphological classification was inconsistent with genetic clusters, suggesting that similar morphological traits may have arisen in parallel in similar habitats. The long tubular ray floret variation was confirmed in multiple taxa and was found in relatively harsh habitats, such as riverbanks, coastal areas, and serpentine soils. The frequency of rosette reformation varied among populations: it was not observed in grassland populations but tended to be higher in riverbank and serpentine populations. Furthermore, iteroparity was confirmed in A. kantoensis and A. hispidus var. tubulosus.

PA3-31
From theory to macroecological evidence: a global test of island syndrome in plant floral traits
島嶼症候群と花形質進化のグローバル検証
Ruiqi Zhang*1, Shota Sakaguchi1
Plant island syndrome predicts that adaptation to islands promotes self-compatibility and simplified floral attraction traits. Previous studies have supported increased self-compatibility in island plants, yet floral traits are less consistent: floral size does not always decrease on islands and may even increase in tropical and subtropical systems. Thus, floral simplification on islands may emerge only under particular ecological conditions rather than a general rule. It remains unclear whether this reflects geographic filtering, or arises from shifts in pollinator environments and self-compatibility. Here, I tested the ecological conditions and pathways underlying floral trait simplification across global island floras. I compiled a global dataset of island floras integrating island area, distance to continent, GBIF-based Bombus spp. climatic unsuitability, and floral and reproductive traits. Floral color, floral form, pollination mode, and self-compatibility were collected and standardized with the assistance of large language models. Analyses were restricted to animal-pollinated species. For each island, I calculated the proportions of inconspicuously colored flowers (white, green, or brown), open or brush-type flowers (actinomorphic, brush-type, or composite), and self-compatible species. For north-temperate islands, I compared four Bayesian piecewise path-model scenarios using LOO-CV: (1) Geographic Filtering, in which isolation and area directly predict floral traits; (2) Selfing Syndrome, in which isolation promotes self-compatibility, which in turn shapes floral traits; (3) Full Mediation, in which Bombus climatic unsuitability drives self-compatibility, which then leads to floral simplification; and (4) Partial Mediation, in which Bombus climatic unsuitability additionally exerts direct selection on floral color independently of self-compatibility. Partial Mediation performed best. More isolated islands showed greater Bombus climatic unsuitability, which in turn predicted higher self-compatibility. Self-compatible floras had higher proportions of both inconspicuously colored flowers and open or brush-type flowers. Bombus climatic unsuitability also directly increased inconspicuously colored flowers, but showed little direct effect on floral form. Smaller islands tended toward stronger floral simplification. When the north-temperate pathway was projected to tropical and southern non-tropical islands, predictive accuracy declined, suggesting that Bombus climatic unsuitability does not explain animal-pollinated island floras globally. In tropical and southern temperate regions, alternative pollinators such as birds and tropical butterflies may maintain bright colors and complex floral forms. Whether similar unsuitability operates for other pollinators remains untested. Together, these results indicate that floral island syndrome is condition-dependent, expressed most strongly in north-temperate islands where pollinator unsuitability and self-compatibility jointly shape floral trait composition.
（要旨集 p.346）
PA3-32関連
Trait filtering reduces proboscis length in pollinator communities on oceanic islands
海洋島における送粉者口吻長の形質フィルタリング
海洋島の昆虫形質フィルタリングで島嶼進化と関連
Masayoshi K. Hiraiwa*1, Atushi Ushimaru2
Fauna of historically isolated oceanic islands usually decreases in species richness with increasing distance from the nearest continent or continental island. Faunal trait composition has been hypothesised to be biased on isolated oceanic islands, such that traits which allow long-distance dispersal and lower resource requirements, e.g. small body size, dominate in each animal group. These changes in species richness and trait composition may alter species interactions and consequently affect ecosystem functioning. Pollinator communities are ideal subjects to test these predictions because they interact with plants and the pollination function is strongly influenced by their functional traits. We therefore aimed to determine which factors influence assembly of pollinator species and trait composition in oceanic island ecosystems by comparing the species richness and trait composition of five major pollinator groups (bees, wasps, flies, lepidopterans, and beetles) between continental and oceanic islands. We surveyed flower-visiting insects at three coastal sites on the Japanese mainland and five oceanic islands in the Izu Archipelago. Five seasonal surveys were conducted at each site from May to December 2013– 2014, during which flower-visiting pollinators were collected with a net. Using null-model analyses, we evaluated whether species occurrence and abundance on oceanic islands deviated from expectations based on the mainland species pool while accounting for differences in species abundance. We then tested relationships between colonization success and functional traits, including body size, larval habit, sociality, feeding type, and proboscis length. Most oceanic islands exhibited significantly lower pollinator species richness than expected from the mainland species pool. Pollinator occurrence and abundance were associated with several functional traits. In particular, long-tongued pollinators were underrepresented on oceanic islands. These functionally important pollinators were frequently absent or occurred at much lower abundances than expected, resulting in a reduction in community-level proboscis length. Because proboscis length was positively associated with body size and differed among pollinator groups, trait filtering associated with colonization and establishment processes may have contributed to this pattern. Our previous work revealed that absence or reduced abundance of long-tongued pollinators altered plant– pollinator interactions and reduced pollination function in this oceanic island system. Thus, trait filtering associated with colonization and establishment processes may reduce the representation of long-tongued pollinators on oceanic islands, with cascading effects on plant–pollinator interactions and pollination function.
（要旨集 p.347）
PA3-33
Relationship between leaf trait diversity and habitat environment in Metrosideros polymorpha across the Hawaii islands
ハワイ諸島におけるメトロシデロス葉形質の多様化
Ryota Futamura*1, Kaede Konnrai1, Gaku Amada2, Ayako Izuno2, Yuji Isagi1, Kanehiro Kitayama3, Yusuke Onoda1
Metrosideros polymorpha is an endemic, dominant tree species that has widely diversified across the Hawaii archipelago. While significant variations in leaf traits—such as leaf mass per area (LMA)—have been documented along environmental gradients (elevation, precipitation, and soil age) on the island of Hawaii, few studies have investigated the extent of this diversification across the older islands of the archipelago. Furthermore, despite conspicuous morphological variations, leaf shape has yet to be quantitatively analyzed. This study aims to quantify leaf trait variations, with a specific focus on leaf shape, across the M. polymorpha species complex to gain insight into the mechanisms driving adaptive radiation in this foundation species. Leaves were sampled from 1,326 individuals across 79 sites spanning four Hawaii islands, capturing gradients in elevation (0 to 2,500 m), annual precipitation (400 to 6400 mm), and substrate age (the present to 4 million years). Leaf shape was quantitatively evaluated using geometric morphometrics, establishing coordinates for 10 landmarks per leaf to derive five distinct shape indices. Additional functional traits, including leaf area, LMA, and leaf dry matter content (LDMC), were also measured. Consistent with previous literature, LMA and leaf size were strongly correlated with air temperature. Crucially, however, leaf shape was more strongly associated with soil age than with temperature; specifically, leaf tips became progressively more acute (pointed) as substrate age increased. These findings reveal uncoupled evolutionary or plastic responses between physiological and morphological leaf traits, and we are currently investigating the ecological significance of this shape variation across the geological age gradient of the Hawaii islands.

PA3-35
Morphology and thermal physiology between two elevational populations in Takydromus tachydromoides on Yakushima Island
屋久島トカゲ標高集団の形態・温度生理比較
Gumma Kubo*1, Shouta Iyoda1, Teppei Jono1
Thermal environments strongly influence the ecology and evolution of ectotherms. Recent studies have suggested that thermoregulatory behavior can buffer the evolution of thermal physiological traits, such as preferred body temperature, from natural selection by selecting the microhabitat that provides preferred thermal conditions and enable to maintain body temperature within the adapted range. However, such a behavioral change can expose other traits to the new selection pressure, thereby it may also have a role as a driver of the evolution. In Anolis lizards, the species inhabiting cold high-elevation environments and those inhabiting warm low-elevation environments often show little divergence in thermal physiology despite marked differences in microhabitat use and external morphology. These findings suggest that when thermal environment changes, shifts in microhabitat use may compensate for evolutionary constraints on thermal traits, promoting morphological evolution. However, because such conclusions are largely based on interspecific comparisons involving relatively few species, the influence of phylogenetic relationships remains a potential confounding factor. To test this hypothesis within a single species, we examined elevational variation in the Japanese grass lizard, Takydromus tachydromoides, on Yakushima Island, Japan, which possesses a steep elevational gradient within a relatively small geographic area. Species of the genus Takydromus distributed in warmer southern regions tend to exhibit arboreality, and T. tachydromoides utilizes a wide range of microhabitats from the ground surface to herbaceous vegetation. Therefore, assuming that thermal physiology is subject to evolutionary constraints, we predicted that the low-elevation populations, which utilize herbaceous plants more frequently, would possess longer limbs and tails that are advantageous for locomotion on vegetation, whereas the high-elevation populations would lack these traits. In 2026, we collected T. tachydromoides from low-elevation (<100 m elev.) and high-elevation (>1000 m elev.) sites on Yakushima Island to measure snout–vent length, forelimb length, hindlimb length, and tail length. In addition, laboratory experiments using a thermal gradient arena were conducted to evaluate thermal physiological traits. Contrary to our prediction, neither external morphology nor thermal physiology differed significantly between high- and low-elevation populations. The process of invasion is complex and involves various stages that are theoretically distinct but are hard to tease apart in practice: Introduction, Naturalization, and Invasion. While the outcomes of naturalization and subsequent invasion can be observed and are now documented in globally comprehensive databases, information on introductions (especially when species fail to naturalize) is often not recorded or lost to time. Lack of information on introduced species that fail to naturalize is problematic for invasion biology because it is often unclear whether the factors associated with increased invasion success may reflect anthropogenic biases during introductions. In the case of plants, cultivation is the primary pathway for introduction. We therefore compiled a geographically explicit database of cultivated plants across the Caribbean to fill this important information gap. The Caribbean is global biodiversity hotspot with high proportions of and impacts from introduced species. It is also a region with an extensive and complex history of colonization that is reflected in the species introduced for cultivation. Compiling published cultivation checklists of annotated flora lists from across the region, the database includes cultivated species for every island in the Greater Antilles, most of the Lucayan Archipelago, and many Lesser Antilles and Virgin Islands. With each entry representing a species cultivated in a specific island or country we current include over 2,800 entries representing 1,609 unique species. We plan to use this database to study how geographic distributions, plant traits, ecologic and anthropogenic factors influence the invasion process. We have already analyzed recorded plant uses within the Caribbean cultivated flora and found that plants with more uses, as well as those used in lanscaping or animal feed, had a higher likelihood of naturalization. This resource will be useful not only to future studies in invasion ecology, but in diverse fields including botanists, etnobotanists, cultural geography, environmental history, and environmental science.

The daily average temperature inside the tree cavity (20.7±5.1℃) was lower than outside (21.3±5.0℃). The daily average relative humidity inside the tree cavity (97.7±2.9%) was higher than outside (91.3±6.3%). During the winter, the Tin was around 15.4±2.1℃, while it was 25.2±0.5℃ in the summer. Furthermore, use of eight patches (72%) ended when mature seeds had consumed by rats, indicating that patch use was closely associated with seeds availability.
