PG3-02
The biological and conservation value of the canary cedar (Juniperus cedrus) in Gran Canary Island (Canary Islands, Spain)
グランカナリア島のビャクシン属樹木の保全価値評価
Agustín Naranjo-Cigala*1, Manuel Nogales2, Patrick Mäder3, Abraham Araña-Padilla2, Yurena Arjona2, Juli Caujapé-Castells4, David Gutiérrez-Larruscain5, Mercedes López-González2, Javier Martin-Carbajal2, Javier Morente-López2, David P. Padilla2, Miguel Sequeira6, Guillermo Sicilia-Pasos7, Aditya Jethliya3, Pablo Vargas8, Jana Wäldchen9, Jairo Patiño2
The Canary Island cedar, Juniperus cedrus, is one of the most emblematic relict trees of the Canary Islands and a key component of the archipelago’s natural heritage. Once more widespread across the islands, centuries of human exploitation (including logging, charcoal production, wildfires, and the use of cedar wood for traditional purposes) have drastically reduced its distribution and abundance. On Gran Canaria, the species now survives in a small and fragmented population, raising concerns about its long-term viability and the conservation of its evolutionary potential. Understanding the historical and ecological processes that have shaped these remnant population is essential for developing effective conservation strategies. In this study, we combine population genomics, climatic niche modelling, and artificial intelligence approaches to investigate the evolutionary history, demographic dynamics, and environmental drivers influencing the persistence of cedar populations. Our analyses reveal that J. cedrus populations of Gran Canaria represent a distinct genetic lineage relative to populations on Tenerife, La Gomera, and La Palma, highlighting their unique evolutionary significance within the species. The results also provide new insights into the processes that have contributed to their differentiation and persistence despite centuries of habitat loss and fragmentation. Protecting the canarian cedar of Gran Canaria is crucial not only for preserving biodiversity but also for maintaining an irreplaceable component of the evolutionary history of the Canary Islands in the face of accelerating global change.
（要旨集 p.284）
PG3-04関連
Habitat Limitation Factors of the Tsushima Leopard Cat: Effects of Forest Management and Rodent Responses
対馬ヤマネコの生息地制限要因と森林管理の影響
対馬固有亜種だが系統地理でなく生息地管理の話
Shuki Kikuchi*1, Yushin Asari2, Takuma Hashimoto1
The Tsushima leopard cat (Prionailurus bengalensis euptilurus) is a critically endangered subspecies of the leopard cat endemic to the Tsushima Islands, Japan. In recent decades, abandoned forests have been increasing in Tsushima. These forests often lack understory vegetation, which is critical for the survival of small mammals, the primary prey of the Tsushima leopard cat. Consequently, the proliferation of abandoned forests has been identified as a significant challenge for the conservation of this species. This study aimed to investigate the distribution of small mammals and examine appropriate forest management practices. Forests were classified into six types based on tree species composition and management history, and small mammal trapping surveys were conducted in June 2025 using Sherman live traps. To analyze the relationships among capture rates, forest types, and coarse woody debris (CWD), generalized linear models (GLMs) were constructed. The survey captured 18 Japanese wood mice (Apodemus speciosus) and 24 small Japanese field mice (A. argenteus). The catch per unit effort (CPUE) of small mammals was highest in abandoned artificial conifer forests, with a value of 3.86 individuals per 100 trap nights. However, no clear relationship was observed between forest type and CPUE. Positive correlations were found with understory vegetation coverage, whereas negative correlations were observed with the number of residual thinning logs and fallen trees. These results suggest that understory vegetation coverage is a critical factor in small mammal habitat selection. Conversely, residual thinning logs and fallen trees are typically perceived by small mammals as refuges from predation; however, this study showed negative correlations. This discrepancy may be attributed to the presence of predators influencing small mammal behavior on Tsushima Island. On Tsushima, overpopulation of sika deer (Cervus nippon) has severely impacted understory vegetation, potentially homogenizing forest floor environments regardless of management history. This may explain the lack of correlation between forest type and CPUE. While abandoned artificial forests are generally considered undesirable from the perspectives of biodiversity conservation and land management, socio-economic changes have made their active utilization increasingly difficult. Under such circumstances, we suggest the strategic preservation of forests that are geographically difficult to utilize as protected areas, emphasizing their potential role in biodiversity conservation.
（要旨集 p.286）
PG3-05関連
Recent cases of poaching and illegal export of endangered animals in the Ryukyu Archipelago, Japan
琉球諸島における希少動物の密猟・違法輸出の現状
琉球固有動物の密猟問題、分類群重なるが政策寄り
Masako Izawa*1, Mamoru Toda1, Shun Kobayashi1
Poaching of rare insects such as the Yanbaru long-armed scarab beetle Cheirotonus jambar has long been a conservational problem in the Ryukyu Islands. This activity was not limited to collection for personal collections; illegal online trade was also taking place, both on an individual and commercial basis. In recent years, there have been several cases of poaching and illegal export abroad targeting reptiles and amphibians. In 2018, the illegal export of the Ryukyu black-breasted leaf turtle Geoemyda japonica, a National Natural Monument (NNM) and a National Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (NESWFF), was uncovered in Hong Kong. Also in 2018, Ryukyu black-breasted leaf turtles kept at Okinawa Zoo were stolen. Even during the COVID-19 pandemic, when human traffic had drastically decreased, incidents occurred in which the Amderson’s crocodile newt Echinotriton andersoni, a NESWFF, was illegally listed on online auctions. Subsequently, as human traffic recovered and the number of domestic and foreign visitors increased, incidences of poaching and illegal export has expanded in frequency and scale. Indeed, in 2025, large-scale poaching incidents involving turtles and geckos, including NNM and NESWFF, were uncovered in northern part of Okinawajima Island and Iriomotejima Island, both designated as Natural World Heritage sites, as well as on Kumejima Island, a small island home to many rare species. This year, pet dealers were arrested for poaching eyelid geckos and other animals. In addition to rare species, there have been cases of wild animals being found at airports, shipped via courier services, and sold at pet shops, and these issues also need to be addressed. These cases are likely just the tip of the iceberg, and vigilance against similar poaching and illegal exportation will be necessary going forward. In this presentation, we will summarize the uncovered cases and current countermeasures, and outline future challenges.
（要旨集 p.287）
PG3-07
Eradication of the mongoose on Amami Oshima Island: How was the eradication on one of the largest islands in the world been successfully completed?
奄美大島におけるマングース根絶成功の報告
Masaki Asano*1, Takuma Hashimoto1, Yoshiyuki Ryuzaki1,2, Yoshihito Goto1,2, Tamotsu Matsuda1,2, Shin Hosokawa1,2, Goro Majima1,2, Toshinori Kawaguchi1, Kenji Kitaura1, Tomonori Kawamoto1, Tomomi Aratani1, Shuki Kikuchi1, Takahiro Morosawa3,1, Shintaro Abe4, Amamigunto National Park Office, Ministry of the Environment5
On September 3, 2024, the Ministry of the Environment Government of Japan declared the eradication of Urva auropunctata on Amami-Oshima Island, Japan. Eradication of a widespread medium-sized mammal species on a large island such as Amami-Oshima Island is rare case at the global level, and this became the largest-scale mongoose eradication effort in the world. Mongooses were released on Amami-Oshima Island around 1979. Subsequently, it became apparent that they had impact on the island ecosystem, including predation of native species. Since 1993, local governments had been implementing mongoose control programs to prevent damages on agricultural products, and the Ministry of the Environment had been implementing an eradication program since 2000. The Act on the Prevention of Adverse Ecological Impacts Caused by Designated Invasive Alien Species came into effect in 2005, initiating the eradication program under the Act and establishing the Amami Mongoose Busters (AMB) to carry out these control operations. To capture mongooses, AMB set approximately 35,000 traps across the entire island. In 2008, we had introduced mongoose detection dogs from New Zealand and carried out efficient mongoose detection and capture operations by using these dogs. As a result of continuous trapping efforts, no mongooses have been observed since the last one had been captured in April 2018. Subsequently, the probability of its eradication and other factors were calculated by using six years of monitoring data. Based on these results, the eradication of mongooses on the Amami-Oshima Island was declared. Forty-five years have passed since the time when mongooses had been introduced, and twenty years have passed since eradication program had been initiated under the Act. We will review and synthesize how such a globally significant achievement was accomplished.
（要旨集 p.289）
PG3-08
Current status and challenges of invasive rodent eradication on islands in Japan
日本の島嶼における侵略ネズミ類根絶の現状と課題
Takuma Hashimoto*1, Ryuichi Minato1, Shuki Kikuchi1, Ogasawara Ranger Office2, Kushiro Nature Conservation Office3
Islands are important sites for biodiversity conservation. In many islands are inhabited many endemic species, serve as breeding grounds for endangered seabirds, and develop unique ecosystems. One of the greatest threats to island ecosystem conservation is predation by invasive rodents, and proactive measures are needed. In Japan, since the eradication carried out on Nishijima Island in the Ogasawara Islands in 2006, attempts have been made to eradicate rodents from islands such as the Ogasawara Islands and Yururi and Moyururi Islands in Hokkaido. To date, eradication in Japan has been carried out using diphacinone, a first-generation anticoagulant, and has achieved success in rodents eradication while avoiding impact on non-target species on small islands with simple topography. Among the islands where eradication has been successful, Higashijima Island in the Ogasawara Islands has shown significant results in ecosystem recovery, such as the confirmation of breeding of endangered seabirds. Over a 20-year period, eradication atempts aimed at eliminating invasive rodents were carried out on 20 islands. However, complete eradication was only achieved on 7 islands; on the other islands, individuals either survived or reinvaded from surrounding islands after eradication. Thus, current Japanese rodent control techniques rarely achieve eradication on islands with an area of 2 km² or more, indicating the need for various technical improvements. Areas for improvement include the introduction of second-generation anticoagulants, improvements in aerial dispersal techniques, and the development of methods to predict and mitigate impacts on non-target species. Although the introduction of second-generation anticoagulants and new aerial dispersal technologies presents significant challenges in terms of legal regulations and costs, these issues must be addressed in order to promote biodiversity conservation on islands. This research was conducted with funding from the Environment Research and Technology Development Fund (JPMEERF20254001).
（要旨集 p.290）
PG3-09
Soil erosion can limit grassland plant establishment via alternation of soil chemical properties in the Ogasawara islands even eradication of feral goats
小笠原諸島のヤギ根絶後も続く土壌侵食と植生回復阻害
Kenji Hata*1,2, Takeshi Osawa3, Syuntaro Hiradate4, Naoki Kachi5
Overgrazing and trampling by invasive feral goats often cause vegetation degradation and soil erosion, disrupting the ecosystem functions of oceanic islands. Soil erosion can alter in soil chemical properties, which can limit vegetation recovery even after goat eradication of goats. We evaluated the effects of soil erosion on plant establishment through a field survey in Nakodo-jima Island —located in a subtropical archipelago in the northwestern Pacific Ocean —and laboratory experiments. The field survey revealed that soil erosion and the exposure of deeper soil horizons were more pronounced in areas with low vegetation cover, and this subsoil exhibited lower nutrient content and extremely high acidity. The occurrence of herbaceous species dominating grassland vegetation on the island was significantly and negatively correlated with amounts of soil nutrient levels and acidity. Laboratory experiments further revealed that these exposed soils had fewer nutrients and an extremely low pH, limiting the initial growth of the herbaceous species. This growth limitation was primarily driven by phosphorous availability; which depended on soil pH, with the trend of dependency varying among species. Our results suggest that soil erosion prior to goat eradication would create a nutrient-poor and acidic soil environment, inhibiting the establishment of herbaceous plants even after the removal of the goats.
（要旨集 p.291）
PG3-10
Towards understanding the spread of an invasive moss on a tropical oceanic island
レユニオン島における侵略コケ植物の拡大メカニズム
Claudine Ah-Peng*1,2, Nicholas Wilding1, Saioa Ricou--Dreneuc1, Nemo Fontanié3, Nada Nikolic1, Haruna Fimmel4, Vincent Jacob1, Terry Hedderson5, Yoan Coudert6
Biological invasions are a major cause of biodiversity loss on oceanic islands, yet the processes driving bryophyte invasions remain poorly understood. The moss Pseudoscleropodium purum (Hedw.) M. Fleisch., introduced to Réunion Island during the twentieth century, has become one of the most successful invasive bryophytes in the Mascarenes. Once largely restricted to disturbed habitats, it is now spreading into protected native ecosystems and forming extensive monospecific mats that threaten indigenous bryophyte communities. We present an overview of ongoing research examining the ecological success of P. purum on Réunion. Combining field surveys, species distribution modelling, architectural analyses, and experimental studies, we identify several mechanisms that contribute to its invasion. Distribution models based on more than 250 occurrence records show that suitable habitat covers a large proportion of the island’s uplands, including much of the National Park. Elevation is the strongest predictor of occurrence, indicating substantial potential for further expansion into native habitats. Recent observations reveal a remarkable shift from a primarily terrestrial to an epiphytic growth habit. Architectural analyses show that epiphytic individuals produce more shoot reiterations, longer primary axes, and greater rhizoid development, traits that facilitate colonisation of tree trunks. This novel growth form allows P. purum to threat Réunion’s diverse epiphytic bryophyte flora. Surveys have recorded the species overgrowing at least 50 native bryophyte species, while growth rates measured on Réunion are up to six times higher than those reported in its native European range. Experimental studies further demonstrate that volatile organic compounds (VOCs) emitted by P. purum affect native bryophytes under controlled conditions. VOC exposure altered growth and physiological performance in a species-specific manner, including increased shoot elongation in Pyrrhobryum spiniforme and changes in chlorophyll fluorescence in Leptodontium longicaule. Chemical analyses identified a diverse blend of sesquiterpenes and other VOCs associated with plant–plant interactions, suggesting that chemical communication may influence invasion dynamics in addition to direct competition. Together, these studies indicate that the invasion success of P. purum results from a combination of high growth performance, architectural innovation, niche expansion, and potentially VOC-mediated interactions with native species. Our findings challenge the traditional perception of bryophytes as ecologically passive organisms and highlight the need to incorporate cryptogam invasions into conservation strategies for tropical island ecosystems. Understanding the mechanisms driving the spread of P. purum is essential for predicting its future impacts and for developing effective management actions to protect Réunion’s exceptional bryophyte diversity.
（要旨集 p.292）
PG3-12関連
Differences in antipredator behavior between two native toad species and the invasive cane toad in Taiwan
台湾の在来・外来ヒキガエル類の対捕食者行動比較
離島の捕食回避行動、進化的に関連性はやや低い
Kiyoto Sawada*1, Takashi Kamijo1, Tein-Shun Tsai2
Island ecosystems are hotspots for the generation of endemic species, and understanding the ecological traits of these organisms provides important insights into evolutionary biology. In particular, numerous studies have demonstrated that ecological release due to reduced predation pressure on islands leads to the reduction of both physical defense traits, such as morphology, and chemical defense traits, such as toxicity. In contrast, although there is some evidence that islands organisms tend to exhibit reduced wariness and bolder behavior compared to their mainland counterparts, empirical knowledge remains limited, especially in terms of interspecific comparisons. In this study, we compared antipredator behavior among species and across temperature conditions, focusing on toads in Taiwan: the endemic Central Formosa toad (Bufo bankorensis), the native Asian common toad (Duttaphrynus melanostictus) distributed in Taiwan and southern Asia including mainland Asia, and the invasive cane toad (Rhinella marina) native to southern and mainland Central America. Individuals were collected in the field in Taiwan (B. bankorensis: n = 12; D. melanostictus: n = 11; R. marina: n = 17). Antipredator behavior experiments were conducted under three temperature conditions (17°C, 22°C, and 27°C). Behavioral responses were assessed by gently tapping the dorsal side of each individual with a sponge-tipped stick at 3-second intervals for 1 minute. Each response to the stimulus was categorized into multiple behavioral types, such as “fleeing”, “immobile”, “defensive vocalization”, “legs-driving away”, “crouching down”, and “cloacal discharge.” As a result, antipredator behavior varied markedly among species and across temperature conditions. In all species, “fleeing” and “immobile” accounted for the majority of responses. Bufo bankorensis consistently exhibited a relatively high proportion of “immobile” across all temperature treatments. In contrast, D. melanostictus and R. marina showed increasing frequencies of “defensive vocalization” and “fleeing” with rising temperatures, respectively. These findings indicated that the endemic B. bankorensis tends to rely on immobility as an antipredator strategy, whereas mainland-derived species exhibit more active antipredator responses. Although these patterns clearly reflect species-specific traits, further experiments are needed, such as comparisons with populations of the same or closely related species distributed on the mainland, to determine whether these characteristics are influenced by the island syndrome.
（要旨集 p.295）
PG3-13
Juvenile Schooling in Chimaeras in Suruga Bay
駿河湾のギンザメ類幼魚の時空間的集群パターン
Akinori Teramura*1
My team has been conducting continuous commercial trawl surveys in Suruga Bay, during which I discovered sites where large numbers of two chimaeras, Chimaera phantasma Jordan & Snyder, 1900 and Hydrolagus mitsukurii (Dean,1904), hereafter referred to as “colonies”. Both species are endemic to the northwestern Pacific Ocean and are listed on the IUCN Red List as “Vulnerable” for C. phantasma and “Near Threatened” for H. mitsukurii. If fisheries continue to operate without recognizing the existence of such high-density sites, there is a possibility that serious impacts on the maintenance of their populations may occur. In this study, we compared the spatial and temporal patterns between sites where C. phantasma and H. mitsukurii were present and those where they were absent. As a result, the colonies were found to occur on gently sloping areas in the western part of Suruga Bay and appeared primarily from winter to spring. In both species, these colonies consisted almost exclusively of immature individuals, and no significant sex ratio bias was observed among the specimens collected. Furthermore, all specimens of H. mitsukurii collected from the colony were found to prey on the same species of small bivalve, suggesting that they had aggregated around a common food resource. Studies investigating the existence and formation mechanisms of such colonies will help fill gaps in the ecological knowledge of chimaerid fishes and provide important information for the development of future conservation strategies.
（要旨集 p.296）
PG3-14
Osteological comparison of insular leopard cat populations: A functional morphological approach
イリオモテヤマネコなど島嶼ネコ類の頭骨機能形態比較
Nozomi Nakanishi*1, Masako Izawa2
The Iriomote cat (Prionailurus bengalensis iriomotensis), an insular population of the leopard cat inhabiting diverse environments from tropical to subarctic zones, is found on Iriomote Island, the world’s smallest island supporting a viable population of felids. Previous studies have reported that, unlike other populations where rodents are the primary prey, the Iriomote cat utilizes a variety of prey species across different taxonomic groups, including reptiles and amphibians. Due to the unique morphology of its skull, the Iriomote cat was once described as a new genus and species in 1967; these morphological characteristics were thought to be related to its diet and foraging behavior. Therefore, the aim of this study was to clarify the Iriomote cat’s adaptation to the island environment by comparing skull morphology and diet among three populations: the Iriomote cat, the Tsushima cat (P. b. euptilurus), and the Taiwan leopard cat (P. b. chinensis). The morphological peculiarities of the Iriomote cat’s skull, noted by Imaizumi (1967) at the time of the species’ description, were confirmed in juveniles and were found to be congenitally maintained characteristics. Morphological features related to mastication were analyzed using mandibles. The temporal muscle moment arm-to-mandible length ratio was significantly larger in the Tsushima and Taiwan leopard cats than in the Iriomote cat. In contrast, the masseter moment arm-to-mandibular length ratio was significantly larger in the Iriomote cat and the Taiwan leopard cat than in the Tsushima leopard cat, with the Iriomote cat exhibiting the highest value. This suggested that, compared to the Tsushima leopard cat, the Iriomote cat relies more on the masseter muscle than the temporalis muscle for jaw movement and makes greater use of its molars. Analysis of stomach contents revealed that while the Tsushima leopard cat primarily fed on small mammals that could be swallowed in 2–3 pieces, the Iriomote cat also fed on snakes, lizards, and large frogs that required multiple cuts to swallow. Based on these findings, it was concluded that the Tsushima leopard cat uses its temporal muscles to employ its sharp canines to quickly kill fast-moving small mammals, whereas the Iriomote cat has more highly developed masseter muscles for forcefully pushing up on its prey to chew large prey animals captured with its large carnassial teeth. It was also suggested that the Taiwan leopard cat exhibits a chewing style intermediate between those of the two populations.
（要旨集 p.297）
PG3-15
Do diet shifts reshape snake heads? - Head morphological variation in island and urban populations of Elaphe quadrivirgata
食性変化に伴うシマヘビの頭部形態変異の検討
Kohei Kobayashi*1, Harue Abe2
In insular environments, changes in biotic communities and the resulting specialized interspecific interactions are known to drive shifts in morphological and ecological traits. Similarly, urban environments may function as “ecological islands” due to habitat fragmentation and anthropogenic resource conditions. However, the extent to which diet shifts associated with such environmental changes influence morphological divergence in predators remains unclear. The Japanese endemic snake, Elaphe quadrivirgata, is a generalist predator that primarily feeds on frogs in typical habitats. In contrast, insular populations consume fish, whereas urban populations utilize different prey resources such as turtle eggs and lizards, depending on the region. In this study, we examined head shape variation among rural, insular, and urban populations exhibiting different dietary preferences using geometric morphometrics based on 18 cranial landmarks. Shape variation was quantified using multivariate analyses to assess population-level divergence. The results revealed significant differences in head morphology among regions, with insular populations exhibiting distinct morphological characteristics compared to other groups. Moreover, morphological differences were also detected among populations within urban environments, suggesting fine-scale spatial heterogeneity even within anthropogenically modified habitats. These findings indicate that head shape divergence is associated not only with broad environmental differences but also with variation in local resource use. This study provides new insights into how dietary shifts promote phenotypic diversification in predators by comparing island and urban environments as contrasting forms of ecological isolation.
（要旨集 p.298）
PG3-16
Resource Subsidy in the Sky Islands of the Northern Japanese Alps: An Alpine Ecosystem Supported by Aphids
日本アルプス高山生態系をアブラムシが支える資源流入
Ishii Yamano1, Daichi Iijima2, Masashi Murakami*3
Anthropogenic climate change is profoundly altering ecosystem dynamics, especially across ecosystem boundaries at where trophic connections link adjacent ecosystems. Alpine ecosystems, functioning as isolated "sky islands" with unique biodiversity, could be particularly vulnerable to these disruptions. Many alpine consumers such as birds and arthropods predators heavily rely on resource subsidies from surrounding lower-elevation forests. In the Northern Japanese Alps, this critical cross-ecosystem subsidy is mediated by the massive transfer of winged subalpine aphids. However, global warming threatens to destabilize these transfers, potentially triggering cascading effects on alpine food webs. While these insect subsidies are vulnerable to both the direct impacts of warming and indirect phenological shifts, few studies have comprehensively evaluated these dual effects. To address this, we investigated the subalpine aphid species Euceraphis ontakensis and E. caerulescens on Mt. Norikura, Japan. These aphids serve as a primary food source for alpine birds and arthropods, playing a crucial role in supporting the alpine ecosystem. We conducted three-year field surveys and laboratory experiments to assess how temperature and the phenology of their host plant (Betula ermanii) influence aphid populations. Our field surveys revealed that both aphid and host plant phenological events were primarily driven by temperature. Aphid abundance increased at temperatures above 6 °C but showed a marked decline when temperatures exceeded 13 °C. Laboratory experiments confirmed that aphid survival decreased significantly above 12 °C. Furthermore, while aphid locomotor activity increased with temperature, it reached a plateau at approximately 19 °C and then decreased. Conversely, rearing experiments demonstrated that aphids could utilize host plant resources across all leaf developmental stages, suggesting a broad phenological window and a low likelihood of a phenological mismatch with their host. These findings indicate that these subalpine aphids are highly sensitive to thermal stress rather than host plant mismatches. If global warming progresses, rising temperatures may directly cause a spatial contraction of their distribution range and a severe decline in aphid abundance. This would drastically reduce the resource subsidy flying into the "sky islands," undermining the foundation of the alpine food web. Given the complexity of cross-ecosystem interactions, understanding these direct thermal constraints is crucial for predicting the future of biodiversity and ecosystem functioning in unique alpine environments under climate change.
（要旨集 p.299）
PG3-17
Two-decade changes in the relationships among structural diversity, species diversity, and aboveground biomass in evergreen forests on Okinawa Island, southwestern Japan
沖縄島常緑林の構造・種多様性と現存量の20年変化
Tsutomu Enoki*1
We assessed the effects of tree species diversity and aboveground structural diversity on biomass in an evergreen broad-leaved forest in northern Okinawa Island and examined changes over a 20-year period. We measured the diameter at breast height (DBH) of trees with a diameter of 4 cm or greater within 20 m × 20 m plots established at 70 locations in the Yona Field at the University of the Ryukyus. In this study, we analyzed measurement data from 1980 and 2000. In 1980, stand density, mean DBH and total basal area (BA) across all plots were 7,342 trees/ha, 7.3 cm, and 41.8 m²/ha, respectively. By 2000, stand density had decreased (4,406 trees/ha), while mean DBH (10.2 cm) and total BA (49.0 m2/ha) had increased. The skewness of the DBH distribution decreased, as the abundance of small-diameter trees observed in 1980 declined due to growth and mortality. Overall, the stand is considered to have been moving toward maturity. This change may reflect recovery from natural disturbances, such as typhoons, and human disturbances, such as logging, that occurred prior to 1980. We used structural equation modeling (SEM) to evaluate the effects of stem density, species richness, species diversity, the number of DBH classes, and DBH diversity on BA. In 1980, BA was primarily explained by stem density and DBH diversity. However, 20 years later, standardized regression coefficients of stem density and DBH diversity had decreased, suggesting that the relative importance of stem density and DBH diversity had diminished. This indicates that the determinants of BA may have shifted toward factors other than stem density and DBH diversity. Although median species richness and species diversity remained similar, the number of plots with high species richness decreased, likely due in part to reduced stem density. In contrast, the number of DBH classes and DBH diversity increased; however, variation in DBH diversity among plots declined. These indicate that the contribution of DBH diversity to BA has decreased. The reduced variation in DBH diversity among plots may suggest that the stand structure was converging toward a specific state.
（要旨集 p.300）
PG3-19
Spinescence variation in Smilax china on the Izu Islands in relation to leaf mottling
伊豆諸島サルトリイバラの棘変異と葉班の関係
Yumiko Higuchi*1, Takuro Ito2, Shoki Murakami3
Islands often differ from their mainland counterparts in environmental and faunal conditions, which can influence the evolution of multiple plant traits. Reduced expression of presumably costly defensive traits, such as spinescence and secondary metabolites, has been considered an example of the "island syndrome" in plants. However, recent studies indicate that empirical evidence for this pattern is not as consistent as previously thought and remains debated. Loss or reduction of spinescence has also been suggested in a few plant species on the Izu Islands of Japan. Smilax china (Smilacaceae) is a vine species widely distributed in East and Southeast Asia, including Japan. Although S. china usually bears prickles on its stems, unprickled or weakly prickled individuals have been observed on the Miura Peninsula, the Izu Islands, and the Ogasawara Islands. Yet, it is unclear whether spinescence reduction happens quantitatively in natural populations and whether it is related to other potential defensive traits. In this study, we quantify spinescence variations among field-collected young shoots of S. china in the Izu Islands and nearby mainland areas. We measure total phenolics and condensed tannins as putative chemical defensive traits. We also focus on leaf mottling on young leaves of S. china, as leaf mottling in some plants has been proposed to function as a visual defense signal against herbivores. We further infer population genetic structure using MIG-seq to assess genetic differentiation in S. china around the Izu Islands. According to preliminary field data in June 2025 from two mainland areas (the Izu and Miura peninsulas) and two island areas (Izu Oshima and Hachijo islands), both island populations showed lower incidences of spinescence and leaf mottling than the mainland populations. Total phenolics and condensed tannins showed less clear relationships with spinescence than did leaf mottling and showed greater variability, but tended to be lower in plants from Hachijo Island. Although further investigations, such as increasing the number of geographic populations and conducting a common garden experiment, are necessary to confirm the pattern, our observations may help better understand the diversity of S. china on the Izu Islands.
（要旨集 p.302）
PG3-20
Pollination mutualism of the native Veronica undulata in Japan
在来ミズトラノオの送粉共生と外来種との競合
Motoharu Hayase1, Fu Takayanagi1, Misaki Ohta1, Ayami Satou1, Shunsuke Serizawa2, Shizuka Tsuneki*1
Veronica undulata, a native annual aquatic plant of the family Plantaginaceae, is a common emergent species inhabiting wetlands and stream margins in Japan. However, owing to habitat degradation and the impacts of the introduced species Veronica anagallis-aquatica, its populations have declined in recent years, and it is currently listed as Near Threatened. Understanding its life history is therefore important from a conservation perspective. To investigate the current status of hybridization and ecological competition within mixed populations in Aichi Prefecture, we examined growth stage, stem height, and genome size using flow cytometry. In addition, we studied the behavior of floral visitors and the life history of associated insects in two populations consisting solely of V. undulata. Our results suggested that the introduced V. anagallis-aquatica flowered, fruited, and attained greater plant height earlier than the native V. undulata. Relative nuclear DNA content was measured for 40 individuals of V. anagallis-aquatica, 138 individuals of V. undulata, and 67 putative hybrids identified based on external morphology. Among the putative hybrids, 65 individuals were identified as first-generation (F₁) hybrids, two individuals were classified as later-generation hybrid descendants, and three individuals of V. undulata were determined to be novoploid. Furthermore, frequent flower visitation by hoverflies of the genera Sphaerophoria and Melanostoma was observed in two populations composed exclusively of V. undulata. Pollen grains were found attached to the bodies of visiting insects. We also observed mating and oviposition behavior of hoverflies on V. undulata. Larvae collected from the plants were identified using molecular methods. Of the 71 larvae successfully analyzed, 52 individuals were identified as belonging to the genus Sphaerophoria, whereas 19 individuals belonged to the genus Melanostoma. These findings suggest the presence of both ecological competition and genetic disturbance through hybridization between the native V. undulata and the introduced V. anagallis-aquatica. In addition, V. undulata appears to benefit not only from pollination services provided by floral visitors but also from biological control of aphids, as pollinators complete their life cycle within V. undulata stands and their larvae prey upon aphid pests. This study highlights a multifaceted mutualistic relationship between V. undulata and its hoverfly visitors, encompassing both pollination and biological pest control.

To conduct population genetic analyses, we extracted data from 507 SNP loci. The analyses revealed no significant variations in genetic diversity indices among populations. Although some genetic variations among populations were found, no clear genetic differentiation between main and oceanic island populations was detected. Moreover, no significant genetic isolation by distance was found. Analysis of four floral traits (petal length, corolla tube length, and pistil/stamen length) showed that mainland populations had significantly smaller flowers than island populations, with significant trait differences between the two groups. Furthermore, trait differences between population pairs were not correlated with the degree of neutral genetic differentiation, suggesting a dissociation between phenotypic traits and neutral loci. These results suggest that the floral enlargement observed in C. soldanella on the Izu Archipelago reflects independent and rapid adaptation of floral traits on each island to the oceanic island environment characterised by the predominance of small bees.

Sado Island is located approximately 32 km off the coast of mainland Honshu, Japan. Although close to the mainland, no evidence of a historical land bridge connection with Honshu has been found, and the island has remained isolated for long periods. This study focused on Sado Island and the adjacent mainland region of Niigata Prefecture (Echigo). Several plant species are common on Sado Island but exhibit restricted distributions in the Echigo region. Many of these species are centered in western Japan or on the Pacific side, and Niigata lies near the margin of their ranges. We examined whether these contrasting distribution patterns can be explained by environmental conditions, colonization history, or both. We also aimed to identify the spatial scales of environmental conditions important for species distributions. Twelve species, including Daphne jezoensis, Syringa reticulata, Spiraea nipponica var. nipponica, Acer ginnala var. aidzuense, and Viburnum sieboldii var. obovatifolium, were analyzed. Environmental conditions were classified into local topographic-hydrological conditions at the 50-m scale (slope, curvature, topographic wetness index, and distance from rivers) and regional climatic conditions at the 1-km scale (air temperature, precipitation, snow depth, distance from the coast, and topographic heterogeneity). Environmental conditions at occurrence sites were compared. Daphne jezoensis was characterized by cold and snowy environments, whereas Acer ginnala var. aidzuense was characterized by moist habitats. Spiraea nipponica var. nipponica and Syringa reticulata were associated with distinctive environmental conditions at both the 1-km and 50-m scales. Relationships with environmental conditions were less clear for Viburnum sieboldii var. obovatifolium and Cornus macrophylla. These results suggest that species differ in their relationships with environmental conditions and that the spatial scales important for species distributions also vary among species. Furthermore, some distributions could not be explained solely by environmental conditions, suggesting that colonization history should also be considered. On Sado Island, environmental elements such as ridges, valleys, wetlands, and cliffs are concentrated within a small area, whereas similar environments are distributed more widely in the Echigo region. Therefore, Sado Island may represent a compressed environmental mosaic of mainland Honshu and provide suitable habitats for species near the margins of their distribution ranges in a limited area. Such a compressed environmental mosaic may contribute to the contrasting distribution patterns between Sado Island and the Echigo region. Future studies incorporating intermediate spatial scales (e.g., 250 m) will allow a more detailed evaluation of the spatial structure of environmental mosaics and their relationship with colonization history.

The species most likely evolved from a common ancestor with T. diversifolia rather than originating directly from T. diversifolia itself. Overall, from a genetic perspective T. ulleungensis can be considered as an extremely isolated peripheral Tsuga population, the last remnant of a once more widespread species that occurred around the Japan Sea. Sagami Bay as an Evolutionary Terminal: Adaptation and Diversification of Tropical Fishes in Temperate Waters

Despite its openness, Sagami Bay, located along the Pacific coast of the Japanese Archipelago and at the terminal region of the Kuroshio Current, is home to several endemic marine fishes. This study investigates the evolutionary mechanisms underlying such endemism by integrating taxonomy and phylogenomic analyses. We examine the Gunnellichthys monostigma complex (Gobiiformes: Microdesmidae) as a model, as its population in Sagami Bay exhibit morphological discontinuities and habitat specialization that differ from those of its tropical relatives. Historical fluctuations in the Kuroshio Current likely produced repeated cycles of colonization, overwintering, mortality and selective persistence, enabling cold-tolerant individuals to survive climatic bottlenecks. We propose that Sagami Bay functions as an “evolutionary terminal,” where tropical fishes undergo long-term filtering and divergence. This framework provides new insights into the formation of marine biodiversity associated with islands and the evolutionary consequences of oceanographic variability.

APL4関連
Islands as natural laboratories for understanding biodiversity, ecological complexity, and global change
島を自然の実験室とした生物間相互作用ネットワーク研究
Anna Traveset
Biodiversity is declining globally at an unprecedented rate, and islands are among the most threatened environments on Earth. Although they occupy only a small fraction of the planet’s surface, islands contain nearly one-third of the world’s biodiversity hotspots and account for about 80% of documented extinctions, most involving endemic species. Yet much of their biodiversity remains poorly understood, especially the complex interaction networks that have evolved under geographic isolation, limited species pools, and strong evolutionary pressures. Understanding these interactions is essential for predicting the consequences of biodiversity loss and informing conservation strategies. In this talk, I present recent research conducted across diverse island systems—including the Balearic and Canary Islands, Galapagos, Seychelles, Ogasawara, and other archipelagos worldwide—to show how islands serve as exceptional natural laboratories for studying ecological and evolutionary processes. Rather than viewing biodiversity simply as a collection of species, these studies highlight ecological interactions as the foundation of ecosystem functioning. A central focus is the use of multilayer ecological networks, an emerging framework that integrates multiple interaction types—including pollination, herbivory, seed dispersal, plant–fungal associations, plant–nematode interactions, and predator–prey relationships—within a single analytical structure. By linking ecological functions traditionally studied separately, this approach reveals previously hidden dimensions of ecosystem organization. Across a wide range of island systems, multilayer analyses consistently identify a small number of multifunctional keystone species that connect otherwise separate ecological processes and contribute disproportionately to community cohesion and resilience. Ecosystem stability frequently depends on these species because they link several functions simultaneously, irrespective of their abundance. The research also highlights the uniqueness of island biodiversity. Studies of root-associated fungi reveal highly distinct biogeographic assemblages among distant archipelagos, while global analyses of soil nematodes show that host plants exert strong and consistent influences on belowground communities. Together, these findings emphasize the importance of species interactions in generating ecological differentiation and shaping evolutionary trajectories in isolated environments. At the same time, the studies demonstrate the pervasive influence of human activities, particularly biological invasions and habitat modification. Introduced species can restructure pollination, seed-dispersal, and other interaction networks, reducing the ecological importance of native species and increasing dependence on a few generalist invaders. In Ogasawara, multiple invaders can act synergistically, causing cascading effects across trophic levels and altering ecosystem functioning. Conversely, restoration efforts, particularly in Galapagos, show that invasive-species removal can re-establish native interaction networks and recover key ecosystem processes. Overall, this work demonstrates that island biodiversity is defined as much by interactions as by species themselves. By uncovering hidden ecological architecture and the mechanisms sustaining ecosystem functioning, multilayer network approaches provide powerful tools for understanding, conserving, and restoring island ecosystems in an era of rapid environmental change.
（要旨集 p.7）

AS5A-01目安 10:20関連
A review of island biology in the Anthropocene
人新世における島嶼生物学パターンの総説
島嶼生物学の総説、系統地理的視点を含むが抽象的
Thomas J. Matthews*1,2, Ferran Sayol3,4,5, Filipa C. Soares6,7,8, Julia H. Heinen9, Osanna Chu1, Natàlia Martínez-Rubio10,11, Joseph P. Wayman1, Søren Faurby12,13
Islands have long been foundational to the development of ecological and evolutionary theory, serving as model systems for studying patterns of biodiversity. However, pervasive anthropogenic impacts ‒ particularly species extinctions and introductions ‒ have significantly altered island ecosystems, complicating inferences drawn from contemporary data. Here, we review how these human-driven changes have reshaped key biodiversity patterns on islands, including patterns of species richness, community composition, evolutionary dynamics, and species interaction networks. We show that many current ecological and evolutionary patterns observed on islands reflect not just natural processes but also a legacy of human-induced change spanning millennia. Extinction and introduction processes ‒ often non-random and trait-dependent ‒ have altered classic island biodiversity patterns such as the species‒ area and species‒isolation relationships, driven biotic homogenisation across islands, obscured the prevalence of certain island syndromes and modified the structure of island species interaction networks. Approaches that incorporate palaeoecological and molecular evidence, along with improved databases and modelling techniques, can help better reconstruct pre-human biodiversity baselines on islands.

AS5A-02目安 10:35
First human arrival and activities on 1,400 islands globally and their impacts on biodiversity
1400島における人類初到達と生物多様性影響のデータベース構築
Julia Heinen*1, 2
Islands hold roughly 20% of the world's species but account for more than 60% of historical vertebrate extinctions. Across nearly every island where the record is good enough to test, the turning point for native biotas is the same: the first arrival of people and the species they took with them. Yet the global picture of when humans reached islands, who arrived, and what they brought has been patchy and Pacific-dominated, leaving conservation baselines and reconstructions of "natural" island communities resting on uneven ground. The ArchaeoGLOBE Islands database, compiled with more than one hundred archaeologists, provides the first global, temporally resolved record of human colonisation, species introductions, and native extinctions across 1,400 islands worldwide, spanning all major island types from continental shelf to oceanic volcanic, ancient continental fragments, atolls, and raised coralline. Subsistence technology (foraging vs. farming) shaped not only where and when people settled, but what they introduced: foragers arrived with few commensals, while food producers carried full domesticate and commensal assemblages, with food production a near-prerequisite for permanent settlement on remote oceanic islands and atolls. From first arrival, ecological transformation followed a consistent sequence: introduction of commensals and domesticates, loss of native vertebrates, and a restructuring of island communities in which introductions, not extinctions alone, drove functional remodelling. Pinning the timing of first arrival globally is a prerequisite for any meaningful pre-human baseline, and provides the temporal framework against which functional change, homogenisation, and biodiversity loss on islands can be assessed.

Therefore, we tested for changes in vegetation trait composition following human arrival in Macaronesia. We reconstructed functional composition and similarity from trait spaces during pre-human times, first human presence and European colonisation based on assemblage-weighted trait means inferred from pollen proportions. We evaluated the importance of climatic and human drivers by formulating competing generalised linear mixed models of temporal trends of individual trait variables. The trait spaces of all archipelagos changed with ongoing human influence. In the Azores and Canaries, a shift towards shorter plants with high leaf nitrogen content coincided with declines of endemic trees. Variation in functional composition declined across Macaronesia after European colonisation, but functional similarity increased only marginally between the Azores and Cabo Verde. Using pollen-defined ecological zones as a measure of vegetation persistence and turnover, we investigate how rates of ecosystem reorganisation have changed through time. Zone durations progressively shortened towards the present, while the frequency of vegetation reorganisations increased, indicating accelerating ecological turnover across island ecosystems through the Holocene. These trends are evident across multiple island bioregions, with particularly high rates of ecological turnover in Arctic islands and weaker but comparable increases in temperate and tropical systems. Against this long-term baseline, many islands experienced vegetation compositions during the Late Holocene that have no clear analogue in the preceding record. These reorganisations are associated with shifts in plant community composition, including declines in woody vegetation, reduced canopy dominance, and increasing representation of herbaceous taxa. Our results indicate a widespread shift from relatively persistent vegetation assemblages to increasingly frequent ecosystem reorganisation. Despite biogeographical differences, accelerating ecological turnover emerges as a common feature of island ecosystem dynamics. Ferran Sayol*1,2,3, Maria W. Jorgensen4, Natàlia Martínez-Rubio5,6, Roberto Rozzi7,8, Ana M. C. Santos9, Judit Rodrigo5,6, Sandra Nogué5,6, Oriol Lapiedra5, Thomas J. Matthews4

To quantify the cumulative footprint of these changes, we first developed a global database of extirpated (extinct) and introduced (non-native) birds and mammals on islands. For 64 island assemblages worldwide, we compiled records of extinct, extant and non-native species from published literature, fossil and archaeological evidence, and existing biodiversity databases, allowing each island community to be reconstructed both before and after human arrival. We calculate beta diversity across three spatial scales (within archipelago, within region and globally) and partition the contribution to overall beta-diversity change by taxon and process, distinguishing how the extinction and introduction of birds and mammals contributes to either an increase or decrease in between-island compositional similarity. Across all scales, we found an overall homogenisation (i.e., increase in island similarity). Only at the archipelago scale we found two archipelagos with net differentiation (i.e. decreased island similarity). While at the global scale we see a somewhat equal contribution of birds and mammals to homogenisation and the majority of homogenisation from introduction of non-native species, the results are less straightforward at smaller scales. With decreasing scales we see a lot more variability between sites of both taxa and process. In conclusion, the almost ubiquitous homogenisation seen here is cause for concern. Although archipelagos vary in their response to human impact, islands worldwide are converging in composition, steadily eroding the distinctive biodiversity that has long defined island life.

Accumulating extinction debt on islands under future sea-level rise
将来の海面上昇による島嶼植物の絶滅債務を予測
Julian Schrader* 1, David Coleman 1
Sea-level rise (SLR) is expected to become one of the most pervasive threats to coastal ecosystems over the coming centuries, yet its consequences for island biodiversity remain poorly quantified. Islands harbour a disproportionate share of global plant diversity, including many endemic species with restricted distributions and limited opportunities for range shifts. Here, we combine global projections of sea-level rise with a database of vascular plant assemblages from more than 1,400 islands to assess the biodiversity consequences of future land loss. We first quantify changes in island area under multiple sea-level rise scenarios extending to 2300 and evaluate how these changes vary across islands globally. We then estimate the potential extinction debt associated with area loss using species‒area relationships and identify islands where plant assemblages may be particularly vulnerable to future declines. Finally, we assess the exposure of protected areas to inundation and examine how the loss of protected habitat may further increase risks to island biodiversity. Our analyses provide a global assessment of the potential impacts of sea-level rise on island plant diversity. By linking projected changes in island area to biodiversity responses, we identify regions where extinction debt may accumulate and where conservation challenges are likely to intensify. The resulting datasets will support efforts to prioritize monitoring, conservation planning, and adaptation strategies for island ecosystems under future climate change.

Passive acoustic monitoring of migratory birds across an archipelago: roles of stepping-stone pathways and direct immigration in community dynamics
伊豆諸島での渡り鳥の踏み石的移動を音響モニタリングで解明
日本列島(伊豆諸島)の島間連結性と生物地理学的手法
Mitsuki Funahashi*1, Tsukasa Taniguchi2, Takashi Kamijo2, Daichi Iijima2
Island biogeography theory has emphasized connectivity between mainland source areas and islands, yet connectivity among neighboring islands may also shape insular biological communities. Species use islands close to the mainland not only as breeding sites but also as migratory stopover sites, with these islands facilitating movement through archipelagos as stepping-stones. However, the island characteristics that promote their use as stepping-stones, and interspecific differences in such movement patterns, remain poorly understood. Here, we elucidate the spatiotemporal movement patterns of migratory birds within an archipelago using passive acoustic monitoring in the Izu Islands, Japan. Recordings were conducted from March to June 2025 at two to five forest sites on each of seven islands: Oshima, Niijima, Kozu, Miyake, Hachijo, Hachijo-kojima and Aogashima. Dynamic occupancy models for three focal species̶the Ijimaʼs leaf warbler Phylloscopus ijimae, Narcissus flycatcher Ficedula narcissina and Lesser cuckoo Cuculus poliocephalus̶revealed marked interspecific variation in movement patterns. The Ijimaʼs leaf warbler, which breeds mainly in the southern Izu Islands, maintained high occupancy probabilities on Miyake and islands farther south after April. In contrast, occupancy probability increased temporarily on Kozu, a northern island, suggesting that northern islands may function not only as breeding sites but also as migratory stopover sites. The Narcissus flycatcher, whose main breeding range is on the mainland, showed a transient increase in occupancy probability in mid-May only on the northern islands closer to the mainland, indicating the use of these islands as stopover sites. By contrast, the Lesser cuckoo, which breeds across all islands, exhibited an almost synchronous increase in occupancy probability across the archipelago in mid-May and subsequently maintained high occupancy, suggesting that this species may arrive directly on each island rather than moving through the archipelago via stepping-stone pathway. At the community level, analyses using βsim, an index of species turnover, showed that turnover frequency tended to decrease with increasing isolation, indicating that isolated islands maintained stable composition while less isolated islands showed more frequent compositional change during migratory passage. These patterns suggest stepping-stones are primarily located closer to the mainland. Together, our results provide empirical evidence for inter-island connectivity during migration, clarifying that proximity to the mainland enables stepping-stone function and that movement strategies reflect species' breeding distributions. Conserving insular biodiversity, including island-endemic species such as the Ijimaʼs leaf warbler, will require comprehensive conservation strategies across entire archipelagos, rather than management focused on particular islands, with explicit consideration of migratory stopover sites.
（要旨集 p.63）

Does variation in predator communities shape learning abilities in island lizards?
伊豆諸島のオカダトカゲで捕食者相と学習能力の関係を検証
伊豆諸島のトカゲ、系統地理でなく行動進化が主題
Ryotaroh Yanagihara*1, Teppei Jono1
Behavioral plasticity enables organisms to adjust to rapid environmental changes, with learning serving as one of its underlying mechanisms. Because learning is expected to be costly, learning ability may decline under stable environments. However, how learning evolves under different ecological conditions remains poorly understood. Isolated natural populations with varying environmental stability provide an ideal opportunity to address this question. We focused on Okada's five-lined skink (Plestiodon latiscutatus), native to the Izu Peninsula and the Izu Islands, Japan. Previous studies have shown that P. latiscutatus populations are exposed to three major predator types: birds, snakes, and mammals. Predator assemblages vary among islands, ranging from islands with only avian predators to islands with all three predator types. Hatchlings typically possess a conspicuous blue tail that deflects predator attacks towards the autotomizable tail, increasing escape probability. Previous studies have also shown that the tail coloration varies among islands in association with differences in predator assemblages. In simple predator environments, individuals are repeatedly exposed to similar predator stimuli, whereas in diverse predator environments, the stimuli likely change rapidly. Thus, populations with different predator assemblages may vary in learning ability to adjust antipredator behaviors. We hypothesized that predator diversity drives divergence in learning ability and behavioral plasticity. To test this, we conducted a learning experiment using simulated predator attacks. We collected individuals from four populations spanning a gradient of predator diversity. In each trial, lizards were presented with a choice between a safe and an unsafe refuge following a simulated attack. Selecting the unsafe refuge resulted in an additional stimulus as punishment, after which the trial continued. Learning performance was quantified by the number of incorrect choices. From the beginning of the experiment, individuals from diverse predator assemblages made fewer incorrect choices, with learning curves remaining flat across trials. By contrast, populations from simpler predator assemblages initially made significantly more errors but progressively improved, reaching comparable error rates to other populations. Although our hypothesis was partially supported, we found no clear evidence that the population only with avian predators had lower learning ability. However, initial error differences indicate divergence in immediate behavioral flexibility in response to predator stimulation. These findings highlight predator diversity as a key driver shaping the evolution of behavioral plasticity.

Hiroto Terashima*1, Shun Ito2, Takashi Kamijo1
Island ecosystems are widely recognized as global biodiversity hotspots, and their conservation is considered highly important. Soil fauna, which form the foundation of island food web structures, serve not only as a prey resource for terrestrial animals but also underpin island ecosystems fundamentally through various ecosystem functions. However, soil fauna can be affected by predation and competition from invasive species, sometimes resulting in marked declines in abundance and shifts in taxonomic composition. Clarifying the status of soil fauna communities on islands and elucidating how their composition changes in the presence of invasive species, therefore provides important insight for the conservation of island ecosystems. The Izu Archipelago consists of oceanic islands located in the Pacific Ocean, each of which has developed its own distinct ecosystem. Furthermore, due to differences in the extent of invasive species establishment, the Izu archipelago exhibit food web structures with different top predators from island to island. Hachijo-kojima is the only uninhabited island in the archipelago that has remained almost entirely free of invasive species, retaining a typical Izu Archipelago ecosystem. In contrast, the neighboring Hachijo-jima has been invaded by multiple invasive species, raising concerns about their significant impact on the soil fauna community. Comparing the soil fauna communities of Hachijo-jima and Hachijo-kojima therefore makes it possible to indirectly assess the impact of invasive species on soil fauna. This presentation focuses on Hachijo-kojima and Hachijo-jima, two geographically adjacent islands that nonetheless exhibit markedly different food web structures, and compares the diversity and taxonomic composition of their soil fauna. Soil fauna were collected using the hand-sorting method, with both the litter layer and the surface soil layer sampled. Soil fauna were identified to at least the order level, and to the species level where possible. A comparison of the soil fauna communities of Hachijo-jima and Hachijo-kojima revealed distinct differences in both abundance and taxonomic composition. Land snails in particular differed markedly between the two islands. On Hachijo-kojima, numerous small and micro land snail species, including endemic and rare species, were confirmed, and land snails accounted for a high proportion of the overall taxonomic composition. On Hachijo-jima, by contrast, large species and non-native land snails were conspicuously present, and land snails accounted for a low proportion of the overall taxonomic composition. These results indicate that the soil fauna of the Izu Archipelago is highly diverse, while also suggesting that this diversity is under threat from invasive species.

Kazuki, Higashitani*1, Kiyoto Sawada2 and Takashi Kamijo2
Introduced mammalian predators are among the major drivers of biodiversity loss on islands because island species often evolve in the absence of mammalian carnivores and consequently exhibit limited anti-predator responses. The Japanese weasel (Mustela itatsi) is a mustelid endemic to Japan, with a natural distribution on the Japanese mainland and nearby islands. During the twentieth century, it was intentionally introduced to several islands of the Izu Archipelago for rodent control and is now regarded as a domestic invasive species. Established populations occur on Miyake-jima, Toshima, Hachijo-jima, and Aogashima. Following their introduction, predation on native fauna became a major concern, particularly on Miyake-jima, where declines of the Izu Islands sub-endemic Okada's blue-tailed skink (Plestiodon latiscutatus), the only native reptile of the islands, and the endemic Izu thrush (Turdus celaenops) have been reported. Because the islands differ substantially in size, vegetation, habitat structure, and predator communities, the ecological impacts of introduced weasels are expected to vary among islands. To evaluate the feeding habits of introduced Japanese weasels, we analyzed 1,513 fecal samples collected from four islands of the Izu Archipelago. Samples from Miyake-jima were collected between December 2019 and November 2020, whereas samples from the other three islands were collected between July 2023 and May 2025. Prey items were identified by microscopic examination, and statistical analyses were conducted to examine seasonal changes in prey occurrence and compare prey composition among islands. Prey composition showed two broad patterns: Miyake-jima, Hachijo-jima, and Aogashima were characterized by insect-dominated diets, whereas Toshima showed greater reliance on vertebrate prey. Beetles and cockroaches were the dominant insect groups on most islands, while birds and mammals became important prey on Toshima during winter and spring. These differences in prey occurrence were also confirmed by statistical analyses. On Miyake-jima, comparisons with previous dietary studies revealed a dietary shift. Okada's blue-tailed skinks, which were major prey in 1984, became rare in 1993 and were absent from the present study. In contrast, insects increased further in importance, and introduced weasels frequently consumed invasive insects, including the outdoor cockroach species Opisthoplatia orientalis. These findings suggest that Japanese weasels are opportunistic generalists that flexibly exploit locally available prey resources and that invasive insects may facilitate the persistence of weasel populations by providing an additional food resource.

Invasive species on islands can severely affect biodiversity, while island environments may also drive rapid phenotypic change as invaders adapt to novel conditions. The Eastern Japanese common toad (Bufo formosus) has recently invaded several regions of Japan as an invasive species. On Hokkaido and Sado Island, range expansion has been reported, and the speciesʼ predatory behavior and their parotoid gland toxin strongly affect native ecosystems. In the Izu archipelago, the species has invaded Oshima, Nii-jima, Miyake-jima, and Hachijo-jima Islands, but its ecological impacts and phenotypic changes remain poorly understood. This study therefore investigated the ecological traits of B. formosus on four islands and examined whether it differs among islands, through distribution surveys, relative density surveys, and morphometric measurements. For the distribution survey, route censuses were conducted and locations were recorded. The occurrence data were aggregated into 100 m × 100 m grid cells, and species distribution models were built using MaxEnt for Oshima and Miyake-jima. These two models were then used to predict the potential distribution across the entire Izu archipelago. For the relative density survey, 9‒13 survey points were established on each island, and the number of individuals encountered and the distance searched during a 10-minute search were recorded; the encounter rate (individuals encountered per km), used as an index of relative population density, was compared among islands. For morphometric measurements, body length (SVL), parotoid gland length and width, and body mass were measured. SVL, parotoid gland area standardized by SVL, and a body condition index calculated from body mass and SVL were then compared among islands. The distribution survey showed that B. formosus was widely distributed on all four islands. The MaxEnt models indicated high potential distribution probability on both island and forest area percentage and elevation were important. In addition, although the two models showed different potential distribution maps when applied to the entire Izu archipelago, they appeared to complement one another in explaining for the occurrence records of B. formosus. Encounter rate was highest on Miyake-jima. Morphological comparisons revealed differences among islands, with individuals on Oshima having the largest SVL and parotoid gland area. These results suggest that B. formosus has the potential to invade and establish throughout the Izu archipelago, and that its morphology may be changing following island invasion. Shusei Koga1*, Yusuke Magome1, Rio Obata1, Daichi Iijima1, Takashi Kamijo1, Kiyoto Sawada1
Invasive species can profoundly alter trophic interactions on oceanic islands. Although invasive prey may provide novel food resources for native predators, toxic invasive species can instead cause poisoning and population declines. Some predators nevertheless exploit toxic prey by selectively consuming less toxic body parts, yet the extent to which such behavior allows native predators to benefit from abundant toxic invaders remains poorly understood. On Miyake-jima, an oceanic island in the Izu archipelago of Japan, the Eastern-Japanese common toad Bufo formosus has been introduced and now occurs at high density. The species produces toxic secretions concentrated around the parotoid glands, and its roadkill is abundant along the islandʼs main roads. We investigated how native scavengers use this novel toxic food resource during May‒July and September 2025 and February 2026. We recorded temporal changes in roadkill abundance along the islandʼs approximately 30 km main road to estimate the proportion removed before noon and by sunset. We also placed toad carcasses in an open site adjacent to forest and used camera traps to identify scavengers and quantify carcass use and feeding behavior. Feeding locations were classified as the head, trunk or limbs, and differences between adult and juvenile predators were evaluated. Scavenging birds were additionally observed directly on roads. Of 105 toad roadkills recorded, 96% removed before noon and 99% by sunset. The camera-trap and the observation in the road revealed that the large-billed crow Corvus macrorhynchos was the only species observed feeding on toad carcasses. Crows predominantly consumed the relatively non-toxic limbs and frequently accessed carcasses from the ventral side. Adults showed these selective handling patterns more strongly, whereas juveniles consumed the toxin-bearing head more frequently. These findings demonstrate that large-billed crows were the sole observed consumers of this abundant toxic invader and exploited it extensively through selective carcass handling. The age-related differences suggest that efficient exploitation may be strengthened through experience or learning. Rather than acting solely as an ecological threat, the introduced toad has become a frequently exploited and highly predictable food resource for a native island scavenger. More broadly, this case illustrates how behavioral responses by native species can determine whether introduced organisms function primarily as threats, resources or both, thereby reshaping trophic interactions on oceanic islands.

Atsushi Takashima*
Yakushima Island and Okinawa Island, located in Ryukyu Archipelago, are frequently struck by strong typhoons. They also experience heavy rains, leading to sporadic landslides. Cryptomeria japonica forests on Yakushima Island and the subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forests on Okinawa Island are maintained despite disturbances caused by typhoon winds and heavy rains. Cryptomeria japonica forests on Yakushima Island experienced logging activities from the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries. Consequently, the current forests consist of a large number of small diameter individuals that regenerated after logging, interspersed with a small number of large-diameter individuals that escaped logging at the time. Many of these large-diameter individuals are over 1,000 years old. Since the bedrock of Yakushima Island is granite, C. japonica exhibits slow growth due to nutrient-poor soil, but this slow growth results in high resin content, making their trunks resistant to decay. Furthermore, most old-growth C. japonica individuals lost their crown tops, resulting in significantly reduced tree height. Such chemical characteristics of the wood resulting from slow growth, along with the tree's morphological response to strong winds (the breakage of the treetops), enable the longevity of C. japonica on Yakushima Island. The subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forests on Okinawa Island are dominated by Castanopsis sieboldii. This forest also experienced extensive logging between the late 1940s to the 1970s. Currently, patches of mature non-clearcut forest remain scattered across the central mountainous area surrounded by secondary and plantation forests. Typhoons cause severe impacts on these forests. After a strong typhoon in 2012, the total basal area of living stems in a permanent plot established in a mature forest decreased to 80% of pre-disturbance levels in 2017; however, it recovered to 90% in 2025. In contrast, the number of living stems initially decreased to 94% of pre-disturbance levels in 2014; however, it increased to 138% in 2025. The decrease of basal area and the temporary decrease in stem number were primarily caused by the dominant C. sieboldii. Conversely, C. sieboldii also accounted for a large proportion of the subsequent increase in stem number, a process to which regeneration was contributed by sprouts. The mortality and subsequent regeneration of C. sieboldii were highly dynamic after typhoon disturbances. Thus, C. japonica forests on Yakushima Island and the subtropical evergreen broad-leaved forests on Okinawa Island share a common characteristic: both are under effect of the typhoon disturbances, however maintain their forests by establishing unique mechanisms centered on dominant tree species.

Hitoshi Sakio1,2*, Harue Abe2, Motohiro Kawanishi3, Tubasa Endo4
Rhododendron indicum (Satsuki) is a prominent rheophilic shrub that typically establishes specialized populations in high-disturbance riverine habitats like gravel bars and rocky riparian zones. However, anecdotal accounts from mountain guides suggested this species might also inhabit high-altitude mountain environments. To investigate this ecological anomaly, this study examined the geographical distribution of R. indicum across Yakushima Island to verify its presence outside traditional riverine ecosystems and elucidate the underlying mechanisms enabling it to thrive in contrasting habitats. Extensive field surveys confirmed R. indicum is widely distributed from coastal river mouths to upstream areas of major rivers. Overturning conventional ecological assumptions, thriving populations were also discovered on numerous low-altitude mountain summits (locally called "Maedake") below 1,478 meters. On these summits, the species specifically occurs in canopy-free zones characterized by intense direct solar radiation and heavily exposed bedrock. This unique environmental profile structurally mirrors riverine environments, where recurring disturbances suppress tall tree establishment, allowing R. indicum to root within rock crevices. Crucially, the species was entirely absent from the highest central peaks ("Okudake"), as well as from any locations on the Maedake summits that are heavily shaded by dense, mature forests. Comparative measurements of key leaf traits̶length, width, thickness, and petiole dimensions̶revealed distinct morphological differences. Summit leaves were significantly shorter and thicker than riverine ones, serving as an adaptation to withstand violent winds and physiological drought. To evaluate genetic relationships, MIG-seq analysis utilizing genome-wide single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) was conducted. The results demonstrated an extremely low expected heterozygosity (He=0.00432) across all 24 sampled locations. Strikingly, no significant genetic differentiation or population structure was detected between riverine and summit populations, or even among isolated river basins. This lack of genetic divergence conclusively indicates that the observed morphological variations represent a high degree of phenotypic plasticity in response to localized growth conditions, rather than fixed genetic adaptation. Furthermore, this highly uniform genetic structure strongly suggests that current populations across the island underwent a rapid, recent expansion. This expansion likely originated from a single localized southern refuge where a small population managed to survive the devastating Kikai caldera pyroclastic flow approximately 7,300 years ago.

Within this snowy island environment, extreme snowfall acts as a recurrent physical disturbance in cool-temperate montane riparian forests, exerting pressure on tree trunks and branches every winter, and appears capable of generating forest structures found nowhere else. To clarify how extreme snowfall shapes such forests, we compared community composition, forest structure, and growth of dominant tree species between dwarf montane riparian forests under extreme snowfall (maximum snow depth 5 m) and tall-tree montane riparian forests under heavy but less extreme snowfall (maximum snow depth 2 m) in the Tadami region of Japan. Both forest types were dominated by two characteristic species of Japan's cool-temperate montane riparian zone: the high-sprouting Pterocarya rhoifolia and the low-sprouting Aesculus turbinata. Under extreme snowfall, however, the two species showed distinct responses to the added disturbance pressure. P. rhoifolia produced numerous smaller sprout trunks, with a maximum bent trunk length of about 18 m but a height of only 10 m, a strategy that appears to help the stool persist under repeated snow damage. A. turbinata instead grew as a single, creeping trunk, reaching 30 m in length while remaining only about 5 m tall. These results show that although P. rhoifolia and A. turbinata dominate montane riparian forests under both heavy and extreme snowfall, they rely on different strategies̶sprouting, dwarfing, and layering̶ to persist under intensified, chronic snow disturbance. These findings suggest that the extreme snowfall found in parts of the Japanese archipelago maintains montane riparian forests through tree species specifically adapted to withstand recurrent, long-term snow disturbance, representing a distinctive facet of island forest diversity.

Plant‒animal interactions affecting plant reproductive success during post-eruption forest recovery on Miyake-jima Island: The roles of Camellia japonica and Zosterops japonicus
