The Center for Wildlife Conservation of the Tokyo Zoological Park Society (TZPS), which coordinates and oversees conservation activities across Tokyo metropolitan zoos and aquariums, marks its 20th anniversary this year. Since its establishment, the Conservation Center has advanced conservation efforts for wildlife in local habitats, as well as for threatened species both in Japan and overseas. Over the past two decades, we have developed diversified conservation approaches that incorporate in-situ conservation work, collaboration with external organizations, research and studies, and environmental education and outreach to support the long-term survival of threatened species. Our conservation initiatives focusing on island endemic species reflect our sustained commitment and play a fundamental role in zoo- and aquarium-based conservation activities. Key taxa targeted by these efforts include the Lidth’s jay (Garruluslidthi) and Amami spiny rat (Tokudaia osimensis) of Amami Oshima Island; the Miyako grass lizard (Takydromus toyamai) of Miyako Island; the Tsushima leopard cat (Prionailurus bengalensis euptilurus) of Tsushima; and several species native to the Ogasawara Islands, such as the Ogasawara greenfinch (Chloris sinica kittlitzi), the red headed wood pigeon (Columba janthina nitens), and threatened land snails. Through collaboration with the Ministry of the Environment’s Conservation and Breeding Programs and local conservation communities, we maintain viable populations of these island endemic species that can be used to support population reinforcement and reintroduction efforts when needed. Establishing and improving species specific husbandry and breeding techniques has been one of the core pillars of our conservation mission. The biology of those species was often poorly understood, requiring the accumulation of knowledge to build effective conservation strategies. The gradual development of basic husbandry protocols, diet formulations, reproductive management, and veterinary approaches forms the essential foundation for zoo- and aquarium-based conservation programs. In recent years, we have given priority to research activities made possible only under controlled captive conditions. Studies in reproductive biology, behavioral ecology, genetics, and health assessment have generated fundamental insights that inform both in-situ and ex-situ conservation planning. These findings will help fill critical knowledge gaps and strengthen evidence-based decision making within multi-institutional conservation frameworks. Celebrating its 20th anniversary, the Center for Wildlife Conservation continues to integrate zoo - and aquarium-based expertise, collaborative networks, and scientific research to enhance the resilience and recovery of Japan’s island endemic species. We will further develop these approaches to guide future directions in our conservation mission.

In birds, trends like the island rule have been reported for body and bill size, and ecological factors associated with islands have been suggested as potential drivers of these changes. For example, Sittiparus varius had larger bill size in the southern Izu Islands, the Tokara Islands, and Sado Island compared with mainland populations. Notably, Zosterops japonicus exhibited morphological variation associated with island geological origin, with differences in the extent of morphological change among volcanic, limestone, and continental fragment islands relative to mainland populations. In addition, Horornis diphone showed morphological change on an oceanic island, although this pattern was restricted to females. The species distribution models predicted areas of habitat suitability with very limited overlap across Japan, indicating clear spatial separation in predicted suitable areas between the two lineages. Kurihara samples showed sporadic occurrences, while other sites (e.g., Karigane Park, Tome) exhibited minimal seed presence, possibly reflecting differences in habitat use or feeding behaviour. Overall, our results demonstrate that migratory geese in Japan can act as vectors for the dispersal of economically important agricultural weeds, even if dispersal events are infrequent at the level of individual droppings. Given the high abundance, mobility, and field use of geese, such low-frequency events may scale up to meaningful landscape- level connectivity among rice paddies. These findings highlight the need to integrate waterfowl- mediated dispersal into weed management strategies, particularly in regions with intensive rice cultivation and large overwintering goose populations.

Seed dispersal is a fundamental process for the regeneration and persistence of tree populations. Animal-mediated dispersal enables seeds to escape density-dependent mortality near parent trees and colonize distant sites, thereby influencing forest community structure and biodiversity. Scatter-hoarding by rodents and birds is particularly important for tree species producing large seeds or nuts. However, many islands in ocean lack typical scatter-hoarding dispersers, raising the question of how populations of scatter-hoarded tree species persist in such environments. As a mainland comparison, an additional site was established at the Botanical Gardens of Osaka Metropolitan University in Osaka Prefecture. To identify seed users, camera traps were installed on the forest floor for the two trees, and in tree canopies for S. japonicus, to record animal visits, seed handling, and seed removal events. Among these, four canopy species and seven ground-dwelling species physically interacted with seeds. Mucuna gigantea (Fabaceae) is a woody vine distributed throughout tropical and subtropical regions, with the Ryukyu Archipelago representing the northernmost limit of its range. Mucuna flowers are pollinated through "explosive opening," a process in which a visitor presses down the wing petals, exposing the concealed stamens and stigma. Animals that trigger this process are termed “explosive openers”. These results suggest that reduced pollen availability and pollen viability may be factors contributing to the low fruit set of M. gigantea on Okinawa Island.

PA5-07

Yuta Sunakawa*1, Kazuya Takeda2, Ko Mochizuki1, Atsushi Kawakita1
Bulbophyllum boninense is an endemic epiphytic orchid restricted to the oceanic Ogasawara Islands in Japan, a remote archipelago characterized by high endemism and distinctive biota. The orchid genus Bulbophyllum includes many species with fetid floral scents that have been hypothesized to attract sapromyiophilous flies through mimicry of dung or carrion. However, direct observations of pollination remain scarce for most species, particularly among oceanic island endemic species. Behavioral observations indicated differences among fly taxa in their interactions with the flower, particularly in their responses to the mobile labellum, which mechanically trapped visitors and facilitated pollinarium attachment and removal. Furthermore, the extremely low fruit set observed in natural populations may indicate low pollination success in the current island’s ecosystem. Potential explanations include low pollinator abundance, inefficient pollination behavior, and indirect effects of invasive species. Since plant–pollinator interactions significantly influence plant mating success, intra- or interspecific differences in these interactions may reflect species-specific adaptations to the local pollination environment. plant–pollinator interactions significantly influence plant mating success, intra- or interspecific differences in these interactions may reflect species-specific adaptations to the local pollination environment. Some plant species exhibit spatial or temporal segregation of the stigma and the anther within an individual to enhance outcrossing and prevent selfing (e.g., herkogamy or dichogamy). Such mating systems are expected to maximize reproductive success when pollinators are abundant. However, their effectiveness under pollinator-limited conditions remains unclear. Alpinia (Zingiberaceae) flowering plants exhibit flexistyly, a floral mechanism where the style physically moves over time to switch the flower's sexual function. In southern Japan, two native Alpinia species (A. japonica and A. intermedia) occur on various-sized islands ranging from temperate to subtropical regions. Since island plants often suffer from pollinator deficiency, Alpinia provides an ideal model case for exploring the adaptation mechanisms of flexistylous plants in a pollinator-inadequate environment. In this study, we addressed the following questions. ・Do native Japanese Alpinia species exhibit flexistyly? ・What kinds of pollinators contribute to outcrossing in these Alpinia species? ・How do native Japanese Alpinia species reproductively adapt to island pollination environments? Contrary to previously studied species, the female phase was considerably shorter in protandrous flowers than in protogynous flowers; nevertheless, fruit set did not differ significantly between the two floral morphs. In contrast, A. intermedia was pollinated by multiple insect taxa, including lepidopterans, hymenopterans, and dipterans, with lepidopterans showing particularly high visitation frequencies. On the other hand, the stigmas of the Amami Island population were shorter than those on the mainland, suggesting that autonomous selfing is likely to occur in this population. Mutualisms between species are universal and diverse across various ecosystems, playing an indispensable role in their functioning. Therefore, understanding such interactions is essential to understanding ecosystems. Plants of the family Phyllanthaceae and moths of the genus Epicephala form a pollination mutualism in which the plant and its seed-feeding pollinator are strongly interdependent. Adult female Epicephala moths actively pollinate the host plant's female flowers before laying their eggs inside the ovary. The hatched larvae consume only a few of the multiple seeds within the fruit before reaching maturity, allowing the plant to reproduce through the seeds that escape larval herbivory. Two Epicephala species, Epicephala obovatella and Epicephala corruptrix, share the Phyllanthaceae plants Glochidion obovatum and its sister species Glochidion rubrum as hosts. G. obovatum is distributed from the Okinawa Islands northward, while G. rubrum occurs from the Yaeyama Islands southward; consequently, the host used by each moth population varies by geographic location. Despite sharing a host, however, the two Epicephala moths exhibit mutually exclusive distributional patterns across most of their range. Amami-Oshima Island is one of the few regions where the coexistence of the two Epicephala species has been confirmed. Behavioral interference has increasingly recognized as a key mechanism driving the displacement of native species by invasive species, alongside the more widely studied processes of exploitative competition and hybridization. The population-level consequences of behavioral interference depend on the relative abundance of the interacting species. During the early stages of invasion, when native species remain numerically dominant, behavioral interference is expected to favor the native species at the population-level. In contrast, once the invasive species becomes established and abundant, the same mechanism may instead favor the invader. Furthermore, previous studies have shown that individuals responses can vary depending on whether population is allopatric or sympatric through character displacement. Despite, these potential temporal dynamics at both population- and individual- levels, most previous studies have focused solely on individual-level interactions overlooking these temporal relationships change over time. In this study, we investigated the role of behavioral interference in invasion dynamics using the invasive gecko Gekko japonicus and the native G. asahi in Japan. We compared behavioral interactions between individuals from areas where the invasive species has not yet established (allopatric populations) and from areas where the invasion has been established for an extended period (sympatric populations). By linking individual-level asymmetries in behavioral interference with their population-level introduction status, we aimed to comprehensively assess the mechanism of species displacement mediated by behavioral interference. Our results showed that interactions between native and invasive geckos originating from allopatric populations were generally weak and largely symmetrical. These findings suggest that although G. asahi is likely have enjoyed a demographic advantage during the early stages of invasion due to the numerical dominance, it was insufficiently aggressive to exclude G. japonicus at the individual level. Consequently, G. japonicus may have been able to establish initial populations unnoticed, facilitating its long-term persistence and subsequent spread. Maria Akai*1, Masami Hasegawa2,3, Shun Ito4
Predation is a major driver of natural selection in prey organisms. Plestiodon latiscutatus, an endemic species that inhabits the Izu Peninsula and Izu Islands of Japan, exhibits inter-island differences in morphological and life-history traits depending on predator composition. However, only few studies have examined these predatory effects on behavior. In ectotherms such as P. latiscutatus, escape performance to avoid predation depends heavily on body temperature. A previous study reported that the Kozu population, which coexists with snakes as major predators, maintains higher body temperatures than the snake-free Hachijo-Kojima population. In the Hachijo-Kojima population, basking frequency did not differ significantly, whereas basking duration increased significantly in weeks 5 and 9. In contrast, in the Kozu population, basking duration did not change significantly, whereas basking frequency was significantly lower in weeks 5 and 9. Taken together, these findings suggest that differences in predator assemblages may drive variation in thermoregulatory behavior in P. latiscutatus, and that populations may retain different thermoregulatory strategies adapted to their respective predator composition.

Sei Horiuchi*1, Naoki Kanasugi1, Mitsuru Sakai1, Haruka Nakamura2, Tomonobu Nakata1, Akira Sawada1, Masaoki Takagi1
Possessing the ability to recognize kin should be adaptive because it allows avoiding inbreeding or cooperation. Two mechanisms may underline kin recognition: the ability may be acquired through learning, or it may be innate. While the former possibility has been tested in many species, the latter has hardly been tested. One reason is that to testing the latter hypothesis requires detailed information about kin relationships among individuals, which is difficult to obtain in a wild population. We examined whether owlets of Ryukyu Scops Owl (Otus elegans) on Minami-daito Island possess kin recognition ability and how this ability develops―whether they are born with it or acquire it through learning. To test this, we played back three types of males’ hoots to the owlets: (1) the hoot of a familiar kin (a kin male they frequently encounter and hear), (2) the hoot of unfamiliar kin (a kin male they may not have met or heard before), and (3) the hoot of non-kin. The owlets typically emit begging calls upon hearing conspecific hoots. If the owlets possess kin recognition ability from birth, they may either (1) respond equally to the hoots of familiar and unfamiliar kin but differentially to the hoot of non-kin, or (2) respond to hoots of males in a graded manner based on genetic relatedness―for example, showing the strongest response to familiar kin, a weaker response to unfamiliar kin, and the weakest response to non-kin. On the other hand, if they acquire kin recognition ability through learning from familiar kin, they should respond differentially only to the hoot of familiar kin while responding equally to both unfamiliar kin and non-kin. Our results showed no significant differences in the number of begging calls in response to different male’s hoots. These findings suggest that owlets of the Ryukyu Scops Owl do not distinguish kin relationships, at least based on male’s hoots and the kin recognition ability based on male’s hoots is not innate.

Understanding the temporal variation in animal diets is essential for elucidating their ecology, especially for understanding how animals respond to environmental fluctuations and changes in resource availability. Flying foxes (Pteropodidae) are primarily frugivorous, feeding mainly on fruits as well as on leaves and flowers. Several studies have suggested a relationship between their ecology and the phenology of food plants, particularly the patterns of flowering and fruiting. However, few studies have quantitatively examined the relationship between foraging ecology and food plant phenology in insular flying fox populations. Kita-daito Island in the Ryukyu Archipelago, Japan, is a small oceanic island with an area of approximately 12 km² and is home to the Daito flying fox (Pteropus dasymallus daitoensis). This subspecies is restricted to two islands in the Daito Islands and is classified as critically endangered; therefore, a better understanding of its foraging ecology is essential for its conservation. This study aimed to clarify the foraging patterns of the Daito flying fox on Kita-daito Island by combining phenological surveys of food plants with radio-tracking surveys. In addition, radio-tracking surveys were conducted for three individuals across multiple nights to examine their nightly foraging patterns, and direct observations were conducted to record feeding behaviors and the plant species utilized. The results of this study showed that the phenology of food plants was categorized into two patterns; (1) species with long flowering or fruiting periods (>3 months) and (2) species with short flowering or fruiting periods (<3 months). The plant species and frequency used by flying foxes varied among months, and utilization rates were relatively high for species with short flowering or fruiting periods. Direct observations revealed that individuals fed on multiple plant species within a single night and preferentially utilized species that were temporarily available due to short flowering or fruiting periods.

approach using the epigenetic clock-Yuuto Kane*1, Miho Murayama2, Eiji Inoue3, Shizuko Hiryu4, Emyo Fujioka4 , Shoko Fujitani4, Shun Kobayashi5, Yoshie Kanao6, Tomoaki Nakamura6, Etsuko Yamauchi6, Misato Ohonuma7, Toi Yamada7, Dai Fukui1
Age is a primary factor underlying individual variation in animal behavior. However, accurately determining age of wild animals has traditionally been challenging using conventional methods. In recent years, epigenetic clocks—particularly those based on DNA methylation patterns as an indicator—have emerged as powerful alternatives. This study aimed to develop an age estimation model based on DNA methylation rates for the Ryukyu flying fox (Pteropus dasymallus) and to examine the influence of epigenetic age on its home range size on Okinawa Island in the Ryukyu Archipelago, Japan. To construct the age estimation model, wing membrane tissues were collected from captive individuals of known age, and DNA methylation rates were quantified using the methylation-sensitive high-resolution melting (MS-HRM) method. A support vector regression (SVR) model was then constructed using genomic regions correlated with chronological age, and its accuracy was evaluated through cross-validation. To estimate the home range size in wild individuals, GPS loggers were attached and their location data were recorded at 2-minute intervals during the activity period. Wing membrane tissue samples were also collected at the time of capture to estimate the epigenetic age. Home range sizes were calculated from location data, and the effect of epigenetic age on home range size was analyzed using a linear mixed model (LMM). The age estimation model, based on three age-related genomic regions, achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.95 years, which is within 7% of the species’ maximum lifespan. Results of the LMM showed that younger individuals had larger home ranges, whereas older individuals maintained smaller ones. This relationship remained significant after controlling for sex and seasonal effects. The observed age-dependent contraction in home range size may reflect social displacement of subordinate younger individuals, as well as the optimization of foraging efficiency in older individuals through experience and spatial learning. This study provides the first empirical evidence that epigenetic age is a key driver of individual variation in home range size in bats, highlighting life-history stage as a major determinant of spatial utilization dynamics.

The genus Takydromus is widely distributed in Taiwan and exhibits high diversity and endemism, with distinct life history strategies often observed among species and even among populations within the same species. The population of the grass lizard Takydromus viridipunctatus on Guishan Island has been confirmed to exhibit insular gigantism, making it an ideal system for studying life history variation and island syndrome. Previous mark–recapture studies have suggested potential differences in population dynamics between insular and mainland populations; however, the age structure and growth patterns underlying this insular phenomenon remain insufficiently explored. Feeding ecology of the giant mottled eel (Anguilla marmorata) in island streams as a generalist apex predator

Tatsuhiko Maeda*1, Hikaru Itakura2, Ryoshiro Wakiya1, Shingo Kimura1
Introduction Island rivers are typically characterized by low autochthonous productivity owing to their short, steep channels, and their food webs depend on allochthonous subsidies. In these systems, the giant mottled eel (Anguilla marmorata) occupies the apex predator position. Despite this top trophic status, A. marmorata attains the highest biomass density among all resident aquatic taxa, forming an apparent inverted biomass pyramid relative to its prey. How this apex predator sustains such disproportionately high biomass in resource-limited systems remains poorly understood. Characterizing feeding strategy of apex predator is therefore key to resolving this paradox. We examined this strategy using mark–recapture surveys combined with non-lethal stomach content analysis. Methods & Results Field surveys were conducted monthly on Amami–Oshima Island, Kagoshima, Japan from January 2024 to September 2025. A total of 645 individuals were tagged, yielding 1,068 capture events including recaptures, from which stomach contents were obtained 515 times. Stomach contents were collected using a flexible tube and forceps and identified visually to the lowest feasible taxonomic level. Prey items spanned 28 orders across 11 classes, including both aquatic and terrestrial taxa, indicating a broad dietary niche at the population level. Prey composition varied with season, habitat, and body size. Within-individual dietary similarity across recaptures did not differ significantly from between-individual similarity (LMM, p > 0.05), indicating that individuals do not specialize on particular prey types but instead exploit a wide range of prey opportunistically. Discussion These findings suggest that the high biomass of A. marmorata in island rivers is sustained by an opportunistic, individually flexible feeding strategy. Individual eels shift prey use across seasons and ontogenetic stages, and even between successive capture events. Because this strategy depends on prey of diverse origins, the conservation of A. marmorata populations requires the maintenance of connectivity among sea, river, and land. This connectivity supports both the diversity of available prey and the recruitment of diadromous prey species from the sea. Rather than simply consuming locally available prey, A. marmorata may function as a predator that actively links marine, freshwater, and terrestrial compartments through its broad foraging.

Kiminori Fukaya*1, Yuya Fukano1
Urban areas can be regarded as relatively isolated, island-like environments, where urban heat island effects and soil desiccation impose strong environmental stress. Plants growing in urban habitats therefore provide a useful system for examining three processes: first, how plants respond plastically to environmental stress on plants; second, whether they exhibit rapid evolutionary divergence, potentially associated with local adaptation; and third, whether phenotypic plasticity itself evolves. By examining multiple plant species commonly occurring in urban habitats, it is also possible to test whether these plastic and genetic responses show parallel patterns across species or vary among species. In this study, we conducted a reciprocal transplant experiment using three grass species widely distributed across urban and agricultural landscapes: Eleusine indica, Digitaria ciliaris, and Setaria viridis. Seeds were collected from multiple urban and agricultural populations, grown to comparable stages, and transplanted into simulated urban and agricultural environments. We measured early plant length one week after transplanting, as a proxy for early growth, final dry mass as a proxy for biomass production, flowering onset date as a measure of flowering phenology. Using these traits, we statistically tested for three components of plant responses: (i) plastic responses to the cultivation environment, (ii) evolutionary differentiation associated with seed-source environment, and (iii) the evolution of phenotypic plasticity, inferred from the interaction between cultivation environment and seed source environment. The experiment showed that the three species exhibited both (i) plastic responses and (ii) evolutionary differentiation. (i) Plastic responses were detected in plant length and final dry mass. Early plant length was reduced in all three species when plants were grown under the simulated urban environment, where heat and drought stress were relatively high. In contrast, final dry mass was greater in the simulated urban environment, where competition with neighboring individuals was relatively low. (ii) Evolutionary differentiation was detected in plant length, final dry mass, and flowering onset date. Across all three species, urban-derived individuals tended to show shorter early plant length and smaller final dry mass than agricultural-derived individuals. In contrast, flowering onset date showed species-specific patterns. In E. indica, agricultural-derived individuals flowered significantly earlier, whereas in D. ciliaris, urban-derived individuals flowered significantly earlier. In S. viridis, no significant effect of source environment was detected. Together, these results indicate that, in the three species examined, responses to urban conditions appeared as plastic responses and evolutionary differentiation in growth-related traits, whereas flowering phenology showed species-specific differentiation. Future work should quantify how these species-specific patterns affect fitness more comprehensively, including reproductive success and survival.

Bárbara Freitas*1
Acoustic signalling is central to animal communication, mediating mate attraction, territory de-fence, and social interactions. Because acoustic signals often function as premating barriers, their divergence can directly influence speciation. While sexual selection, ecological interactions, and species coexistence shape signal evolution, the ecological drivers of acoustic diversification remain poorly understood at broad taxonomic and geographic scales. Island systems provide natural laboratories for studying evolution. Reduced predation pressure, fewer competitors, and simplified communities may relax selective constraints, potentially promoting increased variability and complexity in communication signals. However, whether island environments consistently shape acoustic trait evolution across taxa remains largely unexplored at broad comparative scales. This project aims to investigate the hypothesis that island populations exhibit more variable and complex acoustic signals than their mainland counterparts. As a first step toward a taxonomically broad global comparative study, I will compile and analyse acoustic recordings from island and mainland populations across multiple taxa. Acoustic recordings will be assembled from publicly available datasets and through collaborations. Conference participants and other researchers with relevant recordings are warmly invited to contribute data and help developing a global acoustic trait dataset. Acoustic variability and complexity will be quantified using measures such as repertoire size, note diversity, temporal structure, and spectral variation. By investigating acoustic divergence across island systems, this work will provide new insights into how relaxed selective regimes shape phenotypic evolution and diversification, while establishing a collaborative resource for future research on island bioacoustics and evolutionary biology.

Quaternary climate changes greatly affected the distributions and phylogeographic patterns of temperate and boreal species. Plebejus argyrognomon is widely distributed in grassland habitats across mid- to high-latitude Eurasia and is likely to have been strongly affected by Quaternary climate changes. In this context, genetic and morphological differences among regional populations have been reported, suggesting the need for taxonomic re-evaluation. To date, Japanese populations have not been genetically examined, and their evolutionary relationship with continental populations remains unclear despite reported ecological and morphological differences. In Japan, P. argyrognomon is locally restricted to central Honshu. In recent decades, grassland habitats along rivers and agricultural areas have declined drastically, and local extinctions of this species have occurred in many areas. The present study aimed to clarify the molecular phylogenetic relationships between Japanese and continental Northeast Asian populations of P. argyrognomon, as well as the genetic population structure within Japan. Genome-wide SNP analyses using the dpMIG-seq method were conducted for 213 individuals collected from Japan (121 individuals), South Korea (49 individuals), and the Russian Far East (43 individuals). PCA and phylogenetic analyses clearly separated the samples into four groups: Japanese populations of P. argyrognomon; continental Northeast Asian populations from South Korea and the Russian Far East, and two congeneric outgroup species, P. argus and P. subsolanus. These results indicated that Japanese populations are genetically distinct. The Japanese and continental northeast Asian populations were estimated to have diverged approximately 180,000 years ago. Furthermore, Japanese populations showed fine-scale subpopulation structure: the Shizuoka, Tochigi, Toyama, and Yamanashi populations each formed distinct genetic clusters, whereas the Nagano population exhibited admixture among multiple clusters. These results indicate that the Japanese and continental Northeast Asian populations of P. argyrognomon are genetically differentiated to the extent that they can be regarded as separate species. Furthermore, Japanese populations have experienced demographic bottleneck and expansion from Nagano to other regions. Overall, the findings suggest that the colonization into the Japanese archipelago from the Eurasian continent dates back beyond the last glacial period, and that Japanese populations have since followed an independent evolutionary history. Currently, butterfly species recognized as endemic to the Japanese archipelago are limited to a few forest-associated species, and thus the evolutionary history of Japanese P. argyrognomon provides new insights into the origin of grassland biodiversity in Japan.

Akihiko Jingu*1, Norio Hirai1, Naoyuki Nakahama1, Shouhei Ueda1
More than 4,000 kilometers of Japan’s coastline consist of sandy beaches, and these environments are habitats for a wide variety of organisms. However, these environments are disappearing due to human activities and environmental changes, leading to habitat fragmentation. Consequently, population genetic studies on coastal insects remain highly limited in Japan. While many species of antlion larvae inhabit sandy areas, non-pit-building species, which do not construct pits, were poorly studied about their ecology and genetic structure due to the difficulty of locating them in the field. Using the obtained sequences, we constructed molecular phylogenetic trees and haplotype networks and calculated the haplotype diversity and nucleotide diversity for each population of both species. In S. japonica, the phylogenetic tree showed small genetic distances between individuals, and little geographic differentiation was observed. The haplotype network exhibited a complex structure, and haplotype sharing was observed between distant populations. In contrast, the phylogenetic tree of D. contubernalis was largely divided into two lineages: clade A primarily occurring on the Pacific side and clade B primarily occurring on the Sea of Japan side. A comparison of haplotype diversity and nucleotide diversity between S. japonica and D. contubernalis revealed that S. japonica unexpectedly exhibited higher values at all populations. In contrast, D. contubernalis showed lower values in some populations. East Asia supports a globally high diversity of Tertiary relict plant species, many of which constitute important components of the region’s biodiversity. The Japanese Archipelago, the Ryukyu Islands, and Taiwan, located at the eastern margin of Eurasia, have experienced repeated connections and separations from surrounding landmasses and therefore provide an ideal system for understanding the historical range dynamics of East Asian relict taxa. Understanding the formation of relict distributions in Tertiary relict species is important for reconstructing the biogeographic history of East Asian temperate forests and informing their conservation. We investigated the genetic diversity, phylogeographic structure, and demographic history of Trochodendron aralioides, a Tertiary relict species endemic to Japan and Taiwan. To cover the major distribution range of T. aralioides, samples were collected from 35 populations in Japan and Taiwan. A total of 16,067 SNPs were obtained using the MIG-seq method and used for subsequent analyses. Genetic diversity was evaluated using heterozygosity and nucleotide diversity indices calculated by the populations program implemented in Stacks v2.66. Phylogeographic structure was assessed using ADMIXTURE, PopCluster, and PCA. In addition, to investigate demographic history of T. aralioides, divergence times and demographic scenarios among regional populations were estimated using DIYABC-RF. Furthermore, species distribution modeling using MaxEnt was conducted based on present and Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) climatic conditions to infer historical distribution shifts. These analyses suggested that genetic diversity was higher in Japanese populations than in Taiwanese populations and that ancestral populations were likely distributed in Japan, followed by range expansion toward Taiwan. In addition, populations from the Ryukyu Islands exhibited intermediate genetic characteristics between Japanese and Taiwanese populations, suggesting that T. aralioides migrated via the Ryukyu Islands. Divergence time estimation using DIYABC-RF further suggested that the timing of population differentiation may be associated with geological events related to the formation history of the Ryukyu Archipelago. Through these analyses, we clarified the phylogeographic structure and demographic history of T. aralioides across its entire distribution range and explored their relationships with geological events that shaped East Asian temperate forests since the Tertiary period. These results suggest that some Tertiary relict taxa distributed in Japan and Taiwan have expanded their ranges via the Ryukyu Islands. In addition, the Ryukyu populations of T. aralioides, which exhibited genetic characteristics intermediate between Japanese and Taiwanese populations, are of particular biogeographic importance. Because these populations are small and locally distributed, they are also considered important targets for conservation.

Kai Tsukamoto*1, Hiroshi Noda2, Chang-Shien Lin3, Yuan-Hao Cheng4, Tae-Soo Jang5, Xiao-Feng Jin6, Yano Okihito7, Koji Takayama1
The Japanese Archipelago, comprising both continental and oceanic islands, provides an ideal setting for investigating insular diversification. While most islands are continental in origin and were repeatedly connected to the Asian continent through land bridges, the archipelago also contains oceanic components, including the Ogasawara Islands, which originated 30–40 Ma, and the Izu Islands, which formed after more recently and subsequently collided with Honshu to form the Izu Peninsula. Elaeagnus (Elaeagnaceae), a genus of evergreen and deciduous trees widely diversified in East Asia, offers an excellent model for examining island endemism, range expansion, and hybridization. In Japan, 11 endemic species and three putative hybrids have been described, yet their evolutionary relationships remain poorly resolved owing to limited phylogenetic data. To clarify the evolutionary history of Elaeagnus, we analyzed genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphisms and complete chloroplast genomes from extensive sampling across Japan and adjacent regions. Nuclear population genetic analyses revealed clear genetic differentiation among species and deep divergence between evergreen and deciduous lineages, corresponding to differences in flowering phenology. Ancestral area reconstruction inferred multiple bidirectional migrations between the Asian continent and the Japanese Archipelago, many of which coincided with periods of land-bridge formation. Within the evergreen lineage, including the widespread E. glabra and E. macrophylla, two major chloroplast haplotype lineages were identified: one extending from Taiwan to western Japan and another distributed in eastern Japan including Izu Peninsula and Izu Islands, shared with the Ogasawara endemic E. rotundata. Cytonuclear discordance detected in eastern Japan is best explained by introgression, suggesting secondary contact among lineages that are currently allopatric. Divergence within the eastern chloroplast lineage coincided with the formation of the Izu Islands, supporting a scenario reverse colonization from oceanic islands to the continental margin via newly formed oceanic islands acting as stepping stones. In addition, extensive interspecific gene flow among E. pungens, E. glabra, and E. macrophylla has generated multigenerational hybrids, including backcrosses. These findings indicate that secondary contact among lineages arriving through different colonization routes promoted hybrid-complex formation, potentially facilitating the generation of genetic diversity and adaptation to insular environments. Overall, our findings reveal a complex history of migration and hybridization in Elaeagnus and demonstrate that islands act not only as sinks but also as important sources of genetic diversity in East Asian floras.

Marine organisms often show high levels of genetic diversity. One of the primary reasons is that many species have planktonic larvae that can disperse over long distances through ocean currents. Intertidal crabs also have planktonic larval stages, suggesting that they can disperse over long distances in the marine environment. The Izu Islands are located off central Japan and extend from north to south; the northern islands are close to the coastal line, whereas the southern ones are located farther away. Therefore, by focusing on this island system, we aimed to examine the effects of island environments on the population genetic structure and dispersal of the intertidal crab Pachygrapsus crassipes. Individuals of P. crassipes were collected from the Izu Islands and from the coast of the Honshu mainland. Genome-wide SNPs data were obtained using next generation sequencing. The data were analyzed using principal component analysis, phylogenetic network analysis, population structure analysis, and isolation by distance analysis. Principal component analysis, phylogenetic network analysis, and population structure analysis did not show clear population structure among the sampling localities. In contrast, isolation by distance analysis demonstrated that genetic differentiation tended to be greater among populations in the Izu Islands than among populations along Honshu. These results suggest that gene flow among island populations may be partially restricted, even in an intertidal crab species with high dispersal potential. In other words, our findings indicate that island environments play a role in geographic isolation among marine organisms living in a seemingly continuous marine environment.

Silvia Harumi Kamazuka*1, Isao Nishiumi2, Toru Nakahara3, Haruki Tatsuta1
The Japanese Pygmy Woodpecker (Yungipicus kizuki) is the smallest woodpecker in Japan and comprises 11 recognized subspecies, nine of which occur across the Japanese archipelago. Because this species is non-migratory and shows limited dispersal ability, it represents a suitable model for island biogeography studies of resident birds. Despite its broad geographic distribution, subspecies delimitation in Y. kizuki has been based primarily on locality, plumage characteristics, and simple morphometric descriptions, with no comprehensive assessment of morphometric variation across populations. Bergmann’s and Allen’s rules are ecogeographical patterns predicting that endothermic animals exhibit larger body sizes and relatively shorter appendages at higher latitudes, respectively, where lower temperatures favor heat conservation, whereas populations in warmer regions tend to be smaller and possess longer appendages to enhance heat dissipation. To evaluate whether morphometric variation follows these ecogeographical patterns or discrete subspecies clustering, this study investigated morphometric variation among Y. kizuki subspecies found in the Japanese archipelago as part of an ongoing integrative project combining morphology, bioacoustics and molecular data. Beak, wing, tail and tarsus dimensions were obtained from 89 specimens of Y. kizuki housed at the National Museum of Nature and Science and the Kitakyushu Museum of Natural History & Human History, as well as from individuals collected with mist nets. Wing length was used to assess body size, while beak and tarsus measurements were used to assess appendage size. Principal component analysis (PCA) did not reveal clear clustering among subspecies, but a MANOVA test detected significant differences between groups. A Mantel test using Mahalanobis distances indicated that geographically distant individuals were also more morphologically distinct than geographically closer individuals. Furthermore, correlations between latitude and morphological traits showed that populations occurring closer to the equator exhibited larger beak dimensions and smaller body size, while tarsus length showed no clear latitudinal trend. These findings suggest that morphological variation in Y. kizuki is better explained by latitudinal clinal variation than by discrete subspecies clustering. The observed pattern of larger body size at higher latitudes and larger beak dimensions at lower latitudes is broadly compatible with the patterns predicted by Bergmann’s and Allen’s rules, respectively.

PA5-37

Tadashi Tokumoto*1, Takato Inoue2, Wataru Kojima1
Anti-predator traits function at different stages of the predation sequence, from reducing detection by predators to enhancing survival after capture. Different habitat structures may favor different combinations of defensive traits. However, how habitat complexity shapes the suite of anti-predator traits remains largely unknown. We studied the association between habitat structures and two types of defensive traits, i.e., escape behavior and chemical defense, across mainland and six island populations of the Japanese toad Bufo japonicus. As habitat variables, we quantified canopy openness and the surrounding landscape for each individual. For escape behavior, we measured field-based escape responsiveness to physical stimuli as well as laboratory-determined running speed. For chemical defense, we quantified the mass of secreted toxin and the total amount of bufadienolides determined by chemical analysis. We found that the mainland and two island populations primarily inhabited forests, whereas the other four island populations utilized a wide range of habitats, including open grasslands and farmlands. Interestingly, a strong association was found between habitat use and escape behavior: forest-dwelling populations initiated escape at earlier stages and exhibited faster running speeds, whereas populations in more open habitats responded more slowly. We also found that chemical defense levels in most island populations, with the exception of Mishima Island, were as high as those in mainland populations, regardless of habitat type. This pattern may reflect an optimal anti-predator strategy depending on habitat complexity. In complex forest environments with ample refuges, rapid escape responses are likely adaptive for avoiding predator strikes. Conversely, in open environments with limited refuges, toads may minimize immediate escape efforts and instead rely heavily on chemical defense. The consistently high level of chemical defense across nearly all populations highlights its critical importance as a "last resort" defense. Notably, we found a marked reduction in chemical defense on Mishima Island. Given that this island lacks mammalian and reptilian predators, relaxed predation pressure has likely led to the degeneration of this costly defense. Overall, our findings demonstrate that the suite of anti-predator traits is shaped by the interplay between habitat complexity and predation pressure.

PA5-39

Ryoga Tanaka*1, Shun Ito2
The Izu Islands are an oceanic island group located more than 20 km from the Japanese mainland. Because of their geographic isolation and unique environmental conditions, many island organisms exhibit distinctive morphological and ecological variation. The large Japanese field mouse (Apodemus speciosus) inhabiting the Izu Islands is no exception; island-specific morphology and behavior have been observed. Previous phylogenetic studies showed that island populations are genetically distinct from mainland populations, suggesting that the island morphotype reflects phylogenetic divergence. The Izu Islands, where A. speciosus occurs on five islands, provide an ideal system for investigating the evolutionary factors associated with island morphotypes. However, it remains unclear whether the island morphotype reflects only historical divergence or also adaptation to island environments. Our study demonstrated that dietary composition formed distinct clusters among mainland Japan, the Izu Peninsula, and the Izu Islands, indicating regional differences in diet. In particular, in the Izu Islands, they consumed island-specific plants such as camellias. In addition, dietary breadth also varied within the Izu Islands, and the Oshima and Kozu Island populations showed a unique pattern not observed in other populations. Although they consumed some moths and other insects, they fed almost exclusively on soil-dwelling invertebrates. In the Izu Peninsula population, soil-dwelling invertebrates were detected in their faeces. In contrast, the Izu Islands populations showed island-specific dietary patterns. These findings suggest that A. speciosus has evolved independently on each island through adaptation to island environment, resulting in island-specific dietary niches.

PA5-41

Jory Teltser*1, Johannes Foufopoulos1
Mediterranean islands support diverse bird, reptile, and amphibian communities that are increasingly exposed to habitat modification, coastal development, hunting-driven overkill, invasive species, human disturbance, and climate-driven environmental change. Although these taxa often occur within the same island habitats, their ecological and life history differences may cause them to respond differently to anthropogenic pressures. Understanding how human-caused stressors are associated with declines across different taxonomic groups is important, not just for sustainable future ecosystem management, but also for identifying how specific conservation actions can benefit one or multiple taxa. This study investigates how anthropogenic stressors have been associated with patterns of decline and extinction in bird, reptile, and amphibian communities across Mediterranean islands over the last century. We compiled island-level data from GPS-verified eBird and iNaturalist records, historical breeding records, documented extirpations and extinctions, species status, habitat characteristics, climate, and patterns of human land use and development. Particular attention is given to whether different forms of landscape modification, including tourism-related development and agricultural land use, are associated with contrasting responses among birds and reptiles. Preliminary analyses suggest that while birds and herptiles are exposed to several overlapping pressures, their responses to these stressors are not congruent. Patterns of species occurrence, historical loss, and conservation concern vary between the two groups, indicating that the relative importance of development, habitat fragmentation, invasive species, and climatic stress are taxon-dependent. PA5-42

Takayasu Amano*1
In the Anthropocene, roads and expressways have often been discussed as sources of negative impacts on wildlife through habitat fragmentation, roadkill, noise, and artificial light pollution. However, for some birds adapted to urban and human-modified environments, such infrastructure may also provide novel opportunities for breeding. This study focused on Barn Swallows (Hirundo rustica), which commonly nest on artificial structures, and examined their use of service areas (SAs) and parking areas (PAs) along Japanese expressways. Although Barn Swallows are representative urban-adapted birds, their broad-scale use of expressway facilities remains poorly understood. In particular, little attention has been paid to whether these facilities provide artificial nesting substrates in mountainous or high-elevation landscapes, where suitable nesting sites may otherwise be limited. This study aimed to clarify the breeding distribution of Barn Swallows using expressway facilities in the Japanese Archipelago and identify characteristics of SAs/PAs with high nest numbers. I conducted a nationwide survey from Hokkaido to Kyushu, covering approximately 13,000 km of driving distance. I stopped at all SAs and PAs along the route and recorded the presence and number of Barn Swallow nests. I also examined relationships between nest numbers and facility type, management region, 24-hour shops, surrounding landscape context, and elevation. Nest numbers were significantly higher at SAs than at PAs, and facilities with 24-hour shops tended to support more nests. Nesting was confirmed from low-elevation coastal sites to facilities around 500 m above sea level. Barn Swallow nesting was recorded mainly from northern Honshu to Kyushu, whereas no nests were found at SAs/PAs in Hokkaido. Moreover, such facilities may function as artificial nesting substrates not only in urban or residential areas, but also in mountainous and topographically complex landscapes, thereby expanding the potential breeding space of Barn Swallows. By viewing the Japanese Archipelago as an insular landscape, this study shows how an expressway network may shape breeding opportunities for urban-adapted birds. The repeated use of SAs/PAs by Barn Swallows suggests the possible emergence of a “highway ecosystem” formed through interactions among artificial structures, human activity, vehicle traffic, lighting, surrounding landscapes, and wildlife. This perspective reevaluates human infrastructure in Anthropocene island landscapes not only as a source of negative impacts, but also as a creator of novel habitat opportunities for wildlife.

Geographic variation in acoustic signals is thought to promote population differentiation and may ultimately contribute to speciation. In birds, geographic variation in song characteristics is considered to arise from a variety of ecological and social factors. In the Cinereous Tit (Parus cinereus) inhabiting the Ryukyu Archipelago, geographic variation in song associated with character displacement has been reported among island populations occurring sympatrically with the Varied Tit (Sittiparus varius). Takayuki Ikegami*1, Akira Sawada1, Naoki Kanasugi1, Hinako Hanzawa1, Sei Horiuchi1, Fuka Takei1, Mitsuru Sakai1, Tomonobu Nakata1, Kosei Ikejiri1, Ayumi Hamakawa2, Masaoki Takagi1

For formulating effective conservation plans for forest birds, understanding large-scale population densities and island-wide total abundance is fundamental baseline information. However, no breeding individuals have been confirmed in the southern part of Okinawa Island. The scarcity of contiguous forests in the southern region may also be a factor contributing to the species’ inability to establish a breeding range there. The objective was to construct a hierarchical spatial model based on distance sampling data covering the entire Island of Okinawa, with the aim of elucidating the spatial distribution characteristics of this species while accounting for forest area and accurately estimating the total island population. We conducted point-transect surveys at 204 locations across Okinawa Island over an approximately one month period from August to September 2025. PA5-46

Since the mid-20th century, rapid global warming has altered the distribution of numerous species worldwide. Birds are particularly sensitive to climate change because of their high mobility. Among them, migratory species are especially vulnerable, and shifts in both breeding and wintering ranges have been reported. The Chestnut-cheeked Starling Agropsar philippensis, the focal species of this study, is a migratory bird that breeds primarily in central and northern Japan. Although some populations breed in South Korea and Russia, most of the breeding population occurs within Japan, and the species is therefore regarded as a near-endemic species. The species can be characterized as an island-associated migrant because both its breeding and wintering ranges are largely distributed across island archipelagos. In the Tohoku region of northeastern Japan, several breeding colonies were recorded in the southern part of the region during the 1970s, whereas breeding records have become scarce there in the 2020s. A model developed using temperature conditions from the 2020s was projected onto past and future climate scenarios to estimate historical and future distributions. Temperature data for the 1970s, 2050s, and 2070s were derived from a global climate model. The results indicated that the current distribution is concentrated in local cities of northern Tohoku. In contrast, projections for the 1970s suggested that southern Tohoku provided more suitable habitat, indicating that the species' distribution has shifted northward over approximately the past 50 years. Future projections suggested that this northward shift will continue under ongoing climate warming, and that lowland areas of Tohoku may become unsuitable for the species within the next 50 years. Japan is a biodiversity hotspot harboring numerous endemic species, while also being characterized by high alien species richness, against a backdrop of intensive socioeconomic activities. The Japanese archipelago comprises both relatively large continental islands and numerous geographically isolated small islands, and it spans a broad latitudinal range. Consequently, ecosystem characteristics and vulnerability to biological invasions vary substantially among regions. In Japan, invasive alien species (hereafter, IAS) are listed in the List of Alien Species that May Cause Damage to Japan’s Ecosystems published by the Ministry of the Environment (MOE; hereafter, the MOE list). However, comprehensive nation-scale analyses of introduction pathways remain limited for species listed in the MOE list across multiple taxonomic groups. Furthermore, the recent distribution and spread of many IAS remain poorly understood. Therefore, this study aimed to analyze the drivers of biological invasions across multiple taxonomic groups in Japan and to provide insights for developing effective measures to prevent both new introductions and spreads of IAS. We focused on the established IAS originating from outside Japan and listed in the MOE list. Pathways were classified for each species based on the CBD Pathways Categorization through a literature review. Across the three taxa (plant, freshwater fish and bird), “Escape” accounted for more than half of the pathways. “Horticulture” (plant) and the “Pet/aquarium” (freshwater fish and bird) were major “Escape” subcategories, both associated with introductions for ornamental purposes. “Release” was the second most common pathway and was mainly associated with intentional introductions for “Erosion control/dune stabilization” (plant), “Fishery in wild” (freshwater fish), and “Hunting” (birds). We also present the temporal pattern of introduction pathways in Japan and compare it with the global trend, and extend similar analyses to additional taxonomic groups. In addition, using records from nation-scale biodiversity monitoring programs, we obtained distribution data for plant, freshwater fish, and bird IAS. We analyze the drivers of biological invasions at the municipal scale using species distribution models and report the results as well.

Understanding whether non-native invasive species maintain their native ecological niche in invaded regions is therefore important for predicting future range expansion and invasion risk. Island terrestrial molluscs are among the animal groups that have suffered the highest numbers of extinctions during the past 500 years. Based on these findings, we conclude that the European rabbit population on Okunoshima has established a unique population structure under specific environmental conditions.

潮間帯における外来巻貝の貝殻が生息場所として果たす機能

Identifying the factors that determine community structure is a central challenge in community ecology, and biological interactions are key factors influencing it. Ecosystem engineers are organisms that influence other organisms by physically modifying ecosystems, and much remains unknown about them, particularly in marine environments. What impact do snail shells have on ecosystems? Hard structures formed by organisms often function as habitat substrates within ecosystems. For example, oysters and mussels that form reefs can be listed. Such habitat-forming actions are considered particularly important in unstable environments like sedimentary bottoms. Specifically, the shells of large gastropods can serve as shelters for other organisms and may help their survival. However, many aspects of snail’s functions as ecosystem engineers remain unclear. After death, snails act as “ecosystem engineers” by providing shells that serve as microhabitats, potentially influencing the community structure of the local area. In other words, in the intertidal zone, gastropod shells can be considered like "islands" that provide niches for organisms. In particular, it is extremely important to clarify the impact of invasive species, which have become a major environmental issue in recent years. This is because invasive species, acting as ecosystem engineers, may be altering the structure of native communities. The objective of this study is to identify organisms that utilize the remains of invasive snails. We collected dead shells of alien snail Laguncula pulchella from tidal flats in the Tohoku region. In addition, we measured the shield length of hermit crabs and identified the flatworms found in the dead shells through genetic analysis. As a result of collecting dead shells of L. pulchella, three species of arthropods, four species of mollusks, and one species of platyhelminthes were collected from the surface and interior of the shells. In nearby tidal flats where L. pulchella is currently absent, dead shells were extremely scarce, and few organisms were collected. This suggests that after death, L. pulchella functions as an ecosystem engineer, providing its shells as microhabitats for other organisms. Measurements of the most commonly collected hermit crab species suggested that the invasion of L. pulchella led to the occupation of larger-sized hermit crabs. The unidentified flatworm collected in this study was identified as Pseudostylochus sp. based on genetic analysis. This study revealed that L. pulchella acts as an ecosystem engineer by providing dead shells as microhabitats. In the future, we will investigate patterns of shell utilization by organisms through field experiments using replicas.

PA5-56

Ecological heterogeneity, including spatial variation in light availability, soil nutrients, and vegetation composition, may influence plant growth and reproductive success. However, its role within a single small island population remains poorly understood. Genetic constraints, such as low genetic diversity and clonal reproduction, may also affect population persistence. We focused on a single small population of the endangered perennial herb Arnica sachalinensis on Rebun Island, northern Japan to investigate whether ecological heterogeneity influences reproductive success and conducted genetic analyses to inform conservation management within a single small population on an island. To evaluate ecological heterogeneity, vegetation conditions (vegetation type and total plant coverage) and environmental conditions (canopy openness, soil carbon and nitrogen contents, and soil pH) were compared between inland and sea-cliff sides. Hierarchical clustering and NMDS of vegetation data identified two distinct vegetation types corresponding to the two sides, which also differed significantly in total plant coverage and soil carbon and nitrogen contents, indicating clear ecological heterogeneity. Reproductive success was evaluated based on flowering probability, and factors affecting flowering probability, including vegetation and environmental factors as well as plant traits of A. sachalinensis, were analyzed using GLMMs. Flowering probability was significantly lower on the inland side than on the sea-cliff side, and GLMMs revealed positive effects of canopy openness and stem length of A. sachalinensis but a negative effect of total plant coverage. Limonium wrightii var. wrightii is a perennial coastal plant distributed from Taiwan to the Ryukyu and Ogasawara Islands. It occurs mainly on rocky shores and is listed as Vulnerable in the Red List of the Ministry of the Environment, Japan. Because its small individuals are sparsely distributed on rocky substrates, its microhabitat remains poorly understood. We investigated its microhabitat characteristics by integrating field vegetation surveys with spatial analysis of high-resolution imagery acquired using an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV). The study was conducted on Iheya and Izena Islands, Okinawa Prefecture, where extensive natural coastlines remain. At nine coastal sites, we established 125 quadrats (1 × 1 m) and recorded vascular plant species and their cover. We also acquired RGB and multispectral imagery using a DJI Mavic 3 Multispectral flown autonomously at an altitude of 30 m. From these images, we generated point clouds, a digital surface model, and RGB and NDVI orthomosaics, and extracted environmental variables including elevation, distance from the shoreline, and surface relief. Field surveys recorded 60 vascular plant species, mainly perennial herbs. Six rocky-shore plant communities were identified, including one for which L. wrightii var. wrightii was the indicator species. Species composition changed continuously along gradients of elevation and shoreline distance, with L. wrightii var. wrightii occurring closest to the sea. The UAV imagery, with a spatial resolution of approximately 1 cm, allowed most small individuals on rocky substrates to be identified from the RGB and NDVI orthomosaics. The species’ distribution was significantly related to elevation, shoreline distance, and surface relief, with the highest occurrence at elevations of 0–5 m. Individuals tended to concentrate in cracks and in sheltered positions behind rocks. Occurrence also varied with geology: it was significantly lower on volcanic rock, and field data indicated a wider elevational range on limestone than on other substrates. These results suggest that L. wrightii var. wrightii occupies the seaward zone of rocky shores, which is exposed to physical stresses such as wave action and inundation, whereas its occurrence landward may be limited by competition with other species. Even within its distribution range, suitable microhabitats appear restricted to cracks and sheltered positions. By integrating field surveys with high-resolution UAV imagery, this study clarified the microhabitat associations of this species across multiple spatial scales and demonstrated an approach applicable to the conservation and monitoring of small, sparsely distributed coastal plants.

The evolution of fruits with different dispersal capabilities within a species is considered an adaptation to fluctuating environments. The coastal shrub Scaevola taccada exhibits inter-individual variation in fruit morphology, with two distinct fruit morphs: one possessing both a fleshy pulp and a cork layer in the pericarp (cork morph), and another possessing only a fleshy pulp layer (pulp morph). The cork morph can be dispersed by both frugivorous animals and ocean currents, whereas the pulp morph relies primarily on frugivorous animals for seed dispersal. These two morphs occur sympatrically within populations, but their frequencies differ among coastal habitats: the cork morph is more common on sandy beaches, whereas the pulp morph is more common on sea cliffs. Our previous studies suggested that differences in seed dispersal ability contribute to these habitat-specific frequency patterns. However, other factors, such as differences in germination traits, may also be involved. Seed germination is generally influenced by seed age and seed or fruit size. Therefore, in this study, we compared germination rate and germination timing between the two morphs and between habitats (sandy beaches and sea cliffs), while also examining the effects of seed age (current-year seeds and one-year-old seeds) and fruit size on germination characteristics. As a result, a significant difference in final germination rate between current-year and one-year-old seeds was detected only in the pulp morph on sea cliffs, with one-year-old seeds showing a lower germination rate. The fruit size of germinated seeds was significantly larger than that of ungerminated seeds only in the cork morph on sea cliffs. A significant negative correlation between fruit size and germination time was observed in the cork morph on both sandy beaches and sea cliffs, whereas no such relationship was found in the pulp morph on sea cliffs. In addition, fruit size tended to be larger in the cork morph on sandy beaches than on sea cliffs. These findings suggest that each fruit morph possesses germination-related traits that are advantageous in the habitat where it occurs most frequently. For example, the larger fruit size, longer seed longevity, and earlier germination associated with the cork morph on sandy beaches may facilitate establishment in sandy beach habitats, which are subject to greater disturbance than sea cliffs, as well as after prolonged dispersal by ocean currents. In contrast, the shorter seed longevity of the pulp morph may not be disadvantageous in the relatively stable environment of sea cliffs.

Since the early 2000s, large-scale outbreaks have been recorded in the southern Izu Islands of Japan, where acorn production has nearly failed for decades. On Miyakejima Island, larval populations of S. castanopsisae were estimated at approximately 158 billion in 2017 and 36 billion in 2018. As a result, two major genetic groups were identified: (1) Kyushu, Korea, and the Yaeyama Islands in the southwestern Ryukyus, and (2) the remaining Ryukyu Islands, the Izu Islands, and Honshu. While multiple haplotypes were detected in Kyushu and the Ryukyu Islands, populations in the Izu Islands and Honshu were characterized by only two haplotypes, both common in the Ryukyu Islands. Site fidelity is widespread across animal taxa and contributes to the long-term stability of home ranges. I analyzed long-term data from the E group, which was observed intermittently between 2004 and 2016. Group composition was recorded in each observation year, with particular attention to age and sex classes. During focal observations, GPS locations of adult individuals were collected to estimate annual home ranges. Site fidelity was quantified by calculating the overlap between 50% and 95% utilization distributions in successive years. In addition, all observed encounters with neighboring groups and their outcomes were recorded to assess intergroup dominance relationships. Throughout the study period, the size of the E group declined after 2011, with its home range gradually shifting northward. A particularly pronounced shift occurred between 2015 and 2016, when the home range moved approximately 1 km northward and showed no overlap between years. Intergroup dominance relationships involving the E group were unclear in 2015, but the group was subordinate in all observed intergroup encounters in 2016. These findings suggest that intergroup competition may contribute to home range dynamics in Japanese macaques and that a reduction in group size may weaken a group's ability to maintain its established home range. Suzuki Setsuko*1, Kyoko Sugai2
The genus Callicarpa in the Bonin Islands comprises three endemic species: the widely distributed C. subpubescens and two species restricted to the Chichijima Islands, C. parvifolia and C. glabra. Previous studies have suggested that C. subpubescens exhibits substantial intraspecific morphological variation. This combination of high species endemism and pronounced phenotypic diversity within a single oceanic archipelago makes this genus an excellent model for studying speciation and adaptive radiation. In this study, we conducted population genetic and phylogenetic analyses of these three species, together with morphological variants within C. subpubescens, to clarify patterns and timing of diversification. We analyzed 14 populations differing in species identity, morphology, and geographic distribution: C. parvifolia, C. glabra, and C. subpubescens sampled across the Chichijima, Hahajima, and Mukojima Island Groups, including populations selected to represent morphological variation. The 14 populations were classified into nine genetic groups. In the Chichijima Islands, three groups corresponded to the recognized species, whereas C. subpubescens was subdivided into four groups in the Hahajima Islands and two in the Mukojima Islands. Analyses also indicated that one Hahajima group originated through hybridization. Excluding this group, demographic analyses of the remaining six groups in the Chichijima and Hahajima Islands revealed that one group from the Hahajima Islands diverged earlier, approximately 170,000 years ago, whereas the other five groups diverged almost simultaneously, approximately 73,000–77,000 years ago. In contrast, the two Mukojima groups are inferred to have arisen through independent colonization events from specific genetic groups of C. subpubescens on the Chichijima and Hahajima Islands at nearly the same time as this rapid diversification event. Detailed analyses showed that the four genetic groups exhibit distinct distributions associated with forest types and environmental conditions on Hahajima, including variation along gradients of forest canopy height, elevation, and light availability. These groups show differences in plant height, growth form, leaf morphology, and flowering phenology, indicating ecological differentiation driven by local adaptation. Based on genetic and morphological evidence, we identified cryptic lineages within the Hahajima Islands and described two new species, C. ogasawarensis and C. hahajimensis, and one new hybrid, C. ×chibusensis. These findings demonstrate that diversification in oceanic islands can be driven by rapid ecological adaptation and genetic differentiation over relatively short timescales.

The Ogasawara Islands are a group of oceanic islands located approximately 1,000 km south of Tokyo in the northwestern Pacific Ocean and harbor many endemic species. However, most of these endemic species are threatened with extinction, highlighting the urgent need for conservation studies and management strategies to maintain the island flora. Among the Melastomataceae found in the Ogasawara Islands, Melastoma tetramerum is endemic to Chichijima Island, while M. tetramerum var. pentapetalum is endemic to Hahajima Island. Both taxa are threatened with extinction. Although conservation efforts are underway for M. tetramerum, recovery of the local population has remained limited. Defining conservation units with an awareness of genetic diversity and population structure is essential for conducting conservation activities. To accurately assess the genetic status of these taxa, we conducted comprehensive genome-wide analyses, and we suggested some candidate conservation units. Between 2017 and 2018, we collected mature leaves of M. tetramerum and M. tetramerum var. pentapetalum from wild populations. The phylogenetic trees, PCA, and clustering analysis indicated that M. tetramerum were distinguished into two genetic groups, which were corresponding to the two relict populations. In contrast, there was no significant genetic group in M. tetramerum var. pentapetalum. In addition, summary statistics indicated that genetic diversity was significantly higher in M. tetramerum than in M. tetramerum var. pentapetalum, and inbreeding was observed in some populations. In contrast, for M. tetramerum var. pentapetalum, establishing a conservation unit based on specific populations was difficult. Oceanic islands like the Azores are biodiversity hotspots, hosting a high proportion of endemic and native species. However, these ecosystems are increasingly threatened by anthropogenic factors, namely light pollution. Within the LIFE Natura@night project, a preliminary assessment of nocturnal insect fauna was conducted in the archipelago. Sampling took place at 26 sites across three islands (Graciosa, São Miguel and Corvo) following standardized methodologies, including UV light traps and complementary techniques (winerope and pitfall traps). A total of 8,583 insects were recorded, with Lepidoptera as the most abundant order (4,954 individuals and 52 different species). In line with the sampling effort, Graciosa yielded the highest number of specimens (6,455 insects; 3,542 Lepidoptera), followed by Corvo (1,241; 802 Lepidoptera) and São Miguel (891; 610 Lepidoptera). Despite fewer individuals, São Miguel and Corvo presented a higher proportion of native and endemic insect species. Light trap was the most effective method for Lepidoptera sampling while pitfall revealed additional diversity in Coleoptera, Hymenoptera, Dermaptera, Hemiptera, Trichoptera, Julida, and Isopoda orders - particularly on Graciosa’s islets. Among Lepidoptera, 15 families were recorded in total, with Crambidae (2,047 individuals), Argyresthiidae (604), Noctuidae (1,016), as the most represented. PG5-10
Heterostyly on Islands: Patterns and Insights from Japan
日本の島嶼における異型花柱性の分布パターンと進化的意義
Kenta Watanabe*1, 2
Heterostyly is a genetically controlled floral polymorphism that promotes outcrossing through reciprocal positions of stigmas and anthers between floral morphs. Although heterostylous species have been estimated to represent only a small fraction of angiosperm diversity, species-based estimates of heterostyly within well-documented regional floras remain extremely limited. Oceanic islands are generally known for a high proportion of dioecy and a low proportion of heterostyly, but the occurrence and evolutionary significance of heterostyly on islands remain poorly understood. Japan provides a useful setting for examining heterostyly on islands because it includes both continental and oceanic islands across a wide climatic range from cool-temperate to subtropical regions, and its flora has been relatively well documented. In this study, I compiled a list of heterostylous species in the native flora of Japan through literature review, herbarium records, and field observations. I compared the number and characteristics of heterostylous species among three island regions: the main Japanese archipelago, the Ryukyu Islands, and the Ogasawara Islands. I also examined growth form, dispersal mode, pollination system, and reported cases of evolutionary modification or breakdown of heterostyly. I recognized 38 heterostylous species in 17 genera and seven families in Japan, corresponding to approximately 0.76% of the native angiosperm flora. The proportion was 0.58% in the main Japanese archipelago, 0.91% in the Ryukyu Islands, and 0.52% in the Ogasawara Islands. In the main Japanese archipelago, heterostylous species were mainly represented by Primulaceae and were often herbaceous with non-animal dispersal. In contrast, in the Ryukyu and Ogasawara Islands, they were mainly represented by Rubiaceae and were often woody with bird or sea-drift dispersal. Pollinators also differed among regions, with bumblebees commonly reported in temperate Japan, whereas more diverse pollinators, including moths, were observed in the southern islands. Many cases of breakdown or modification of distyly have been reported in Japan: in the main Japanese archipelago, these mainly involve the evolution of monomorphism with self-compatibility, whereas in the Ryukyu Islands they also include dioecy and polygamous breeding systems, including monoecy. These patterns suggest that heterostyly on islands provides rich opportunities for studying the diversification of plant reproductive systems. The association of temperate heterostylous plants with non-animal dispersal and bumblebee pollination may help explain the rarity of heterostyly on temperate oceanic islands, where seed colonization and access to suitable pollinators may both be limited. Further comparisons among islands and pollinator communities will deepen our understanding of the evolutionary modification of heterostyly.
