This presentation provides an overview of ICS's seabird monitoring programmes across its island network, highlighting standardised population censuses, breeding success monitoring, colony assessments and species-specific research. Case studies will demonstrate how long-term datasets have improved our understanding of population changes, reproductive performance and responses to environmental pressures, while informing adaptive management and conservation decision-making. Symposium S6E Beyond Darwinian model islands: opportunities from non-canonical islands for island biology theory Organizers: Sebastian Steibl1, Sofía Hayden Bofill2, Luís Valente2
luis.valente@naturalis.nl Traditionally, island biology research has been centred around the study of classic volcanic Darwinian islands, such as the Canary Islands, Galápagos and Hawaiʼi. Research on these systems has been fundamental for developing and advancing influential theories across island biogeography, ecology, and evolution. However, their dominance has also defined the scope of what is considered to be representative or anomalous patterns, processes, and dynamics on islands. Our symposium will showcase how conceptual advances in island biology are being achieved when researchers engage with the full diversity of island types and island-like systems. We bring together contributions from a set of non-canonical island systems that do not fit conventional baseline conditions and assumptions about age, isolation, species-area dynamics, endemicity, connectivity, glacial dynamics, and diversification. We include atolls, land-bridge islands, lakes, as well as the Japanese archipelago as examples of island systems that are providing exciting new conceptual insights into island biology. Each of these systems can illuminate fundamental island-biological processes that inherently cannot be studied on the long-lived and isolated volcanic island models. Atolls offer unique windows into the predictability or contingency of evolutionary processes under repeated cycles of emergence and submergence. They also reveal the boundary conditions under which species-area relationships can emerge at all. Land-bridge islands, due to their recurrent connectivity with continental landmasses, offer an opportunity to explore deviations from classic area and distance assumptions related to the diversity and evolutionary history of their biota. Freshwater lakes are often exceptionally young, yet harbour surprisingly rich endemic biotas. Finally, the Japanese archipelago is the ultimate melting pot of different island types, making it an exciting system for studying evolution and biogeography. The talks will draw from studies across diverse taxa and global geographies. By putting spotlight on these non-canonical island systems, our symposium will show how studies on a broad range of island types are sharpening, testing, and refining island theory. Rather than treating non-model islands as deviations to established patterns and processes, we highlight them as opportunities for building a more inclusive, mechanistic, and global understanding of island biology capable of explaining fundamental dynamics across the full diversity of island types.
（要旨集 p.113）

ES6E-01目安 13:40おすすめ
Continental island dynamics shaped the evolutionary history of terrestrial mammals in the Japanese Archipelago
日本の陸生哺乳類63種の分岐史と海峡形成の関係
日本列島の海峡形成と陸生動物分岐の地史的枠組み
Jun J. Sato*1
The Japanese Archipelago is a continental island system that has repeatedly connected to and separated from the Eurasian continent throughout the Quaternary. This history provides a unique opportunity to examine how geological processes and ecological interactions jointly shape island faunas. To explore the assembly of mammal communities in Japan, I synthesized molecular phylogenetic and phylogeographic evidence for all 63 indigenous non-volant terrestrial mammal species, focusing on divergence-time estimates and distributional patterns. The synthesis revealed that major vicariance events associated with the formation of the Tsugaru and Korea-Tsushima Straits explain much of the evolutionary history of Japanese mammals. Most Hokkaido endemic species originated during the Late Pleistocene, whereas many species endemic to the Honshu‒Shikoku‒Kyushu region diverged during the Middle Pleistocene or earlier, reflecting different histories of isolation from source populations. However, geological history alone cannot account for present-day species distributions. Community assembly processes, including competitive exclusion, ecological sorting, and environmental filtering, also contributed substantially to faunal structure. Many late-arriving colonists were unable to establish persistent populations because ecologically similar resident species were already present or because environmental conditions were not suitable. In contrast, some earlier colonists now exhibit fragmented distributions, possibly reflecting replacement by later immigrants. These results suggest that the Japanese mammal fauna was assembled through the interaction of repeated mainland‒island connections and ecological filtering among species. More broadly, they highlight the importance of viewing continental islands as dynamic systems in which historical biogeography and community ecology jointly shape biodiversity patterns. Recent genome-wide phylogeographic studies of the large Japanese wood mouse (Apodemus speciosus) further demonstrate that repeated cycles of island connection and isolation have left detectable signatures not only in species distributions but also in fine-scale intraspecific genetic structure, including among peripheral islands surrounding the main islands of Japan. The Japanese Archipelago therefore provides a valuable model for understanding faunal assembly on continental islands and demonstrates how dynamic connectivity, rather than persistent isolation alone, can shape island biodiversity.
（要旨集 p.115）
ES6E-02目安 14:05おすすめ
Patterns and drivers of bird diversity and endemism on land-bridge islands
陸橋島における固有性と隠蔽的遺伝的多様性の概観
陸橋島の隠蔽的多様性という概念が琉球研究に応用可能
Sofía I. Hayden Bofill*1, Lu Feng1, Johannes de Groeve2, Kenneth Rijsdijk2, Patrick Weigelt3,4, Ferran Sayol5, Tom Matthews6,7, Martim Melo8, Sonya Clegg9 & Luís Valente1,10
Classic island biogeography theory predicts that species richness increases with island area and decreases with increasing isolation. These patterns are well described for oceanic archipelagos which represent only a quarter of all islands larger than 1km2. The majority of islands are land-bridge islands (LBIs) that were connected to the continent in periods of low eustatic sea-level. Traditionally, LBI biodiversity is assumed to reflect that of the mainland, hosting higher diversity of species but lower levels of endemism than more isolated islands. Yet, emerging cases of morphological divergence and cryptic genetic diversity have shown that LBIs may foster unique lineages, despite their close proximity and intermittent connectivity to the mainland. An overview of island biogeography on LBIs is currently lacking, largely due to the absence of a comprehensive global list of LBIs and the difficulty in compiling island-level species checklists. We present a global analysis of bird species on ~3,500 LBIs, to investigate how avian species diversity and endemism vary with classic island biogeography variables such as island area, isolation and age. We first address the challenges encountered when integrating island and bird range spatial data, and present an approach for estimating LBI age based on past sea-level reconstructions. By examining the role of area, geographic isolation and time of land-bridge severance in a selection of islands, we then discuss the processes that can promote divergence and speciation in LBIs and thus result in higher levels of “hidden endemism ” than previously recognized. Land-bridge islands emerge as unique opportunities to understand global patterns of bird diversity, as well as more nuanced processes of early divergence that occur on this type of islands. With this work, we highlight the relevance of studying insular systems that do not necessarily adhere to classic island biology theory and discuss how these can be used to understand the evolutionary processes that promote and maintain insular biodiversity.
（要旨集 p.116）
ES6E-03目安 14:30関連
Repeating evolution, species-area relationships, and conservation value: lessons from atolls
環礁における反復進化と種数面積関係の考察
島嶼進化論一般だが節足動物・琉球に直接関連薄い
Sebastian Steibl*1,2, Simon Steiger3, Nick Graham4, Luís Valente2,5, James C. Russell1
Oceanic islands are foundational to the study of evolution and biogeography, as well as holding substantial conservation value. Yet the research underpinning this understanding has been shaped disproportionately by volcanic islands, which hold high levels of threatened endemism that drive species-centred conservation. Atolls, which are generally much smaller and shorter-lived than high volcanic islands, represent a contrasting, but comparatively neglected, class of oceanic island system. Repeatedly reorganized by glacial sea-level change and small in land areas, atolls offer complementary insights into how island biotas assemble, evolve, and acquire conservation value. In this talk, I use atolls to make three arguments. First, the recurrent emergence, expansion, contraction, and submergence of atoll islands with glacial sea-level changes creates a natural setting for examining the repeatability of island assembly and evolution. Second, the small islands of atolls provide an opportunity for examining the environmental conditions that are prerequisite for species‒area dynamics to emerge. Third, atolls show that islandsʼ conservation value cannot be judged by endemism and global red-list assessments alone. Although most atoll islands support few endemic species, they are globally important breeding sites for tropical seabirds that drive ecosystem functioning. Atolls therefore complement dominant island-biogeographic and -conservation perspectives by revealing how dynamic, low-endemism islands can provide major insights into evolution, species ‒ area relationships, and opportunities for conservation.
（要旨集 p.118）
ES6E-04目安 14:50
Lakes as islands: a fresh(water) perspective on island biology
淡水湖を『島』とみなした種数面積関係の検証
Luiz Jardim de Queiroz*1,2,3,4, Sarah Zimmermann1, Tim Alexander1,2,5, Daniela Achleitner6, Martin Luger6, Hubert Gassner6, Carmela Doenz1,2,7, Soraya Villalba2,8, Lukas Rüber1,8, Rampal Etienne4, Luis Valente3,4, Ole Seehausen1,2
Island biology has traditionally focused on oceanic archipelagos, leaving the macroecological dynamics of freshwater “inverted islands” largely unexplored. Here, we used a natural experiment of 79 peri-Alpine lakes that emerged in a fishless landscape less than 15,000 years ago after glacial retreat. We ask to what extent island-biology patterns emerged in these young lakes at both regional (γ-diversity) and between-lake (β-diversity) scales. At the regional scale, the lacustrine Island Species-Area Relationship (ISAR) assembled remarkably fast compared to classic oceanic islands. Rather than following a traditional power law, the lacustrine ISAR is governed by an asymptotic rational function, revealing a mechanism of early richness saturation imposed by a limited regional species pool. Human-mediated introductions disrupted this baseline by removing the upper asymptote, shifting the system toward a quasi‒power law as non-native species bypass regional pool constraints. At the between-lake scale, partitioning total β-diversity uncouples two distinct assembly pathways driven by a combination of dispersal limitation and environmental filtering. Species turnover is reinforced by geographic isolation and depth disparities (reflecting spatial and ecological barriers), whereas nestedness is driven positively by elevation and negatively by spatial distance (reflecting colonization hierarchies). Contrary to island biology expectations, lake area plays no role in either process. Mechanistically, a key environmental filter underlying these patterns is a depth threshold at approximately 20 meters, beyond which ecological conditions diverge sharply. Above 20 meters, warm temperatures and high connectivity promote broad community overlap among lakes dominated by mobile, warm-adapted generalists. Below 20 meters, however, perennial cold and thermal uniformity act as an axis of ecological isolation, trapping cold-adapted specialists within lakes and unlocking the ecological opportunity for parallel adaptive radiations. Together, these findings demonstrate that while the postglacial, peri-Alpine lakes partially mirror classic island community assembly, their dynamics are compressed in time and strongly dictated by a three-dimensional environmental complexity, which drives ecological isolation alongside traditional geographic distance.

Cryptops Leach, 1814 is a genus of generally small, blind centipedes that mostly inhabit epigean habitats. With more than 150 species described worldwide, Cryptops is one of the most widespread and speciose genera within the class Chilopoda. Another East Asian species, C. japonicus Takakuwa, 1934, widely occurs on the Japanese Archipelago and Taiwan. Our results suggest that the species richness of Cryptops on East Asian islands is the outcome of both ancient continental relicts and recent radiations, demonstrating that the current diversity and distribution of Cryptops have been shaped by complex spatial and temporal processes.

Ancestral Recombination Graphs (ARGs) offer a powerful alternative: by reconstructing genome-wide genealogies and tracking how lineages coalesce through time, they provide effectively a time-calibrated genealogy at every position across the genome, enabling high-resolution inference of past population dynamics and divergence processes. Throughout the Quaternary (2.6 Ma), repeated glacial-interglacial cycles drove major climatic changes that resulted in significant sea-level fluctuations. In oceanic islands, these variations profoundly altered inter-island distances, occasionally reducing them to zero, which directly impacted species migration. As glacial periods last significantly longer than interglacials, sea levels declined gradually over tens of millennia as ice sheets expanded, but rose abruptly during deglaciation, leading to continuous and temporally asymmetrical variations of migration between neighbour islands populations. Previous empirical research hypothesised that this specific temporal pattern, by modifying the time available for genetic divergence to accumulate, may strongly shape diversification processes in oceanic archipelagos. Theoretical studies have shown that repeated, discrete shifts between phases of geographical isolation and connection can act as a “species pump”, facilitating speciation. During isolation, populations ecologically diverge, while each secondary contact reinforces prezygotic reproductive isolation because of unfit hybrids. However, these models usually assume temporally symmetrical changes in migration rate and/or instantaneous transitions between high and low migration rate. As a result, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we investigate if continuous and temporally asymmetrical fluctuations in connectivity between two populations favor speciation in a species pump scenario. We developed an individual-based model of a sexually reproducing population split across two patches, where migration fluctuates continuously and can be temporally asymmetric. We also examine empirically inspired scenarios by deriving migration variation from Quaternary sea-level changes to assess their impact on speciation. The two patches have different environments, allowing for ecological divergence. Individuals are characterized by an evolving mating trait allowing for assortative mating based on ecological traits. We showed that Quaternary sea-level fluctuations can act as a powerful driver of diversification. More specifically, continuous and asymmetric connectivity fluctuations shape ecological speciation mainly through the duration of low-connectivity phases and the intensity of contact, with prolonged isolation enhancing ecological divergence and brief periods of moderate contact reinforcing reproductive isolation through moderate hybrid production. This combined effect maximizes speciation probability, particularly for less dispersive species that are most sensitive to these historical shifts in island connectivity. Our findings provide a unified microevolutionary framework that explains the diverse levels of diversification induced by sea-level fluctuations, thereby reconciling the "species pump" paradigm with the diversity-reducing "species vacuum" effect. We demonstrate that, despite complex landscape dynamics, speciation likelihood relies on only two fundamental drivers: the duration of recurrent isolations and the intensity of subsequent contact.

However, strong negative interspecific interactions are likely to lead to rapid species exclusion before evolutionary divergence can occur, suggesting that character displacement may not be a common consequence in ecological communities. Here, we examine the patterns of ecological character displacement between two Harmonia ladybird species, H. axyridis and H. yedoensis, in the Japanese archipelago. In sympatric regions in central Japan, H. axyridis is a generalist predator feeding on various aphid species, whereas H. yedoensis is a specialist predator restricted to elusive aphids on pine trees. In contrast, in the Ryukyu Islands, where H. axyridis is absent, H. yedoensis utilizes a wide range of habitats, providing an ideal system to test for character displacement. We compared three life-history traits (egg size, clutch size, and trophic egg proportion) between sympatric and allopatric populations. Contrary to expectations, none of these traits showed significant divergence between sympatric and allopatric populations of H. yedoensis, indicating that the observed pattern does not clearly match predictions of character displacement. We argue that pre-adaptation to pine-feeding in allopatry may have allowed H. yedoensis to coexist with H. axyridis without requiring further evolutionary divergence in sympatry.

琉球の海峡と遺伝分化・気候適応。地史解釈の参考に必聴
Koh Nakamura
The Japanese and Ryukyu archipelagos form one of the world's longest arcs of continental islands. Situated in East Asia, they contain floristic elements ranging from boreal regions to Oceania, and their origin and diversification have long attracted biogeographers. In northern Japan, the Kurils have long been regarded as a migration corridor for arctic-alpine plants, whereas relatively few studies have examined plant migration from the continental Russian Far East and Sakhalin to Japan. In western Japan, attention has focused on the immigration of Northeast China– Korean floristic elements through the Korean Peninsula. However, unlike oceanic islands, where terrestrial plant species generally colonize only once, continental islands may have allowed repeated colonization of the same species via different routes. Our recent phylogeographical studies have revealed several species that colonized northern Japan from the continental Russian Far East and western Japan through the Korean Peninsula. The circular arrangement of the Japanese Archipelago, the Asian continent, and the Korean Peninsula created the East Asian north–south dual-route migration pattern. An intriguing question is the ecophysiological basis of the northern and southern lineages, derived from a common ancestor, becoming components of floras of different climatic zones. Some show secondary contact and genetic admixture between the two lineages within Japan, whereas others remain geographically isolated. Further exploration of this pattern is expected to reveal a continuum of reproductive incompatibility between lineages, providing an exceptional natural system for investigating outbreeding depression and ring species, in which terminal populations expanding around a geographic barrier become reproductively incompatible upon secondary contact. The Ryukyu Archipelago has long served as a model system for continental-island biogeography, where land-bridge formation and subsequent isolation are thought to have shaped plant distributions and genetic differentiation. In particular, Neogene straits have been considered the primary determinants of floristic and phylogeographical divergence. However, phylogeographical studies indicate that marked genetic differentiation across these ancient straits is neither a general pattern shared among plant species nor consistently associated with dispersal mode. The Ryukyus extend over 1,000 km along a pronounced latitudinal climatic gradient, a rare feature among island systems. Climatic adaptation may restrict gene flow and promote genetic differentiation. The Ryukyus therefore provide a unique natural laboratory for evaluating the relative roles of geological isolation and climatic adaptation in shaping geographic genetic structure. Finally, I discuss the implications for conservation. Across the broad latitudinal range of the archipelagos, conservation units are likely to be structured not only geographically but also climatically. Evaluating their vulnerability to the direct and indirect effects of climate change will therefore be essential for effective conservation strategies across the archipelagos.

Oceanic islands are thought to offer nearly ultimate enemy-free space to founders because almost all predators and parasitoids present on the mainland are absent. This reduced predation pressure may facilitate the evolution of unique characteristics in endemic species on oceanic islands. If we can identify closely related species to endemic species distributed in oceanic islands and then identify the traits that play important roles in defense against natural enemies in those closely related species, we may be able to infer the impact of enemy-free space on trait evolution on oceanic islands. “Mines” are feeding traces produced by phytophagous insect larvae that live and feed on internal tissues of plant leaves. Leaf miners exhibit various mine shapes (e.g., linear, blotch, star-like, serpentine, or linear then blotch), but each species constructs a species-specific shape and mine shapes are usually similar within the same genus or higher-taxa. Thus, natural selection and/or limitations in genetic background, which are not yet understood, are thought to constrain the mine shape in each taxon. Here, we report an unusual leaf-miner species, Metacercops sp. 1 (Gracillariidae), in the Ogasawara Islands (oceanic islands), Japan that shows intraspecific variation in the mine shape. Individuals of this species exhibit multiple mine shapes (mainly “fold” or “blotch” types) during the larval stage and there are no genetic differences among individuals that construct distinct mines, even using NGS makers. The putative closest relative, Metacercops sp 2, is found in the Ryukyu Archipelago (continental islands) and exhibits only a single mine shape (fold type), although both species feed on the same host plant, Planchonera obovata (Sapotaceae, Ericales). Interestingly, parasitism rates are significantly lower in sp. 1. These findings lead us to hypothesize that enemy-free space in the Ogasawara has relaxed selection against mine shapes, leading to multiple mine shapes in sp. 1 as phenotypic plasticity. To test this hypothesis, we have established a laboratory successive rearing method for the two species. In this talk, we will: (1) compare distinct parasitoid-community structures and parasitism rates between the two species, (2) assess whether the mine shape differences in sp. 1 are determined plastically, and (3) test whether the “fold” mine, which is the shape sp. 2 exclusively constructs, shows the highest defensive efficiency against parasitoids.

Islands have exceptional levels of endemism, but face disproportionately high extinction rates. For highly diverse ‘dark’ taxa, extinctions may often occur before the species has been collected, let alone formally recognised, at great cost to science. Currently, only four mite species are known from the region. This project investigates the phylogenetics and biogeography of Mesostigmatic mites on LHI, with a focus on understanding the role of symbiosis in island colonisation and faunal assembly. Lord Howe Island is home to a unique range of flora and fauna, including an estimated 1,600 terrestrial invertebrate species, most of which remain undescribed. The island also represents an exceptional system for studying biogeography and island colonization, yet it remains highly vulnerable to human-induced environmental change. More than 500 beetle species have been recorded from Lord Howe Island, the majority of which are undescribed, with over half considered endemic. Beetles play crucial ecological roles in forest ecosystems; however, our understanding of their diversity remains limited because many species are extremely small and understudied. Among leaf litter-inhabiting beetles, the subfamily Pselaphinae, comprising more than 10,000 species worldwide, represents one of the most diverse arthropod groups in leaf-litter ecosystems. As predators of small invertebrates, Pselaphinae are ecologically significant and important for studies of speciation and biogeography. Despite their high diversity, the only formally described species of Pselaphinae from Lord Howe Island is Tiracerus bispinosus Lea, 1918. Since then, no additional Pselaphinae species from Lord Howe Island have been formally described, even in the extensive studies of Australian Pselaphinae conducted by Chandler in 2001. Preliminary analyses suggest that several independent colonization events have occurred within these groups, followed by in situ diversification on the island. Studies of adaptive radiations have been central in developing our understanding of the processes involved in speciation and diversification. The explosive nature of adaptive radiation that results in exceptionally high levels of diversity over a comparatively short time span has provided fruitful grounds for biologists to better understand how divergence between close relatives is attained and maintained, highlighting the complex interplay between ecological and reproductive isolation. Shifts in the ecological opportunities or pressures arising from the colonization of a new habitat have been shown to influence the divergence in ecological traits and are a fundamental element in adaptive radiations. Likewise, divergence in sexual signaling traits has also been shown to play an essential role in the reproductive isolation of many rapidly radiating lineages. However, many of the sexual signals studied to date are deeply intertwined with ecological factors that power ecological divergence. When the divergence in sexual signals overlaps with that of ecological traits, it can be difficult to discern the initial axis of variation, whether it is in the ecological traits or sexual traits. This study focuses on how variations in sexual signaling traits are generated and selected upon using a lineage of Hawaiian Tetragnatha spiders that has diversified across an age-structured and ecologically similar landscape, allowing the process to be examined at different slices in time while controlling for divergence in ecological traits. Using genomic tools in conjunction with chemical analysis of mating pheromones and behavioral responses of males to these pheromones, this study investigates the evolutionary processes underlying sexual signal divergence and reproductive isolation in an adaptive radiation of Hawaiian Tetragnatha spiders.

The family Gobiidae (Teleostei), comprising approximately 1,360 species, is the second-largest taxonomic group of fishes after Cyprinidae (ca. 1,740 species), with at least 423 species known from Japanese waters. The family includes the species which adapted to estuary and to deep-sea habitats exceeding 400 maters in depth, some of which live in association with sessile marine organisms. The coral-reef gobiid genus Pleurosicya Weber, 1913 is characterized by I, 7–9 second dorsal-fin rays; I, 7–9 anal-fin rays; all scales ctenoid; cup-shaped pelvic fin, fused medially with well-developed connecting membrane between innermost rays and thick frenum between spines; one posterior interorbital pore; edge of lower lip free at sides, fused at chin. The genus is currently known to comprise 17 valid species that live in association with hermatypic, and soft corals, sponges, algae and seagrass. In Japanese waters, 10 of these species have been reported. One of these, Pleurosicya mossambica Smith, 1959 (type locality: Mozambique) shares the diagnostic characters of the genus, but can be readily distinguished from all other congeners by having 17– 19 pectoral-fin rays, relatively shallow body depth, scaled nape, and distinct black blotch on the first dorsal fin. Pleurosicya mossambica is distributed throughout the Indo-Pacific, including the Red Sea, and inhabits on soft corals (e.g., Wrightella sp. and Sinularia sp.), hermatypic corals (e.g., Montipora sp., Millepora sp., Tubastraea sp., and Pachyseris sp.), algae (e.g., Halimeda sp.) and sponges. However, our re-examination of specimens identified as P. mossambica from the Izu to Yaeyama islands, Japan revealed that these specimens included two morphologically distinguishable species. Furthermore, each of these two species formed a separate clade based on the neighbor-joining phylogenetic tree using the 16S regions of the rRNA. Additionally, our examination of the type series of P. mossambica revealed that three specimens represent undescribed species, Pleurosicya sp. In Japanese waters, Pleurosicya sp. has been recorded only from the Ryukyu Islands, where it primarily inhabits on Halimeda sp. Chromosomes are a fundamental unit of inheritance, yet their size, structure and number vary dramatically across the Tree of Life. Together, these results offer the first empirical evidence that MSC formation preserves genetic diversity under strong inbreeding. They also demonstrate that sex-chromosome evolution can be strongly influenced by historical migration and habitat fragmentation, especially in archipelagic systems. Geological history and terrain strongly influence genetic diversity of organisms. The Japanese Islands are known to have experienced a complex formation history. Around 20–15 Ma, two different primary landmasses separated from the Eurasian Continent through plate tectonics then collided together in the current “Fossa magna” zone. This complex geological history of the Japanese Islands is due to their location at the intersection four different crustal plates. Therefore, the Japanese Islands are a particularly suitable model for studying how geological events affect genetic diversity. However, studies investigating the genetic divergence associated with the Japanese Islands formation are still scarce. Species having a wide distribution despite low dispersal ability that have survived for a long period are important characteristics to research the relationships between ancient geological events and genetic divergence. Therefore, we focused on springtail (Homidia munda) that is distributed widely in Japanese Islands. Springtails are wingless and vulnerable to drying. So, they have weak dispersal ability. In addition, fossil of the current species has been found between 55–33 Ma layers. Thus, springtails might have experienced a longer evolutionary history than other taxa. In this study, we conducted comprehensive sampling and genetic analyses. Based on mitochondrial DNA analysis (16S rRNA, 12S rRNA), Japanese Islands lineage and Korean Peninsula lineage, each formed monophyletic groups. and the divergence between the Japanese Islands lineage and the Korean Peninsula lineage is very deep. This pattern may be related to the “double-door” opening model of the Japanese Islands’ formation. Furthermore, the Japanese Islands lineage diverged into four geographically structured subclades. In the Chugoku Region located in the western part of the Japanese Islands, these subclades coexist suggesting secondary contact. To examine the possibility of hybridization, we analyzed nuclear DNA markers (28S rRNA, ITS2). Similarly, despite the existence of a coexistence spot, we could not detect any discordance within the mitochondrial DNA and nuclear DNA. This study provides insights into genetic divergence associated with ancient geological events being deeply involved in the mechanisms of biodiversity creation.

To clarify the relationship between geological events and genetic divergence, it is important to focus on organisms that are widely distributed despite having low dispersal ability. The Japanese rhinoceros beetle, Trypoxylus dichotomus, is widely distributed across mainland Japan and surrounding islands. The results showed clear genetic differentiation in island populations with described subspecies, including Tanegashima, Yakushima, Kuchinoerabujima, Kumejima and Okinawa Island. In addition, populations of Tsushima and the Goto Islands, which belong to the mainland Japanese subspecies also showed genetic structures different from mainland Japan. Gene flow was detected between several island populations and Kyushu. However, this gene flow may reflect either natural dispersal or human-mediated immigration, which could not be distinguished in this study. The GLMMs showed no clear difference in non-major cluster assignment between island and mainland populations, and genetic diversity was not clearly explained by island area or surrounding forest area. These results suggest that island populations of T. dichotomus are not necessarily protected from genetic disturbance by geographic isolation. Based on geographical isolation and slight morphological differences, this species has conventionally been classified into five subspecies: P. d. dasymallus (Kuchinoerabu-jima Island and the Tokara Islands), P. d. inopinatus (the Okinawa Islands), P. d. daitoensis (the Daito Islands), P. d. yayeyamae (the Yaeyama and Miyako Islands), and P. d. formosus (Green Island and Gueishan Island in Taiwan). Since the center of distribution for Pteropus species is originally located in the tropics, the Ryukyu Archipelago, where P. dasymallus occurs, represents the northernmost limit of the distribution for this genus. Generally, for many organisms, peripheral regions offer less suitable habitats than central areas, and colonization attempts in such regions often fail even if individuals succeed in reaching new islands. However, bats possess exceptional flight and dispersal capabilities that allow them to cross oceans. This mobility enables them to temporarily leave an island to evade adverse events, such as food resource depletion, and subsequently re-migrate once food conditions improve. Particularly for solitary species like the Ryukyu flying fox, which do not utilize colonial roosts known as "camps" and furthermore rely on spatiotemporally fluctuating ("ephemeral") food resources such as fruits, a mainland-island metapopulation structure facilitates survival, thereby producing geographically complex distribution patterns. Our results were generally consistent with the conventional subspecific groupings; however, they also suggested that the formation of isolated populations has been driven in some areas either by the establishment of new sources through anthropogenic transport or by the emergence of distinct geographic fragmentation resulting from a decline in the species’ dispersal capability.

Island biogeography theory has emphasized connectivity between mainland source areas and islands, yet connectivity among neighboring islands may also shape insular biological communities. Species use islands close to the mainland not only as breeding sites but also as migratory stopover sites, with these islands facilitating movement through archipelagos as stepping-stones. However, the island characteristics that promote their use as stepping-stones, and interspecific differences in such movement patterns, remain poorly understood. Here, we elucidate the spatiotemporal movement patterns of migratory birds within an archipelago using passive acoustic monitoring in the Izu Islands, Japan. Recordings were conducted from March to June 2025 at two to five forest sites on each of seven islands: Oshima, Niijima, Kozu, Miyake, Hachijo, Hachijo-kojima and Aogashima. Dynamic occupancy models for three focal species̶the Ijimaʼs leaf warbler Phylloscopus ijimae, Narcissus flycatcher Ficedula narcissina and Lesser cuckoo Cuculus poliocephalus̶revealed marked interspecific variation in movement patterns. The Ijimaʼs leaf warbler, which breeds mainly in the southern Izu Islands, maintained high occupancy probabilities on Miyake and islands farther south after April. In contrast, occupancy probability increased temporarily on Kozu, a northern island, suggesting that northern islands may function not only as breeding sites but also as migratory stopover sites. The Narcissus flycatcher, whose main breeding range is on the mainland, showed a transient increase in occupancy probability in mid-May only on the northern islands closer to the mainland, indicating the use of these islands as stopover sites. By contrast, the Lesser cuckoo, which breeds across all islands, exhibited an almost synchronous increase in occupancy probability across the archipelago in mid-May and subsequently maintained high occupancy, suggesting that this species may arrive directly on each island rather than moving through the archipelago via stepping-stone pathway. At the community level, analyses using βsim, an index of species turnover, showed that turnover frequency tended to decrease with increasing isolation, indicating that isolated islands maintained stable composition while less isolated islands showed more frequent compositional change during migratory passage. These patterns suggest stepping-stones are primarily located closer to the mainland. Together, our results provide empirical evidence for inter-island connectivity during migration, clarifying that proximity to the mainland enables stepping-stone function and that movement strategies reflect species' breeding distributions. Conserving insular biodiversity, including island-endemic species such as the Ijimaʼs leaf warbler, will require comprehensive conservation strategies across entire archipelagos, rather than management focused on particular islands, with explicit consideration of migratory stopover sites.

This type of speciation, occurring at the distributional margins of widespread species, is referred to as peripatric speciation. This process of peripatric speciation involves genetic drift influenced by strong bottleneck effects. On 3 September 2024, the Ministry of the Environment of Japan officially declared the eradication of the invasive small Indian mongoose (Urva auropunctata) from Amami-Oshima Island. This achievement represents a global conservation milestone, accomplished on the unprecedented scale of a large island (712 km²) in invasive mongoose management. This presentation reviews the history of the mongoose invasion, changing public perceptions, the challenges and breakthroughs in eradication, the recovery of native species, and the lessons from this long-term conservation effort. Mongooses were first introduced to Japan on Okinawa-jima Island in 1910 as a biological control agent against the venomous habu snake. The invasion history on Amami-Oshima differed from that on Okinawa-jima. Mongooses were brought from Okinawa in the 1950s for mongoose–habu shows. They had been kept in captivity before being released into the wild around 1979 for unknown reasons. Their establishment became publicly recognized in 1983, when a local newspaper reported the establishment of a wild mongoose population. Nevertheless, the prevailing perception that mongooses were beneficial delayed management while they expanded into forests inhabited by numerous endemic species. Control efforts led by local government began in 1993. However, early management relied on bounty payments, which failed to apply sufficient capture pressure, particularly in remote forests and along the invasion front. A major turning point came in 2005 with the enforcement of Japan's Invasive Alien Species Act and the establishment of the Amami Mongoose Busters, a professional eradication team. Strategic, data-driven trapping, combined with improved traps and detector dogs, enabled intensive island-wide management and targeted searches for the remaining individuals. The final mongoose was captured in April 2018. After more than six years without confirmed detections, eradication was declared in 2024. During the eradication process, native mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians showed remarkable recovery. The successful eradication of the invasive mongoose from Amami-Oshima represents one of the world's largest invasive mammal eradication programs ever completed and highlights the value of sustained, science-based management for protecting unique island biodiversity and millions of years of evolutionary history.
（要旨集 p.9）
AO6A-0311:00–11:20おすすめ
How to TABS? Biogeographic reconstructions at your fingertips
海水準変動等で島や陸橋の変遷を復元するRパッケージTABS
島・陸橋の時系列復元ツールで琉球古地理解析に応用可能
Johannes De Groeve*1, Sietze J. Norder2, Buntarou Kusumoto3, Moriaki Yasuhara4, Suzette G.A. Flantua5, Eline S. Rentier5, Frank E. Rheindt6, Theo Atkinson6, 7, Luis L. Valente8, Johannes Foufopoulos9, Kenneth F. Rijsdijk1
Quaternary climate fluctuations continuously altered sea levels and forest lines. The resulting shifts in the area, connectivity, and configuration of islands, shelves, and alpine zones are key to understanding present-day biodiversity patterns. Here we present TABS (Temporal Altitudinal Biogeographic Shifts), an R package for reconstructing altitude-bounded biogeographic systems through time. TABS provides a flexible toolkit to calculate, explore and map how islands, shelf seas, coral systems, and alpine zones changed over continuous time. Users can furthermore incorporate local conditions, including local sea level variations induced by the growth and retreat of continental ice sheets, mountain-range specific forest line variations defining alpine zones, and tectonic and geomorphological processes such as uplift, subsidence, volcanism, erosion, and sedimentation. We demonstrate TABS across a range of applications, showing that it enables systematic, standardised, and scalable reconstructions of past landscapes. Through these examples, we seek to foster collaboration and inspire further applications of TABS in biogeography.
（要旨集 p.255）
AO6A-0612:00–12:20おすすめ
Biodiversity conservation and sustainable livelihoods on the Tokara Islands
トカラ列島の固有種保全と持続的利用、隠蔽種の可能性
トカラ列島・琉球弧の隔離と隠蔽的多様性に直結する地域研究
Ayhan Yener*1
The Tokara Islands are a group of small islands in Japan, located in the central part of the Ryukyu archipelago between Kyushu and Okinawa. While small in total land area, the Tokara Island group spans an entire degree of latitude, and constitutes the transition zone between temperate and subtropical ecosystems of the archipelago. Several rare and endemic species are present on these islands, such as the Tokara habu (Protobothrops tokarensis) and tamoto lily (Lilium nobilissimum). There is also strong potential for cryptic diversity, as demonstrated by the recently classified Tokara leaf warbler (Phylloscopus tokaraensis). Ecosystem integrity and sustainable use of natural resources have important consequences for the conservation status of these species. However, geographic isolation, invasive species, and resource constraints pose challenges to maintaining biodiversity and sustainable livelihoods on the islands. Additionally, the effects of global change, including increasing frequency and intensity of stochastic events, threaten vulnerable species populations and increase barriers for ecological monitoring. Reconciling community needs with conservation goals is critical for maintaining ecosystem integrity, and further supports the need for community involvement in monitoring and conservation efforts. At the transition between ecological zones, the Tokara Islands represent the range limit of various taxa and are important stepping stones for species dispersal and evolution across the Ryukyu archipelago. Therefore, population dynamics on these islands have implications for regional patterns of community assembly, species migrations and range shifts under global change scenarios. Case studies highlight current topics in biodiversity conservation and sustainable livelihoods on the Tokara Islands.
（要旨集 p.258）
BO6B-0612:00–12:20おすすめ
Asymmetric acoustic character displacement in two Gekko lizards
Gekko類2種の非対称な音響形質置換と地理的隔離の関係
琉球ヤモリ類の種分化と音声形質置換、島の隔離
Teppei Jono*1, Mamoru Toda2
The subgenus Japonigekko exhibits a mosaic distribution pattern, where areas of multiple species coexistence are intermingled with areas inhabited by a single species. In sympatry, reproductive interference, such as heterospecific courtship or gamete wastage through hybridization, imposes fitness costs. Under these conditions, selection favors individuals that can accurately recognize and select conspecifics, driving reproductive character displacement (RCD) in areas of overlap, while traits remain unchanged in allopatry. In contrast, in some species of Japonigekko that are geographically isolated on islands or in mountainous regions, female discrimination of courtship calls and species-specific male call patterns have been evolutionarily lost. In these isolated lineages, it is hypothesized that the absence of heterospecifics eliminates the need for species discrimination, leading first to the loss of female recognition abilities, and subsequently to the loss of species-specific patterns in male calls despite the persistence of courtship calling behavior. Gekko asahi and G. hokouensis, both belonging to Japonigekko, cooccur in Kagoshima Prefecture, Japan, where low-frequency natural hybridization suggests ongoing mutual reproductive interference. In this study, we verified the occurrence of RCD by comparing courtship calls between sympatric and allopatric populations of both species. For G. asahi, no significant differences were detected between sympatric and allopatric populations in any acoustic parameters (pulse number, pulse length, pulse interval, pulse rate, or dominant frequency). In contrast, sympatric G. hokouensis exhibited a significantly longer pulse interval and a lower pulse rate compared to allopatric populations, shifts that diverge from the acoustic traits of G. asahi. These results suggest that RCD has occurred in G. hokouensis but not in G. asahi. Given that natural hybridization predominantly occurs between G. asahi females and G. hokouensis males, G. asahi may represent a transitional evolutionary state where females have lost species-recognition abilities while males still retain species-specific call patterns. We will discuss evolutionary scenarios for species recognition traits in G. asahi and Japonigekko as a whole, incorporating recent data from female preference experiments.
（要旨集 p.264）
ES6E-0113:40–15:40 シンポおすすめ
Continental island dynamics shaped the evolutionary history of terrestrial mammals in the Japanese Archipelago
日本の陸生哺乳類63種の分岐史と海峡形成の関係
日本列島の海峡形成と陸生動物分岐の地史的枠組み
Jun J. Sato*1
The Japanese Archipelago is a continental island system that has repeatedly connected to and separated from the Eurasian continent throughout the Quaternary. This history provides a unique opportunity to examine how geological processes and ecological interactions jointly shape island faunas. To explore the assembly of mammal communities in Japan, I synthesized molecular phylogenetic and phylogeographic evidence for all 63 indigenous non-volant terrestrial mammal species, focusing on divergence-time estimates and distributional patterns. The synthesis revealed that major vicariance events associated with the formation of the Tsugaru and Korea-Tsushima Straits explain much of the evolutionary history of Japanese mammals. Most Hokkaido endemic species originated during the Late Pleistocene, whereas many species endemic to the Honshu‒Shikoku‒Kyushu region diverged during the Middle Pleistocene or earlier, reflecting different histories of isolation from source populations. However, geological history alone cannot account for present-day species distributions. Community assembly processes, including competitive exclusion, ecological sorting, and environmental filtering, also contributed substantially to faunal structure. Many late-arriving colonists were unable to establish persistent populations because ecologically similar resident species were already present or because environmental conditions were not suitable. In contrast, some earlier colonists now exhibit fragmented distributions, possibly reflecting replacement by later immigrants. These results suggest that the Japanese mammal fauna was assembled through the interaction of repeated mainland‒island connections and ecological filtering among species. More broadly, they highlight the importance of viewing continental islands as dynamic systems in which historical biogeography and community ecology jointly shape biodiversity patterns. Recent genome-wide phylogeographic studies of the large Japanese wood mouse (Apodemus speciosus) further demonstrate that repeated cycles of island connection and isolation have left detectable signatures not only in species distributions but also in fine-scale intraspecific genetic structure, including among peripheral islands surrounding the main islands of Japan. The Japanese Archipelago therefore provides a valuable model for understanding faunal assembly on continental islands and demonstrates how dynamic connectivity, rather than persistent isolation alone, can shape island biodiversity.
（要旨集 p.115）
ES6E-0213:40–15:40 シンポおすすめ
Patterns and drivers of bird diversity and endemism on land-bridge islands
陸橋島における固有性と隠蔽的遺伝的多様性の概観
陸橋島の隠蔽的多様性という概念が琉球研究に応用可能
Sofía I. Hayden Bofill*1, Lu Feng1, Johannes de Groeve2, Kenneth Rijsdijk2, Patrick Weigelt3,4, Ferran Sayol5, Tom Matthews6,7, Martim Melo8, Sonya Clegg9 & Luís Valente1,10
Classic island biogeography theory predicts that species richness increases with island area and decreases with increasing isolation. These patterns are well described for oceanic archipelagos which represent only a quarter of all islands larger than 1km2. The majority of islands are land-bridge islands (LBIs) that were connected to the continent in periods of low eustatic sea-level. Traditionally, LBI biodiversity is assumed to reflect that of the mainland, hosting higher diversity of species but lower levels of endemism than more isolated islands. Yet, emerging cases of morphological divergence and cryptic genetic diversity have shown that LBIs may foster unique lineages, despite their close proximity and intermittent connectivity to the mainland. An overview of island biogeography on LBIs is currently lacking, largely due to the absence of a comprehensive global list of LBIs and the difficulty in compiling island-level species checklists. We present a global analysis of bird species on ~3,500 LBIs, to investigate how avian species diversity and endemism vary with classic island biogeography variables such as island area, isolation and age. We first address the challenges encountered when integrating island and bird range spatial data, and present an approach for estimating LBI age based on past sea-level reconstructions. By examining the role of area, geographic isolation and time of land-bridge severance in a selection of islands, we then discuss the processes that can promote divergence and speciation in LBIs and thus result in higher levels of “hidden endemism ” than previously recognized. Land-bridge islands emerge as unique opportunities to understand global patterns of bird diversity, as well as more nuanced processes of early divergence that occur on this type of islands. With this work, we highlight the relevance of studying insular systems that do not necessarily adhere to classic island biology theory and discuss how these can be used to understand the evolutionary processes that promote and maintain insular biodiversity.
（要旨集 p.116）
